title: 📚 Era 6 Works: The Modernist & Inter-War Era
subtitle: Verify publication dates, summaries, characters, storylines & exam traps for 298 works

items.title: "The Wanderings of Oisin" (1889) — W. B. Yeats

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Oisin tells Saint Patrick of three magic islands and three hundred years with Niamh.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1889 is correct. Kegan Paul, Trench and Company published the volume in London in 1889.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Oisin (The Fenian hero who narrates his wanderings); Niamh (The fairy woman who takes Oisin to the islands); Saint Patrick (The Christian saint who hears and answers Oisin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The aged Oisin has returned to an Ireland ruled by Saint Patrick.
He tells of leaving with Niamh, a fairy woman, across the sea.
They visit three islands, of joy, of victory, and of forgetfulness.
He thinks three years have passed, but three centuries have passed.
When he touches the mortal ground, his youth falls away.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young officer jumps from a ship and spends his life seeking honor.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Blackwood's Magazine ran the serial from October 1899 to November 1900. William Blackwood published the book in October 1900. The database span 1899-1900 matches the serial. The book year is 1900.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jim (The young officer who jumps from the Patna); Charles Marlow (The narrator who follows Jim's life after the inquiry); Jewel (The woman Jim loves in Patusan); Doramin (The Patusan chief whose son dies because of Jim's failure); Gentleman Brown (The pirate whose raid breaks Jim's peace)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a psychological novel of Conrad. Originally published as a serial in Blackwood's Magazine, but published in book form in 1900.
Jim, the protagonist (a young British seaman) becomes first mate on the Patna, a ship full of pilgrims travelling to Mecca for the hajj.
When ship started rapidly taking into water and disaster seemed imminent, Jim joins his captain and other crew members in abandoning the ship and its passengers.
Later the Patna and its passengers were also saved.
In the court of inquiry, the court strips the navigation command certificate for his dereliction of duty.
Jim is angry with himself, both for his moment of weakness and for missing an opportunity to be a hero.
At the trial he befriends a sea captain, Charles Marlow.
Whenever the memory of the 'Patna' becomes fresh in Jim's mind he abandons his place and moves further east.
Later Marlow (Jim's friend) placed Jim as his factor in Patusan, a remote island settlement with a mixed Malay and Bugis population where Jim past can remain hidden.
While living on this island he acquires the title Tuan (Lord).
Here Jim wins the respect of the people and becomes their leader by reliving them from the predations of the bandit Sherif Ali and protecting them from the corrupt local Malay chief Rajah Tunku Allang.
Jim wins the love of a woman named Jewel, who is of mixed race and he is really satisfied.
The end comes a few years later when the town is attacked by marauder "Gentleman" Brown. Jim returns to Doramin, the Bugis leader and willingly takes a fatal bullet in his chest from him as a retribution for the death of his son. (As Doramin's son was slain in the attack).
Jim, a young mate, dreams of heroic deeds at sea.
He abandons the pilgrim ship Patna, thinking it will sink.
The ship is saved, and a court cancels his certificate.
Marlow helps him, and Jim becomes a leader in Patusan.
A later failure leads to his death before Doramin.

items.title: "The Wind Among the Reeds" (1899) — W. B. Yeats

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A volume of symbolic lyrics on love, the Sidhe, and the mood of the 1890s.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1899 is correct. Elkin Mathews published The Wind among the Reeds in London in 1899.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aengus (The speaker who pursues a vision from the hazel wood); The Sidhe (The fairy host that rides and calls the living away)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poems speak through masks such as Aedh, Hanrahan, and Michael Robartes.
The Song of Wandering Aengus follows a vision from a hazel wood to old age.
The Hosting of the Sidhe calls mortals away with the fairy host.
Desire, dream, and Irish otherworld belief run through the book.
The language is rich and symbolic, before his later plain style.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A public poem on the Easter Rising and the change made by the executions.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Yeats finished the poem in 1916. Clement Shorter printed about 25 private copies in 1917. The New Statesman printed it on 23 October 1920. It was collected in Michael Robartes and the Dancer in 1921.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A voice close to Yeats, counting the dead and the change); Constance Markievicz (The woman whose sweet voice grew shrill in politics); Patrick Pearse (The man who kept a school and rode the winged horse); Thomas MacDonagh (Pearse's helper and friend); John MacBride (The man Yeats calls a lout, yet still numbers in the song)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a poem by Yeats.
In it the poet remembers friends and companions who died for Ireland in the Easter rising.
Famous line: "All changed, changed utterly, a terrible beauty is born".
The speaker remembers meeting the rebels with only polite, empty words.
The Rising of Easter 1916, and the executions, change his judgement.
He pictures Constance Markievicz, Patrick Pearse, and Thomas MacDonagh.
He also includes John MacBride, though he had hated him.
The refrain says a terrible beauty is born.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: This is the original Bengali Gitanjali of 1910, a book of devotional songs and poems.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Bengali Gitanjali is 1910. The English Song Offerings is 1912. The genre is poetry.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A devotee who sings to God)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Bengali book came out on 4 August 1910.
It has 157 poems.
Many of them became Rabindra Sangeet (Tagore's songs).
Its main theme is devotion to God.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first book of poems, mixing wit, color, death, and the power of imagination.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1901 is only the period label. Knopf published Harmonium in 1923. Representative Poetry Online dates that edition 7 September 1923. There were about 1,500 copies and 85 poems. The 1931 book is the second edition. The Man with the Blue Guitar is a separate book of 1937.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The woman in Sunday Morning (A speaker who thinks of death, Sunday quiet, and earthly beauty); The voice in The Emperor of Ice Cream (A speaker who orders a plain funeral and rejects soft illusion)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Stevens gathered poems he had placed in magazines from about 1914 to 1923.
Alfred A. Knopf published the book in New York in 1923, when Stevens was 44.
Sunday Morning sets beauty and change against the hope of a Christian afterlife.
The Emperor of Ice Cream tells the reader to face a real death, not a pretty show.
Other famous pieces include Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird and Anecdote of the Jar.
A 1931 edition dropped three poems and added fourteen.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Dublin tenement family is ruined by a false legacy during the Civil War.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Abbey Theatre premiered the play on 3 March 1924. Macmillan of London first printed it in 1925, inside Two Plays, with The Shadow of a Gunman.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Juno Boyle (The mother, named for the month of June, who keeps the family alive); Captain Jack Boyle (The paycock, a boastful loafer who pretends he once was a sea captain); Joxer Daly (Boyle's drinking mate, who flatters him and then mocks him); Mary Boyle (The daughter, a striker who is abandoned while pregnant); Johnny Boyle (The son, wounded in the fighting and later taken away and shot)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the second play of the Dublin trilogy that deals with contemporary historical events in Ireland.
The play was first staged at the Abbey Theatre in Dublin in 1924. It is in three acts.
Sean O'Casey has taken the characters of Juno and the Paycock from Greek Mythology.
Juno is the name of a Roman goddess, who is the protector of suppliants and the jealous wife of Jupiter.
However Juno Boyle in the play is a Dublin housewife, an earthly human figure who struggles for hard life.
Juno's husband Captain Jack Boyle is drawn from Shakespeare's Captain Jack Falstaff, because of Captain Boyle's handsome dress he is depicted as Paycock.
Boyle's family consists of four people:.
Captain Boyle.
Juno Boyle.
Johnny (their son)
Mary (their daughter)
It is labeled as tragic-comedy.
In the play Captain Jack is a loafer who claims to be unable to work because of pain in his legs.
The mother Juno is the only worker member in the family as daughter Mary is on strike and son Johnny is disabled, having lost his arm in the war of independence.
The play examines men's relationship to his environment primarily in terms of money.
Juno is so called "Juno" because all of the important events in her life took place in June.
Last line of the play: "The whole world in a terrible state of chassis".
Other characters:.
Mrs. Tancred.
"Needle" Nugent.
Furniture Removers.
Maisie Madigan.
Charles Bentham The Shadow of a Gun-Man (1923)
It is a play by Casey and the first in his "Dublin Trilogy". The original title of the play was "On the Run".
It is set during the Irish War of Independence.
The play centers on the mistaken identity of a building tenant who is taught to be an IRA (Irish Republican Army) assassin.
Main characters:.
Donal Davoren: A poet of about 30, living with Seumus in the tenement. Some of the residents suspect, he has an affiliation with the IRA.
Seumus Shields: A broken down lazy peddler of about 35, disillusioned over the nationalist cause. He only supports those who wish the conflict will end.
Adolphus Grigson.
Minnie Powell The Plough and the Stars (1926)
It is the third play in the Dublin trilogy of Sean O'Casey.
Firstly, it was performed in the Abbey Theatre in 1926. It is in 4 acts.
The first two acts take place in Nov 1915 looking forward to the liberation of Ireland.
The last two acts are set during the Easter rising in April 1926.
Major Characters:.
Jack Clitheroe: A brick layer and former member of the Irish citizen Army.
Nora Clitheroe: House wife of Jack Clitheroe.
Peter Flynn: A laborer and Nora's uncle.
Bessie Burgess: A street fruit vendor and protestant.
Mrs. Gogan: A charwoman Cock-a-Doodle Dandy (1949)
Sean O'Casey regarded it as his best play.
It is a dark comedy fantasy in which a magic cockerel appears in the Parish of Nyadnanave and forces the characters to make choices about the way they live their lives.
It is a parable of midcentury Irish rural life, symbolizing the struggle between repression and liberty.
Initially it was regarded as anti-Catholic and was banned from professional public performance in the UK by Lord Chamberlain.
So the world premiere of this play took place at the people's theatre.
The play was reviewed as "A play to arouse both anger and pity" in the Irish newspaper Irish Times.
The Boyle family lives in a Dublin tenement in 1922, during the Irish Civil War.
Juno works and holds the house together, while Captain Boyle drinks with Joxer Daly.
Mary is on strike, and Johnny fears punishment for betraying a comrade.

items.title: "Long Day's Journey into Night" (1956) — Eugene O'Neill

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: One day in 1912 shows the Tyrone family wrecked by drink, drugs, and blame.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is only a period label. O'Neill finished the script in 1941. He asked that it wait 25 years after his death. Yale University Press published it in February 1956. The first performance was on 2 February 1956 in Stockholm. Broadway opened on 7 November 1956. The Pulitzer Prize followed in 1957.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: James Tyrone (The father, a touring actor based on O'Neill's father); Mary Tyrone (The mother, addicted to morphine); Jamie Tyrone (The older son, a cynical drunk); Edmund Tyrone (The younger son, a portrait of the young O'Neill)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The play covers a single August day in the Tyrone summer home.
James Tyrone is a famous actor who is also tight with money.
Mary has returned from a cure, but she slips back to morphine (a strong drug).
Jamie drinks and mocks them, while Edmund learns he has tuberculosis (a lung disease).
At midnight Mary enters with her wedding gown, lost in the past.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jim Burden remembers Antonia Shimerda, a Bohemian girl on the Nebraska prairie.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1901 is only the period label. Houghton Mifflin published My Antonia in Boston in 1918. The Willa Cather Archive dates the first edition 21 September 1918. A 1926 edition shortens the introduction. That later book is not the first publication. The epigraph is Virgil's line, Optima dies prima fugit.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jim Burden (The narrator, a lawyer who looks back on his Nebraska childhood); Antonia Shimerda (The Bohemian immigrant girl, later a farm wife named Cuzak); Mr Shimerda (Antonia's father, a homesick musician who kills himself); Lena Lingard (A hired girl who later runs a dress shop in Lincoln)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Orphan Jim Burden leaves Virginia and goes to his grandparents in Nebraska.
On the same journey he meets the Shimerda family from Bohemia.
The first winter breaks Mr Shimerda, who kills himself.
Antonia works the farm, then works in town as a hired girl.
A man deserts her, and she returns home with a child.
Years later Jim visits her farm, where she is a strong wife and mother.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Bigger Thomas kills a white woman in Chicago and is sentenced to death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1901 is only the period label. Its own note already says 1940. Harper and Brothers published the novel on 1 March 1940, and the Book of the Month Club took it then. A stage version opened in 1941. The Library of America printed a restored text in 1991. That later book is not the first publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bigger Thomas (A poor young Black man who kills Mary and then Bessie); Mary Dalton (The daughter of his white employers, smothered in her bedroom); Mrs Dalton (Mary's blind mother, whose entrance causes the panic); Bessie Mears (Bigger's girlfriend, whom he murders during the flight); Boris Max (The lawyer who defends Bigger and blames the society that made him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bigger Thomas, a poor young man of 20, shares one room with his family in Chicago.
The rich Dalton family hires him as a driver.
He smothers their daughter Mary with a pillow when her blind mother enters the room.
He burns the body in the furnace and sends a false ransom note.
He then kills his girlfriend Bessie, is caught, and is sentenced to death.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1914 book of talking poems about work, grief, and walls in rural New England.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia says David Nutt of London published the book in 1914. The Academy of American Poets dates the Henry Holt edition 1914. The Road Not Taken is not in this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Country speakers (New England voices who talk, argue, and remember); The neighbor in Mending Wall (The man who keeps saying that good fences help neighbors)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Frost published this second book in London in 1914.
Most poems sound like short plays or talks between country people.
Mending Wall sets a speaker against a neighbor who trusts fences.
The Death of the Hired Man and Home Burial show family pain.
After Apple Picking and other poems mix labor with tired dreaming.
None of the poems is titled North of Boston.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two migrant friends chase a farm dream that ends in a killing.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The New York book edition appeared in February 1937. The play opened in New York on 23 November 1937. The title comes from Robert Burns, To a Mouse.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: George Milton (The small, sharp friend who cares for Lennie and tells the dream.); Lennie Small (A huge, gentle man with a childlike mind who loves soft things.); Curley (The boss's angry son, who picks fights.); Curley's wife (A lonely woman on the ranch. Lennie kills her by accident.); Candy (An old worker who wants to join the farm dream.); Slim (The respected mule driver who understands George.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a tragedy written in the form of a play. It's title is taken from Robert Burn's poem "To a Mouse"
The story is about two travelling ranch workers, George and Lennie trying to work up enough money to buy their own farm/ranch.
George Milton and Lennie Small travel together for ranch work in California.
Lennie is very strong and has a childlike mind.
They dream of a little farm where Lennie will tend rabbits.
On a new ranch, Lennie's strength leads to trouble with Curley and Curley's wife.
Lennie kills Curley's wife by accident.
George shoots Lennie himself, to save him from a mob.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A play in blank verse in which Perseus saves Andromeda from a sea monster.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database says only that publication sits in collected editions, and it sorts the play at 1901. A manuscript note dates one scene to 21 June 1906. The weekly Bande Mataram printed it from 30 June to 20 October 1907. A book printing of 1908 was destroyed. Collected Poems and Plays (1942) used the 1907 text, with some scenes missing. Those scenes were restored in 1955.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Perseus (The Greek hero who rescues Andromeda); Andromeda (The princess offered to the sea monster)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Aurobindo retells the Greek legend of Perseus and Andromeda.
The main classical source is Book 4 of Ovid's Metamorphoses.
Andromeda is offered as a sacrifice to a sea monster.
Perseus rescues her and defeats the powers that hold her.
The weekly Bande Mataram printed the play in parts in 1907.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her first book, a set of hard sea poems in the Imagist style.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Constable published the London book in 1916. Houghton Mifflin published a Boston edition in the same year. Some poems had first appeared in Poetry and The Egoist.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A voice that addresses the sea, flowers, wind, and gods.); Hermes (The Greek god of boundaries in the poem Hermes of the Ways.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker turns away from safe, pretty gardens.
She praises harsh flowers, such as the sea rose and the sea lily.
Wind, salt, sand, and rock press on every scene.
Greek figures such as Hermes appear beside the shore.
The poems keep the image and throw away extra talk.
This book fixed her fame as an Imagist.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1923 book that mixes prose and free verse about a new American spring.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year is only the period label. Contact Publishing Company in Paris issued it in 1923. Maurice Darantiere printed it at Dijon. Many copies were stopped at the border, so the book stayed rare.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (The poet voice that looks closely at ordinary things); Elsie (A young woman named in the poem To Elsie)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Williams had the book printed in France in 1923.
Prose sections say that poems should make the world feel new.
The title poem watches spring start near a hospital road.
The Red Wheelbarrow looks hard at one plain farm object.
To Elsie looks at hard American lives and still seeks hope.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A play about a long strike in which both stubborn leaders lose.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The queue had no work year, only the period label. He wrote the play before it was staged. It opened at the Duke of York's Theatre, London, on 9 March 1909. Duckworth published it in 1909 in a volume with The Silver Box and Joy. New York saw it on 17 November 1909.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Anthony (Elderly company chairman who wants an iron rule over the men); David Roberts (Leader of the striking men, as stubborn as Anthony); Annie Roberts (Roberts's sick wife, who dies during the strike); Enid Underwood (Anthony's daughter, married to the works manager); Simon Harness (Union official who wants a compromise); Edgar Anthony (The chairman's son, who pities the starving families)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Workers at the Trenartha Tin Plate Works have been on strike for months.
The works stand on the border of England and Wales.
Chairman John Anthony and strike leader David Roberts both refuse to bend.
The trade union, led by Simon Harness, has already dropped the strike.
Annie Roberts dies, and both sides then accept the old compromise.
Anthony and Roberts are thrown out by their own people.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Short prose poems that make ordinary objects feel strange and new.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and Britannica both date the book 1914. It was her second published book.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Stein began these pieces in 1912 and published the book in 1914.
The three parts are Objects, Food, and Rooms.
She wanted words to match what the eye sees, not old names.
The first poem is about a carafe, a glass bottle for water.
Meaning stays open, so readers must look instead of translate.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Newland Archer loves Ellen Olenska but stays inside the marriage rules of old New York.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1901 is only the period label. Pictorial Review printed the novel in four parts in 1920. D. Appleton and Company published the book in 1920. Wikipedia dates the book 25 October 1920. It won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1921. The story is set in the 1870s, which is not the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Newland Archer (A young New York lawyer who loves Ellen but marries May); May Welland (His wife, trained to be a perfect society lady); Ellen Olenska (May's cousin, a countess who has left her husband); Mrs Manson Mingott (The powerful grandmother of May and Ellen)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In the 1870s, lawyer Newland Archer is engaged to the gentle May Welland.
May's cousin, Countess Ellen Olenska, returns from a bad marriage in Europe.
Newland falls in love with Ellen, whose freedom shocks New York society.
He still marries May.
Ellen will not break that marriage.
May tells Ellen she is pregnant, and Ellen goes back to Europe.
Years later, after May's death, Newland stands outside Ellen's Paris home and does not go up.

items.title: "The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas" (1933) — Gertrude Stein

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Stein's own Paris life, told as if her partner Alice were writing it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates the writing to October and November 1932 and publication to 1933 by Harcourt, Brace. Britannica also dates the book 1933.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Alice Toklas (The named narrator and Stein's life partner); Gertrude Stein (The real subject, seen through Alice's voice); Pablo Picasso (A painter friend whose work hangs in the Paris home); Ernest Hemingway (A young writer the book both helps and criticizes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Stein wrote the book in about six weeks in 1932.
Alice is the narrator, but the life on the page is mostly Stein's.
The story moves from San Francisco to the Paris home at 27 rue de Fleurus.
Painters, including Picasso and Matisse, fill the Saturday gatherings.
Young writers such as Hemingway appear, and some friends disliked their portraits.
The book became her first bestseller and made her famous in America.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A family chronicle of the rich Forsytes, who cling to property and respectability.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The queue had no work year, only the period label. The Man of Property is 1906. In Chancery is 1920. To Let is 1921. The interludes are Indian Summer of a Forsyte (1918) and Awakening (1920). The title The Forsyte Saga names the one volume Heinemann published in May 1922. Later Forsyte groups are separate books.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Soames Forsyte (The man of property, a solicitor who wants to own beauty and people); Irene Forsyte (Soames's first wife, who refuses to be treated as property); Philip Bosinney (The architect Irene loves, who dies during the first novel); Old Jolyon Forsyte (The family patriarch, based partly on Galsworthy's father); Young Jolyon Forsyte (An artist son who later shares his life with Irene); Fleur Forsyte (Soames's daughter in the later part of the Saga)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Man of Property (1906) shows Soames Forsyte treating his wife Irene as property.
Irene loves the young architect Philip Bosinney, who dies.
Indian Summer of a Forsyte (1918) shows the quiet last days of Old Jolyon.
In Chancery (1920) follows divorce, new marriages, and family quarrels.
Awakening (1920) and To Let (1921) move the story to the next generation, including Fleur.
In May 1922 Heinemann issued the novels and interludes together as The Forsyte Saga.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The Joad family loses a farm and seeks work in California.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Viking published the novel in April 1939. The title comes from The Battle Hymn of the Republic, which uses the Bible image of the grapes of wrath. The book later won the Pulitzer Prize. A film followed in 1940.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tom Joad (The eldest son, who moves from private anger to a wider fight.); Ma Joad (The mother who holds the family together on the road.); Jim Casy (A former preacher who becomes a labor organizer and is killed.); Rose of Sharon (Tom's sister, whose final act offers food to a starving man.); Pa Joad (The father, who loses his old authority on the journey.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is set in Great Depression and describes a family of sharecroppers, the Joads who were driven from their land due to the dust storms of the dust bowl.
The source of the novel is "The Harvest Gypsies".
Protagonist - Tom Jood.
The Dust Bowl (a 1930s drought) and the banks push them off their Oklahoma farm.
They drive west toward promised jobs in California.
Tom Joad, just out of prison, travels with Ma, Pa, and the preacher Jim Casy.
The family meets hunger, crowded camps, and hostile growers.
Casy is killed while helping strikers.
Tom kills the attacker and must hide.
The book ends with the family still poor, but still bound to other sufferers.

items.title: "The Home and the World" (1916 (Bengali book, Ghare Baire)) — Rabindranath Tagore

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: This is Tagore's novel Ghare Baire, about a love triangle during the Swadeshi movement.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It is a novel. The Bengali book is 1916, with Indian publication in 1915 and 1916 per the Gutenberg edition. The English translation is 1919.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bimala (Nikhil's wife, torn between home and the world); Nikhilesh (Her husband, a kind landlord who hates violence); Sandip (A fiery nationalist leader who attracts Bimala); Amulya (A young follower of Sandip)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nikhil is a kind landlord who wants his wife Bimala to see the outside world.
Sandip, a nationalist speaker, comes to stay with them.
Bimala is drawn to Sandip and his fiery words.
She slowly sees that Sandip is selfish and wants money and power.
Violence breaks out and the story ends in tragedy.

items.title: "The Hound of the Baskervilles" (1902) — Arthur Conan Doyle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Holmes uncovers a human plot behind the legend of a demon hound on Dartmoor.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Strand ran it from August 1901 to April 1902. George Newnes published the book in 1902. The case is set before The Final Problem, so Holmes is still alive in the story.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sherlock Holmes (The detective who hides on the moor and springs the trap); Dr John Watson (The narrator who guards Sir Henry on Dartmoor); Sir Henry Baskerville (The heir threatened by the family legend); Stapleton (A neighbour who is secretly a Baskerville and the villain); Dr Mortimer (The doctor who brings Holmes the hound legend)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dr Mortimer brings Holmes the legend of the Baskerville hound.
Sir Charles Baskerville has died, and Sir Henry is the new heir.
Watson watches the moor while Holmes seems to stay away.
The hound is a real dog, used to frighten heirs to death.
Stapleton, a hidden Baskerville, wants the estate and is exposed.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Lily Bart falls from rich New York society and dies poor and alone.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1901 is only the period label. Scribner's Magazine began the serial in January 1905. Charles Scribner's Sons published the book in 1905. Wikipedia dates the book 14 October 1905. The Mount and the Academy of American Poets also date the novel 1905. The title comes from Ecclesiastes.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lily Bart (A beautiful socialite who cannot secure a rich marriage); Lawrence Selden (The lawyer who loves Lily but does not save her in time); Bertha Dorset (A married woman who spreads the rumor that destroys Lily); Gus Trenor (A married man who gives Lily money and then expects favors); Simon Rosedale (A rich newcomer who offers marriage on hard terms)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lily Bart is 29, beautiful, and poor, and she needs a rich marriage.
She likes the lawyer Lawrence Selden, but he has too little money.
Gossip, gambling debts, and a bad gift of money from Gus Trenor spoil her chances.
Bertha Dorset ruins Lily's name during a yacht trip.
Lily sinks into poor work, takes a sleeping drug, and dies of an overdose.
Selden arrives to propose and finds her already dead.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A salesman tells barroom dreamers to drop their lies, then confesses a murder.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is only a period label. O'Neill completed the play in 1939. It was published in 1946 and opened at the Martin Beck Theatre in New York on 9 October 1946. He was still alive. The 1956 success with Jason Robards came after his death.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Theodore Hickman (Hickey) (Hardware salesman who urges the drinkers to abandon their lies); Harry Hope (Owner of the saloon and rooming house); Larry Slade (Former anarchist who claims he only watches life); Don Parritt (Young man who betrayed his mother and then kills himself)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The regulars at Harry Hope's saloon live on drink and pipe dreams (false hopes).
Those false hopes make a failed life feel bearable.
They wait for Hickey, a salesman who usually brings a wild party.
Hickey arrives sober and pushes each person to face the truth.
He confesses that he killed his wife, and the others crawl back to their dreams.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A realistic novel of two sisters, Constance and Sophia Baines, from youth to old age.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Chapman and Hall published the novel in January 1908. Bennett began it in 1907, from a memory of an old woman in a Paris restaurant in 1903. Britannica also dates the novel 1908. A 1921 film came later. The book itself is not a play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Constance Baines (The sister who stays in Bursley and marries Samuel Povey); Sophia Baines (The sister who elopes to Paris and later returns); Samuel Povey (The shop assistant who becomes Constance's husband); Gerald Scales (The travelling salesman who takes Sophia away and then deserts her); Mrs Baines (The mother who runs the shop while the father is ill)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a novel by Arnold Bennett published in 1908. Maupassant's "Une Vie" inspired Bennett to write this novel.
It deals with the lives of two very different sisters Constance and Sophia Baines following their stories from their youth, working in their mother's draper's shop into old age.
It is set in Burslem and Paris and covers a period of 70 years (1840-1905).
Constance, sober and sensible, marries the Humdrum and reliable Samuel Bursley.
The passionate and romantic Sophia elopes with Gerald Scales, a rich and charming commercial traveller, an unscrupulous rascal; he compromises Sophia and is forced to marry her.
He takes her to Paris where after some time he deserts her.
After a large struggle Sophia establishes herself as a successful lodging housekeeper and lives through the Siege of Paris (1870 Franco German War).
Ultimately she returns to Bursley and spends the rest of her life with her sister Constance.
'The Old Wives Tales' is also written by George Peele (1595).
The Baines sisters grow up in their parents' draper's shop in Bursley, one of the Five Towns.
Constance stays, marries Samuel Povey, and lives out a quiet local life.
Sophia elopes with the salesman Gerald Scales and goes to Paris.
Gerald wastes their money and abandons her.
Sophia survives by running a boarding house.
In old age Sophia returns to Bursley, and the sisters end their lives in the same house.

items.title: "The Plough and the Stars" (1926) — Sean O'Casey

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Tenement neighbours face love, looting, and death during the 1916 Easter Rising.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Abbey opened the play on 8 February 1926. A riot followed on a later night of that first run. Macmillan of London published the book in 1926, with a stated first edition in April 1926.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jack Clitheroe (A bricklayer and commandant who leaves home to fight in the Rising); Nora Clitheroe (Jack's wife, who tries to keep him home and later loses her reason); Bessie Burgess (A Protestant street seller who scolds the rebels and dies helping Nora); Fluther Good (A carpenter, full of talk, who loots and also helps the neighbours); The Young Covey (A socialist who mocks nationalist speeches)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
8- The Silver Tassie (1927); It is a four act play about World War I.
The first two acts are set in November 1915, in a Dublin tenement and a pub.
Nora has hidden the letter that made Jack Clitheroe a commandant in the Citizen Army.
A figure in a window speaks Patrick Pearse's words about bloodshed while a prostitute waits in the pub.
Jack and his comrades march out under the Plough and the Stars, the flag of the Irish Citizen Army.
During Easter week Nora searches for Jack, loses her baby, and breaks down.
Jack is killed.
Bessie Burgess is shot while trying to pull Nora from the window.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A speaker looks at two similar paths and later claims one made all the difference.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia says the Atlantic Monthly printed it in August 1915. Wikisource agrees it was first published in 1915 and revised in Mountain Interval in 1916. It is a poem, not a play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The traveler (The speaker who must choose one road and will later retell the choice)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
"Two Roads diverged in a yellow wood and sorry I could not travel both And be one traveler, long I stood and looked down one as far as I could To where it bent in the undergrowth".
These are the opening lines of the poem published in 1916.
It is the first poem in the collection "Mountain Interval". (ii)
The speaker stands in a yellow wood where two roads divide.
He looks down one road, then takes the other.
He admits the two paths were worn about the same.
He doubts he will ever come back to try the first road.
Years later, he expects to sigh and call his choice the less traveled one.
Frost linked this teasing speaker with his friend Edward Thomas.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A vision of a collapsing age and a rough beast moving toward Bethlehem.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The poem was written in January 1919. The Dial printed it in November 1920. It was collected in Michael Robartes and the Dancer in 1921.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A prophetic voice watching an age come apart); The rough beast (A beast like a sphinx, set to replace the Christian age)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
13- The Tower (1928); It includes Sailing to Byzantium, Leda and Swan and Among the School Children.
Important Quotations: 1- "Turning and turning in the widening gyre The falcon cannot hear the falconer Things fall apart; the center can't hold Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world" 2- "The best lack all convictions, while the worst are full of passionate intensity" 3- "The darkness drop again but now I know That twenty centuries of stony sleep Were vexed to nightmare by a racking cradle".
It is one of the most important poems of Yeats written in 1919, first printed in "The Dial" and afterwards included in his 1921 collection of verses "Michael Robartes and the Dancers".
It describes the atmosphere of post war Europe as it was written after World War I.
Initially it was titled "The Second Birth".
A falcon turns in a widening gyre and cannot hear the falconer.
The centre fails, and anarchy is loosed on the world.
The speaker feels that some revelation, a Second Coming, is near.
From Spiritus Mundi (the world soul) he sees a pitiless sphinx in the desert.
The poem asks what rough beast slouches toward Bethlehem to be born.

items.title: "Their Eyes Were Watching God" (1937) — Zora Neale Hurston

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Janie Crawford tells a friend how three marriages led her to a life she can claim.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That 1901-1947 span is a period label, not a publication date. J. B. Lippincott published the novel in New York on 18 September 1937.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Janie Crawford (The heroine who tells her life and seeks a love like a pear tree in bloom); Pheoby Watson (The friend who listens on the porch); Nanny (Janie's grandmother, once enslaved, who arranges the first marriage); Logan Killicks (Janie's first husband, an older farmer); Joe Starks (Janie's second husband, the proud mayor of Eatonville); Tea Cake (Vergible Woods, the younger third husband, who dies of rabies)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Janie returns to Eatonville and tells her story to her friend Pheoby.
Nanny marries young Janie to the farmer Logan Killicks for safety, not love.
Janie leaves with Joe Starks, who becomes mayor and silences her for years.
After Joe dies, she marries Tea Cake and works beside him in the Everglades.
A hurricane bites Tea Cake with rabies, and Janie kills him in self-defense.
A jury frees her, and she comes home with her own voice.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ann Whitefield hunts the revolutionary Jack Tanner and makes him marry her.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Shaw finished the play in 1902 and published it in 1903. The Court Theatre staged it on 21 May 1905. That first run cut Don Juan in Hell. The Hell scene was first acted on 4 June 1907. The database year 1903 is the book. The first night was 1905.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Tanner (A fluent revolutionary bachelor, also called Jack, linked with Don Juan); Ann Whitefield (The young woman who pursues Tanner and embodies the Life Force); Roebuck Ramsden (An older liberal who shares Ann's guardianship); Octavius Robinson (Tanner's friend, who loves Ann and loses her); Mendoza (A brigand whose debate role matches the Devil in the dream)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Important Characters:.
Anne Whitefield: A young woman somewhat enigmatic. She corresponds to character Dona Ana in the Don Juan myth.
John Tanner (also called Jack Tanner): He is well educated and well-spoken man, who takes everything seriously, including himself "a political firebrand and confirmed bachelor". He is the descendent of Don Juan.
Octavius Robinson: An amiable young man who is in love with Ann Whitefield and brother of Violet Robinson. He represents Don Octavio from the Don Juan myth.
Roebuck Ramsden: An aging civil reformer and a friend of Mr. Whitefield. He corresponds to the statue in the Don Juan myth.
Mendoza: An anarchist who collaborates with Tanner. She is the "President of the league of the Sierra".
Ann Whitefield's father leaves her in the care of Jack Tanner and Roebuck Ramsden.
Tanner talks revolution and does not want to marry.
Ann stands for the Life Force, Shaw's name for the drive to continue the human race.
A long dream shows Don Juan debating the Devil in Hell.
The 1905 staging cut that dream.
It was first acted in 1907.
Ann wins, and Tanner agrees to marry her.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A silver mine in a South American republic corrupts the people near it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Conrad wrote the novel from 1902 to 1904. The book was published in October 1904. The database year 1904 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nostromo (Giovanni Battista Fidanza, the trusted Italian sailor); Charles Gould (The English mine owner who serves the silver); Emilia Gould (Charles's wife, who sees what the mine costs); Martin Decoud (The skeptical journalist who helps hide the silver)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Full title: "Nostromo: A Tale of the Seaboard".
It is a 1904 novel by Conrad set in the fictitious South American republic of "Costaguana".
Costaguana resembles in real life as Colombia.
In spite of long history of tyranny, revolution and warfare, the place experienced a period of stability under the Dictator Ribiera.
Nostromo is a charismatic Italian seaman who has settled in Sulaco and established a reputation for leadership and daring.
As an employee of the Oceanic Steam Navigation Company, he earns the unofficial title of Capataz de Cargadores or "Head Longhorseman".
Costaguana is a troubled republic, and Sulaco is its port.
Charles Gould reopens the San Tome silver mine.
The sailor Nostromo is trusted with a boatload of silver.
During a revolution he hides the silver and later steals from it.
The mine brings power, but it also brings lies and death.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her first English poetry book, a set of folk songs of Indian life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1905 is correct. William Heinemann of London issued the book in 1905. The dedication names both London, 1896, and Hyderabad, 1905.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The palanquin bearers (Men who carry a bride and sing as they walk); The Indian weavers (Weavers who tell of a child's robe, a marriage veil, and a shroud); The Coromandel fishers (Brothers who call one another out to the sea at dawn)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Arthur Symons wrote the introduction, and the book is dedicated to Edmund Gosse.
William Heinemann published it in London in 1905.
A drawing of the young poet by John Butler Yeats stands at the front.
Folk songs include Palanquin Bearers, Indian Weavers, and Coromandel Fishers.
Workers, weavers, and fishers speak in bright pictures and song like refrains.

items.title: "Where Angels Fear to Tread" (1905) — E. M. Forster

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An English widow marries in Italy, and her family's rescue plan ends in disaster.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1905 is correct. Forster began it in late 1904. William Blackwood and Sons published it in 1905. The working title was Monteriano.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lilia Herriton (English widow who marries Gino in Monteriano and dies in childbirth); Gino (Young Italian husband who loves his baby son); Philip Herriton (Lilia's relative, sent twice to Italy to guard the family name); Harriet Herriton (Philip's sister, who takes the baby and causes the fatal crash); Caroline Abbott (Lilia's companion, who comes to love Gino)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The original title of the novel was "Monteriano".
The title comes from a line in Alexander Pope's "An Essay on Criticism" from the line: "For fools rush in where angels fear to tread." Plot:.
The novel is set in Tuscany in which a widow Lilia Herriton falls in love with two handsome Italians Italy and Gino.
Her dead husband's family send Philip, Lilia's brother-in-law, to Italy to prevent the misalliance but he is delayed and Lilia marries the Italian and becomes pregnant.
Lilia dies after giving birth.
Philip again goes to Italy to save Lilia's child in public eye but actually they have no regard for the child.
Caroline Abbott, Lilia's friend, succumbs to irresistible charm of the inhabitants of Italy.
There is a tragic ending in the novel with the death of Lilia's child.
Philip realizes that he is in love with Caroline Abbott but she denies dramatically, as she is in love with Gino.
Widowed Lilia Herriton travels in Tuscany with Caroline Abbott.
She marries Gino, a younger Italian, before Philip can stop the match.
Lilia dies after the baby is born, and the Herritons want the child.
Harriet takes the baby, and the child dies when the carriage overturns.
Philip loves Caroline, but she loves Gino, so Philip goes home wiser and alone.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Pound's first book of poems, printed at his own cost in Venice.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1908 is correct. The database also marks the book unfinished, as if it were The Cantos. That flag does not fit. Antonini printed the finished book in Venice in July 1908. A full reprint came only in 1965.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Cino (A wandering singer, one of the early masks in the book)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Pound could not find an American publisher for these early poems.
He reached Venice and paid the printer A. Antonini.
The little book appeared in July 1908.
The Italian title means with tapers quenched, a phrase from Dante.
He linked that phrase with the death of his friend William Brooke Smith.
The poems try old music and masks more than the later Imagist sharpness.
Many of the stronger poems were printed again in Personae in 1909.

items.title: "A Room with a View" (1908) — E. M. Forster

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Lucy Honeychurch must choose between a free love in Italy and a proper English match.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1908 is correct. Forster was at work on the Lucy story by 1902. Edward Arnold published the book in 1908.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lucy Honeychurch (Young Englishwoman who learns to choose George over Cecil); George Emerson (Frank young man who loves Lucy); Mr Emerson (George's honest father, who tells Lucy to face her love); Charlotte Bartlett (Lucy's cousin and chaperone, who first blocks the kiss and later helps); Cecil Vyse (Polished fiance who wants Lucy as a pretty possession)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel is about a young woman in the repressed culture of Edwardian era, England.
The novel is set in England and Italy. The story is both a critic of English society and romance.
The novel can also be called a bildungsroman as the protagonist follows a process of development.
Here Forster shows a contrast of the symbolic differences between Italy and England. He idealized Italy as a place of freedom and sexual expression.
It is written in two parts with an appendix. The appendix is entitled "A View Without a Room" (1958) Plot:.
The first part of the novel is set in Florence, Italy.
The novel starts with a visit of Lucy Honey-Church and her cousin Charlotte to a guest house in Florence where they are given rooms that look into the courtyard rather than out over the river Arno.
The novel ends with Lucy's marriage with George and the happy couple remains happy together in Florence Pension, in a room with a view.
Lucy and Charlotte Bartlett reach Florence and are offered rooms with a view.
George Emerson kisses Lucy among violets at Fiesole, and Charlotte stops it.
Back in England, Lucy accepts the snobbish Cecil Vyse.
George kisses her again and says Cecil treats her like an object.
She breaks with Cecil and, after talk with Mr Emerson, marries George.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dialogue on self rule, modern civilization, and nonviolent freedom.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database wording is right on the two dates. The Gujarati text appeared in Indian Opinion in 1909. Gandhi's English translation, called Indian Home Rule, was published in South Africa in 1910. He translated this book himself.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Reader (A questioner who wants fast, even violent, freedom.); The Editor (Gandhi's voice, arguing for self rule and nonviolent means.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gandhi wrote the book in Gujarati on a ship in 1909.
A Reader asks hard questions.
The Editor, Gandhi's voice, answers.
The Editor says India was not taken by English force alone.
He rejects violent revolt and also rejects blind copying of the West.
Railways, lawyers, and doctors appear as part of a sick civilization.
Real swaraj is self rule, gained by satyagraha and self control.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The 1909 London book in which Pound speaks through a set of masks.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1909 is correct for this London book. Elkin Mathews published it in 1909. Do not mix it with Personae: The Collected Poems of 1926.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The personae (Historical and invented speakers whom Pound uses as masks)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Elkin Mathews published Personae in London in 1909.
About half the poems had already appeared in A Lume Spento.
The book opens with the old motto about making strong old dreams.
The speakers are personae, masks taken from other times and lives.
Edward Thomas praised its passion and natural magic.
A later book of 1926, also called Personae, is the collected shorter poems.
That 1926 book is a different publication from this 1909 volume.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three families struggle over a country house that stands for England's future.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1910 is correct. Forster planned it from 1908 and finished in July 1910. Edward Arnold published it on 18 October 1910.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Margaret Schlegel (Thoughtful sister who marries Henry and finally holds the house); Helen Schlegel (Impulsive sister who has a child with Leonard Bast); Henry Wilcox (Rich businessman who learns humility after his son's crime); Ruth Wilcox (First owner of Howards End, who wants Margaret to have it); Leonard Bast (Poor clerk whose death ties the families together)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is considered as a masterpiece of Forster and considered as a social comedy.
On the title page of early editions is the phrase "Only Connect".
In this novel Forster admonishes humankind that it's most significant failure is the reluctance to establish relationship with each other and eliminates the obstacles of prejudice that divides and subjugates individuals.
Helen Schlegel briefly accepts Paul Wilcox, then both draw back.
Ruth Wilcox leaves Howards End to Margaret, but the family burns the note.
Margaret agrees to marry Henry Wilcox, the practical businessman.
Helen has a child with Leonard Bast, and Charles Wilcox strikes Leonard, who dies.
Henry gives the house to Margaret, and Helen's son will inherit it.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her first story book, a set of sharp sketches from a German spa.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1911 is correct. Stephen Swift and Company published it in London in December 1911. That note belongs to The Dove's Nest. She called the book immature and blocked a 1920 reprint.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The English narrator (A quiet young woman who watches the pension guests); Frau Fischer (A talkative guest who presses the narrator about marriage); Frau Brechenmacher (A wife who sees her own hard marriage in a wedding)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After a hard year, Mansfield stayed at a spa in Bavaria in 1909.
Most of these sketches first appeared in the London magazine The New Age.
Stephen Swift published the book in London in December 1911.
An English narrator watches boastful guests, weddings, and tired women.
She later refused a reprint because she found the book immature.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: This is the full English title of the 1912 Gitanjali. It is the same book as the English Gitanjali entry.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database shows 1912; 1913; 1919 and calls it Drama. Only 1912 is the publication year. 1913 is the Nobel year. The genre is poetry, not drama. This entry duplicates the English Gitanjali entry.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A humble singer who offers songs to God)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Song Offerings is the English title of Gitanjali.
The book has 103 prose poems that Tagore translated himself.
Some poems come from other Bengali books, not only from Gitanjali.
The India Society of London published it in November 1912.
It was the main book behind the 1913 Nobel Prize.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her second book of songs about life, death, and the spring.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1912 is correct. Britannica, Wikisource, and the publisher lists agree on 1912. A few catalogues say 1915, which confuses this book with the writing years of The Broken Wing.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The bangle sellers (Sellers who carry shining bangles to the temple fair); The bazaar speaker (A voice that asks Hyderabad merchants what they sell)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Edmund Gosse wrote the introduction.
The subtitle calls the book songs of life, death, and the spring.
It was published in 1912 in London and in New York.
Bangle Sellers and In the Bazaars of Hyderabad are the poems students meet most often.
Markets, brides, and faith fill the songs, with a stronger national feeling than before.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Higgins teaches the flower girl Eliza to speak like a lady, then ignores her future.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Shaw wrote the play in 1912. The first night was in German at Vienna on 16 October 1913. London opened it on 11 April 1914. Everybody's Magazine serialized it in America in November 1914. Constable published the book in 1916. Shaw revised the text in 1941. The database year 1913 is the Vienna premiere.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Eliza Doolittle (A Cockney flower girl who learns upper-class speech); Henry Higgins (A brilliant and rude professor of phonetics); Colonel Pickering (A gentleman of Indian dialects who funds the experiment and treats Eliza kindly); Alfred Doolittle (Eliza's father, a dustman who calls himself one of the undeserving poor); Freddy Eynsford-Hill (A young gentleman Eliza may marry instead of Higgins)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a romantic comedy.
Pygmalion, a play named after a Greek mythological character. It is in V acts.
The title is taken from Ovid's Metamorphosis.
Professor of Phonetics Henry Higgins makes a bet that he can train a bedraggled cockney flower girl Eliza Doolittle, to pass for a duchess at an ambassador's garden party by teaching her to assume a veneer of gentility, the most important element of which, he believes is an impeccable speech.
Colonel Pickering is the person with whom Professor Higgins bet.
The very next morning Eliza appears in Higgins' Laboratory for learning lessons, so that she can speak properly in a flower shop.
Colonel Pickering agrees to pay the cost of experiment of Higgins on Eliza.
Higgins trains Eliza for a number of months and two trials are taken to judge the progress. One at Higgins' mother's home and a second at an Ambassador's party which have been a great success.
Higgins and Pickering are bored now with their experiments that cause Eliza to be hurt.
Eliza throws Higgins' sleeper at him in rage. She returns him the hired jewelry and Higgins accuses her.
Eliza runs away from Higgins home. Mrs. Higgins hided Eliza in the upstairs.
Eliza was thankful to Pickering for always treating her like a lady and threatens Higgins that she will now work with his rival Phonetician "Nepommuck"
Eliza leaves for her father's wedding.
It never became clear that she passed as a duchess or not.
The title recalls Pygmalion, a sculptor in Greek myth whose statue comes to life.
Henry Higgins, a teacher of phonetics (speech sounds), records Eliza Doolittle's London speech.
Colonel Pickering bets that Higgins can pass Eliza off as a duchess.
Eliza wants lessons so she can work in a flower shop.
At a tea party she shocks the guests by saying, Not bloody likely.
After the test succeeds, she asks what is to become of her.
Shaw's ending refuses a marriage between Eliza and Higgins.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Paul Morel struggles to leave his mother's love and to love other women.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1913 is correct. Duckworth published the novel in 1913. Lawrence let Edward Garnett cut a large part of the manuscript.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Paul Morel (The son who cannot easily separate love from his mother); Gertrude Morel (The strong mother who lives through her sons); Walter Morel (The miner father, vital but shut out of the home); Miriam Leivers (The spiritual young woman Paul cannot fully love); Clara Dawes (The married woman with whom Paul has a passion)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is in two parts.
It is third novel of Lawrence, masterpiece and autobiographical novel.
It is dedicated to Edward Garnett (its editor).
It tells the story of Paul Morel who is modeled on youthful Lawrence who in his early age depended hugely upon his mother.
Walter Morel (coal miner) is based upon Lawrence's father, Arthur Lawrence.
Gertrude Morel is Lawrence's tribute to his own mother Lydia.
Miriam is based on Jessie Chamber, Lawrence's girlfriend of adolescent years.
"Sons and Lovers" is also considered the first Freudian novel in English because of its analysis of Oedipus complex tied between Paul and Gertrude.
The Morels live in a Nottinghamshire mining town.
Gertrude Morel turns from her miner husband to her sons.
After the elder son dies, Paul becomes the centre of her life.
Paul loves Miriam, then has a passion with the married Clara Dawes.
His mother's death frees him, but the last pages leave his future open.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: This is a book of English prose poems by Tagore about love, youth and life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database shows 1912; 1913; 1919 and calls it Drama. The Nobel site gives 1913 for The Gardener. The genre is poetry, not drama. The exact month is not confirmed.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tagore made the English versions himself.
The poems do not match one single Bengali book.
The book is dedicated to W. B. Yeats.
It came out in 1913, soon after the English Gitanjali.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1915 book whose famous section is five idealistic sonnets about the war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The year 1914 is the sonnet sequence and the title, not the book date. Brooke wrote the five sonnets in late 1914. Two of them appeared in the Times Literary Supplement on 11 March 1915. The Soldier was read in St Paul's Cathedral on 4 April 1915. He died on 23 April 1915. The book 1914 and Other Poems came out in May 1915, so it is posthumous (published after his death). Earlier poems in the same book, such as Grantchester, date from before the war.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The soldier (The speaker of the fifth sonnet, who pictures his own death in a foreign field)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The opening group is called 1914 and holds five sonnets.
They are Peace, Safety, two poems called The Dead, and The Soldier.
The Soldier says that if he dies abroad, that grave will be a piece of England.
The book also reprints earlier work, including South Sea poems and The Old Vicarage, Grantchester.
Sidgwick and Jackson issued the volume in May 1915, after Brooke had died.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long personal poem about love, London, and the slide toward war in 1938.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia says Faber and Faber published it in May 1939. Britannica also dates Autumn Journal 1939. He finished the poem by early 1939 and did not update the public passages.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet speaker (MacNeice speaking in his own voice as private life and public crisis meet)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
MacNeice wrote it from August 1938 into the new year.
He refused to rewrite public events after later news changed them.
The poem records the Munich crisis and fear of a coming war.
It also remembers school, Birmingham teaching, a broken marriage, and Spain.
One section turns on Ireland, and another on ancient Greek thought.
It ends with the courage of people in besieged Barcelona.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A teenage gangster in Brighton marries a witness and is hunted by a cheerful woman.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That number is the period shelf, not the publication year. Heinemann published the novel in London in 1938. The Viking edition in America also appeared in 1938.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Pinkie Brown (A seventeen year old Catholic gang leader who believes in hell); Rose (A young waitress who loves Pinkie and will not betray him); Ida Arnold (A warm, worldly woman who chases the truth about Hale's death); Charles Hale (A reporter whose murder opens the story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Pinkie's gang kills the reporter Hale in Brighton.
They choke him with a stick of seaside rock candy.
The waitress Rose can spoil their false trail, so Pinkie courts her.
He marries Rose so that she cannot give evidence against him.
Ida Arnold, who met the frightened Hale, follows the case for simple justice.
Pinkie plans a false suicide pact, is blinded by his own acid, and falls from a cliff.
Rose still hopes to hear a loving record, but the record speaks his hate.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1918 book of war poems about failed attacks, smug officers, and broken soldiers.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The queue had no work year, only the period label. William Heinemann published Counter-Attack and Other Poems in London in 1918. E. P. Dutton published the New York edition in 1918. The poems grew out of his 1917 protest and his time in hospital, including his meeting with Wilfred Owen.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The soldier speaker (A voice from the trench who sees horror and hypocrisy); The General (A cheerful officer whose plan of attack kills the men he greeted); Harry and Jack (Two soldiers in The General who die because of that plan)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title poem shows soldiers holding a ruined trench full of the dead.
A counter attack (an enemy strike to retake ground) begins.
A young soldier fires, is hit, and bleeds to death.
The attack fails.
Other poems mock generals, base officers, and patriotic talk at home.
The General smiles at men going up the line, then his plan kills them.
Poems such as Suicide in the Trenches and Does it Matter speak for the wounded.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novella about an aging writer who falls into fatal desire in Venice.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1914 is only the period span. A limited edition and a magazine printing came in 1912. The Fischer trade book came in 1913. Britannica dates the story to 1912.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gustav von Aschenbach (A famous, disciplined writer who loses control in Venice); Tadzio (A beautiful Polish boy whom Aschenbach watches but never meets)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gustav von Aschenbach, a famous writer, leaves home for a holiday.
In Venice he becomes obsessed with a beautiful Polish boy named Tadzio.
He learns that cholera (a deadly disease) is in the city, but he will not warn the family.
He dyes his hair and paints his face so he will look younger.
He dies in his beach chair while watching Tadzio by the sea.

items.title: "Do not go gentle into that good night" (1951) — Dylan Thomas

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Do not go gentle into that good night

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A son begs his dying father to fight against the dark of death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Sources disagree on the writing year. One account says 1947 in Florence. A Welsh timeline says 1951. The journal Botteghe Oscure printed it in 1951. Book form came in 1952, in In Country Sleep and in Collected Poems, 1934-1952. It is not in Deaths and Entrances.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Son (The speaker who urges his father to resist death); The Father (An old man near death, addressed on a sad height)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker tells his father not to slip quietly into death.
Wise men, good men, wild men, and grave men all resist the dark.
Each kind of man returns to one of the two repeating lines.
In the last stanza the son speaks directly to his father.
He asks for fierce tears, a curse and a blessing together.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Fifteen stories of ordinary Dublin people trapped in dull, narrow lives.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Joyce began the stories in 1904 for The Irish Homestead. Three early stories appeared there under the name Stephen Daedalus. The Dead was planned in 1906-07. Grant Richards published the book in London in 1914. The database year 1914 is correct for the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gabriel Conroy (The main man in The Dead, the last story); Gretta Conroy (Gabriel's wife, who mourns a boy from her youth); Michael Furey (The dead boy Gretta still loves)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a collection of fifteen short stories by James Joyce.
They from a naturalistic depiction of Irish middle class life in and around Dublin, in the early of 20th century.
The initial stories in the collection are narrated by children protagonists.
The stories are: 1- The Sisters 2- An Encounter 3- Araby 4- Eveline 5- After the Race 6- Two Gallants 7- The Boarding House 8- A Little Cloud 9- Counter Parts 10- Clay 11- A Painful Case 12- Ivy Day in the Committee Room 13- A Mother 14- Grace 15- The Dead A Portrait of an Artist as a Young Man (1916)
It is the first novel of James Joyce.
It is also called a psychological novel of Joyce.
The theme of the novel traces the religious and intellectual awakening of Stephan Dedalus. It is set in Dublin, Ireland.
In 1903, the portrait began his life as "Stephan Hero".
It is an autobiographical novel consists of 63 chapters.
Ezra Pound serialized this novel in the English literary magazine "The Egoist" (1914-15) and it was published in a book form in 1916.
Epigraph to "A Portrait of an Artist as a Young Man": "Et ignotas animum dimittit in artes" (And he turned his mind to unknown arts).
Opening Lines: "Once upon a time and a very good time it was there was a moocow coming down along the road and this moocow that was coming down along the road met a nicens little boy named baby tuckoo. . . . His father told him that story: his father looked at him through a glass: he had a hairy face. He was a baby tuckoo. The moocow came down the road where Betty Byrne lived: she sold lemon platt". Major characters:.
Stephan Dedalus: He is the protagonist. He goes through long phase of hedonism and deep religiosity. He eventually adopts a philosophy of aestheticism, greatly valuing beauty and art. His surname is taken from Greek Mythical figure "Dedalus".
Simon Dedalus: A former medical student and Stephan Dedalus' father.
Emma Clery: Stephan's beloved, the young girl. Stephan constructs Emma as ideal of femininity.
Charles Stewart Parnell: An Irish political leader who is not actual character of the novel, but his death influences many of its characters.
Cranly: Stephan's best friend at University. He represents a secular confessor of Stephan. Towards the end of the novel he bears witness to Stephan's exposition of his aesthetic philosophy.
The early stories show children and young people facing disappointment.
Middle stories show adults stuck in work, drink, and politics.
Joyce wanted each story to end in an epiphany, a sudden insight.
The last story, The Dead, is set at a party on Epiphany night.
Gabriel Conroy learns that his wife still loves a dead country boy.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A war poem that calls patriotic glory a lie after a gas attack.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Drafted at Craiglockhart in October 1917. The earliest known manuscript is dated 8 October 1917. It was first printed in Poems in 1920, after Owen's death. A New York edition of that book appeared in 1921. The database year 1914 is only the period span.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The soldier speaker (A man who watched a comrade die in a gas attack); The dying soldier (The man who could not fit his gas mask in time)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tired soldiers march back from the front, bent double and coughing.
Poison gas shells fall, and the men scramble for their masks.
One soldier is too slow, and the gas drowns him.
The speaker still sees that death in his dreams.
He says no honest person would tell children that such a death is sweet.

items.title: "Musée des Beaux Arts" (1939) — W. H. Auden

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short poem on how old paintings show suffering while ordinary life goes on.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written December 1938. First printed in New Writing, spring 1939, as Palais des beaux arts. Collected in Another Time in 1940 under the museum title.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A visitor who reads suffering in the paintings of the Old Masters); Icarus (The falling boy in the painting, unnoticed by the working world)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Auden wrote it in Brussels in December 1938, while staying with Christopher Isherwood.
The title is French for Museum of Fine Arts.
It first appeared in spring 1939 in the magazine New Writing, under another museum name.
The Old Masters, he says, understood suffering.
It looks at a Bruegel painting of Icarus falling, while ordinary work goes on.
The poem was then collected in Another Time in 1940.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long novel about orphan Philip Carey, his club foot, and his bondage to desire.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and the novel's own record date the book 1915. An earlier version was called Beauty from Ashes, a title already used, so Maugham took the final title from Spinoza. The book is strongly autobiographical, but Maugham said more of it is invention.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Philip Carey (An orphan with a club foot who studies art and then medicine); Mildred (The waitress who holds Philip in a painful love); Thorpe Athelny (The family man who helps Philip when he is destitute); Sally Athelny (Thorpe's daughter, whom Philip decides to marry)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
5- The Moon and Sixpence (1919): it is based on the life of Paul Gauguin. 6- The Painted Veil (1925); the title is taken from the sonnet of P.B. Shelley. 7- Cakes and Ale or The Skelton in the Cupboard (1930); the title is taken from the remark of Sir Toby Belch to Malvolio in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night. 8- The Razor's Edge; Larry Darrel is the protagonist. 9- The Casuarina Tree (1920): a collection of short stories.
Philip Carey loses his mother and is sent to his uncle, a cold vicar in Kent.
A club foot makes him shy.
He studies in Germany, fails at art in Paris, and turns to medicine.
He falls under the power of Mildred, a waitress who treats him badly.
Poverty, illness, and a false hope of wealth nearly break him.
He qualifies as a doctor and chooses an ordinary marriage over a dream of freedom.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lively defence of Christian belief, written as the positive pair to Heretics.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is wrong. John Lane issued Orthodoxy on 25 September 1908. The London title page is dated 1909, which is why some lists say 1909.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: G. K. Chesterton (The essayist speaking in his own voice)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Chesterton explains how he came to accept ordinary Christian belief.
He says pure logic, cut off from wonder, can itself become madness.
Fairy tales, he argues, keep a person sane and grateful.
He treats Christian ideas as paradoxes that still fit the world.
The book is a companion to Heretics, which had attacked modern slogans.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 13 chapter novel that follows Miriam Henderson's thoughts through her working life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is the period label, not the book date. She began Pointed Roofs in 1912. Pointed Roofs appeared in 1915. The collected title Pilgrimage, with 12 chapters, appeared in 1938. Parts of the last chapter appeared in 1946. March Moonlight was first included in 1967.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Miriam Henderson (The centre of every chapter, a young woman based on Richardson); Hypo Wilson (A writer friend in the novel, based on H. G. Wells)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Pointed Roofs (1915) sends young Miriam Henderson to teach in Germany.
Later chapters follow her work in London, her friendships, and her inner debates.
The reader hears mainly Miriam's thoughts, not a narrator's tidy plot.
