H. G. Wells appears in disguise as the character Hypo Wilson.
Twelve chapters, including Dimple Hill, were gathered as Pilgrimage in 1938.
March Moonlight, still unfinished, was added in the 1967 edition.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The first book of Owen's poems, edited after his death by Sassoon.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year is wrong for this book. Chatto and Windus published Poems in London in 1920. The preface line about pity belongs to a draft Owen wrote for a book he did not live to see. Blunden's 1931 edition is not the first book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The soldier speaker (The voice in many of the war poems, often a man in the trenches)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Owen planned a book of war poems, but he was killed before it appeared.
Only five of his poems were printed while he was alive.
Sassoon edited Poems in 1920, with help from Edith Sitwell.
That book holds 23 poems, including Dulce et Decorum Est.
A larger edition by Edmund Blunden followed in 1931.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Spender's 1933 book of poems on modern life, industry, and social hope.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year is the start of a period label, not the publication year. Wikipedia lists Poems (1933), separate from Twenty Poems (1930). The Poetry Foundation places The Pylons in Poems (1933).

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
T. S. Eliot, then an editor at Faber, took up Spender in 1933.
This book is his first major collection, after the smaller Twenty Poems of 1930.
The poems look at pylons, cities, and people living under the threat of war.
They ask the poet to remember joy and also to face public suffering.
The volume made him known as one of the pylon poets of the 1930s.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1914 volume that turns from dream toward public duty, beggars, and modern Ireland.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1914 is correct for the first book. The Cuala Press at Dundrum issued Responsibilities: Poems and a Play in 1914.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A public voice defending his art and judging modern Ireland)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book opens under an epigraph (a short motto before the poems): In dreams begins responsibility.
Yeats answers critics who blame him for lacking a public theme.
September 1913 attacks the new Irish middle class and mourns Romantic Ireland.
Beggars, hermits, and Paudeen replace the vague roses of the 1890s.
The tone is harder and more argumentative than The Wind Among the Reeds.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A public poem on the Spanish Civil War, later revised and then rejected by Auden.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The 1937 Faber pamphlet is titled Spain. The title Spain 1937 belongs to the revised poem in Another Time (1940). Auden afterwards suppressed it.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Auden visited Spain briefly in 1937, during the Civil War.
Faber published the poem that year as a pamphlet titled Spain.
He gave the profits to the Spanish Medical Aid Committee.
It looks back at the history that led to the war.
It then turns to the war itself and to a possible future after it.
A revised text titled Spain 1937 appeared in Another Time in 1940.
Auden later left the poem out of his collected editions and called it dishonest.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short comic play in which village gossip turns a lost hayfork into a murder.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year is only the period label. The play was first acted on 27 December 1904. That night opened the Abbey Theatre. Yeats's On Baile's Strand was on the same bill. The National Library of Ireland records a Dublin Maunsel edition of 1904. Britannica dates the early comedies in the 1909 book Seven Short Plays, which reprints this play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bartley Fallon (A worried small farmer whom the rumor names as a murderer); Mrs Fallon (Bartley's wife, who defends him until the gossip turns ugly); Mrs Tarpey (A deaf apple seller whose mishearing starts the rumor); Jack Smith (The supposed victim, who returns alive at the end); The Magistrate (An English official who is eager to believe the worst)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A new English magistrate visits a country fair and expects crime.
Deaf Mrs Tarpey mishears talk about a hayfork and a red cloth.
The village decides that Bartley Fallon has killed Jack Smith.
Bartley, who always expects bad luck, is arrested.
Jack Smith walks in alive, and the false story collapses.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long prose book arguing that divine life can evolve on earth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Each part was written just before it appeared in the Arya, from August 1914 to January 1919. The revised Book One came out in November 1939. The revised Book Two came out in July 1940. Britannica dates the book 1939. The exam should keep both the serial years and the 1939-1940 book years.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The chapters first appeared in the monthly Arya from 1914 to 1919.
Aurobindo says the world is a real manifestation of the Divine, not a mere illusion.
Matter, life, and mind are stages in a larger evolution.
The supermind is the link between the infinite and earthly life.
He revised the work into two books, published in 1939 and 1940.

items.title: "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" (1915) — T. S. Eliot

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dramatic monologue about an indecisive man who walks through foggy city streets and fears social judgment.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Those are database errors. This is a dramatic monologue poem. It was written in 1910-1911 and published in June 1915 in Poetry magazine.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: J. Alfred Prufrock (A timid, aging man who feels paralyzed by social fear)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title comes from Rudyard Kipling's "The Love Song of Har Dayal".
Opening Lines: "Let's go then, you and I When the evening is spread out against the sky like a patient etherized upon a table"
The poem follows the conscious experience of a man Prufrock, lamenting his physical and intellectual inertia with the recurrent theme of carnal love unattained.
It was first published in June 1915 issue of poetry "A Magazine of Verse" at the instigation of Ezra Pound.
It appeared as one of the poem in "Prufrock and other Observations" (1917)
The poem's structure was heavily influenced by Eliot's extensive reading of Dante Alighieri.
It is a dramatic monologue in which Mr. Prufrock unloads his mind to his own suppressed self - the you of the poem.
He is torn by conflict between sexual longing and its frustration.
Other famous lines:.
"Do I dare disturb the universe".
"No, I am not Prince Hamlet, nor was meant to be".
"It is impossible to say just what I mean".
This poem is described as "drama of literary anguish".
Eliot dedicated his "Prufrock and other Observations" to Jean Verdenal.
Prufrock invites the listener to walk through cheap city streets under the evening sky.
He visits high society drawing rooms where women talk about Michelangelo.
Yellow smoke and fog roll across the windows of the city streets.
He worries that his hair is growing thin and his clothes look awkward.
He hesitates to ask an overwhelming question because he fears emotional rejection.
He sees mermaids singing on the waves, but he believes they will not sing to him.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long novel about a young man who stays seven years in a mountain clinic.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1914 is the period span, not the book year. Mann began the story in 1912 after a visit to Davos. S. Fischer Verlag published it in November 1924. The English translation came in 1927.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hans Castorp (A young engineer from Hamburg who stays on the mountain); Lodovico Settembrini (An Italian humanist (a thinker who trusts human reason) who argues for progress); Leo Naphta (A radical thinker who argues against Settembrini); Madame Chauchat (A patient whom Castorp loves); Joachim Ziemssen (Castorp's cousin, a soldier being treated at the clinic)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hans Castorp visits his cousin at a clinic in Davos, in the Swiss Alps.
A small illness keeps him there, and seven years pass.
He hears debates between Settembrini, who trusts reason, and the harsh thinker Naphta.
He falls in love with a patient, Madame Chauchat.
When war starts, he leaves to fight, and his fate is left unclear.

items.title: "The Man Who Was Thursday" (1908) — G. K. Chesterton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poet detective joins a council of anarchists and finds the council is a riddle.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is wrong. Arrowsmith published it in February 1908. The subtitle is A Nightmare.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gabriel Syme (Thursday, a poet and undercover policeman); Lucian Gregory (An anarchist poet who challenges Syme); Sunday (The vast president of the council, and the story's deepest riddle)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gabriel Syme, a poet turned policeman, debates the anarchist poet Lucian Gregory.
Syme says order is poetic, and he praises Bradshaw (a railway timetable).
Syme is elected Thursday on a secret council named for the days of the week.
He plans to stop a plot against the world.
He learns that five other members are also policemen in disguise.
Sunday, the huge president, is the man who hired the detectives.
The nightmare ends in Saffron Park, and the terror turns toward wonder.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A story about a salesman who wakes to find he is a giant insect.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1914 is the period span, not the print year. He wrote the story in 1912. It appeared in the magazine Die weißen Blätter in October 1915. The Kurt Wolff book followed in December 1915. He was still alive.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gregor Samsa (A traveling salesman who becomes an insect and loses his human place); Grete Samsa (Gregor's sister, who cares for him and later wants him gone); Mr. Samsa (Gregor's father, who attacks him and returns to work)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a novella by Kafka, published in 1915.
The story begins with a travelling salesman Gregor Samsa, walking to find himself transformed (metamorphosed) into a large, monstrous insect-like creature.
The cause of Gregor's transformation is never revealed, and Kafka himself never gave an explanation.
Gregor attempts to adjust to his new condition as he deals with being burdensome to his parents and sister who are repelled by the horrible verminous creature Gregor has become.
It is written in 3 parts.
Greta is Gregor's young sister, who becomes his caretaker after transformation but ultimately she is tired of taking care of him and realized his burden on each one in the family.
Greta tells her parents to get rid of Gregor and they agreed wishing Gregor would understand them and would leave of his own accord.
Gregor does, in fact understand and determined to rid his family of his presence, he dies.
Gregor Samsa wakes and finds he has become a monstrous vermin.
He cannot go to work, and the chief clerk flees in horror.
His sister Grete feeds him, but the family shuts him in his room.
His father wounds him with an apple, and the family grows tired of him.
Gregor dies alone, and the family feels relief and looks ahead.

items.title: "The Moon and Sixpence" (1919) — W. Somerset Maugham

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel about stockbroker Charles Strickland, who leaves his family to paint.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: William Heinemann published it on 15 April 1919. Britannica also dates it 1919. Maugham said it is not a life of Paul Gauguin. He used the main facts and invented the rest. A visit to Tahiti in 1914 helped him start the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Narrator (A young writer who pieces Strickland's life together); Charles Strickland (A broker in middle age who becomes a ruthless painter); Dirk Stroeve (A kind Dutch painter whom Strickland injures); Blanche Stroeve (Dirk's wife, who leaves him for Strickland and then dies)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A young writer narrates the life of Charles Strickland, a London stockbroker.
Strickland suddenly leaves his wife and children and goes to Paris to paint.
He lives in poverty, uses the people who help him, and cares only for his art.
The narrator later traces Strickland's last years in Tahiti.
Strickland dies of leprosy after painting the walls of his hut, which are then destroyed.

items.title: "The Power and the Glory" (1940) — Graham Greene

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A hunted whisky priest (a drinking priest) keeps serving people in Mexico and is shot.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Heinemann published it in London in 1940. In the same year Viking issued it in America as The Labyrinthine Ways. That is the same novel, not a second book. It won the Hawthornden Prize in 1941.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The whisky priest (A nameless, failed priest who keeps doing a priest's duties while on the run); The lieutenant (An honest, rigid officer who wants the province cleared of priests); Brigitta (The priest's young daughter); The mestizo (Mestizo means a man of mixed birth. He betrays the priest and springs the trap.); Padre Jose (A priest who obeyed the state, married, and will not hear the last confession)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In Tabasco, the state bans Catholic worship and hunts priests.
An unnamed whisky priest stays, though he drinks and has a child.
He meets his daughter Brigitta and still feels unfit for his work.
A stern police lieutenant takes village hostages to trap him.
A man of mixed birth, whom he distrusts, leads him back to a dying man.
The lieutenant admires him as a man but has him shot as a danger.
After the execution, another secret priest arrives in the town.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unfinished novel about a man arrested for a crime nobody names.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1914 is the period span, and it is also near the writing year. He drafted the book in 1914 and 1915 and did not finish it. He died in 1924. Max Brod published it on 26 April 1925. The database does not mark it as posthumous (printed after the writer died). That mark is wrong. The English translation by Willa and Edwin Muir came in 1937.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Josef K. (A bank clerk arrested for a crime that is never named); The priest (A court priest who tells Josef the parable Before the Law); Leni (The lawyer's nurse, who draws Josef away from his case)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a novel by Kafka published in 1925.
It tells the story of a man arrested and prosecuted by a remote, inaccessible authority, with the nature of his crimes revealed neither to him nor to the reader.
On his 30th birthday the chief Financial Officer of a bank Josef K. is unexpectedly arrested by two unidentified agents from an unspecified agency for an unspecified crime.
At the end of the novel K. is stabbed to death and his last words are: "Like a dog". He was killed on his 31th birthday.
On his thirtieth birthday, Josef K. is arrested but not locked up.
Nobody will tell him the charge.
He searches through attic courts, a painter, and a sick lawyer.
A priest tells him a parable about a man who waits at the door of the law.
On the eve of his next birthday, two men take him out and kill him.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An American narrator slowly discovers the lies inside two elegant marriages.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1915 is correct. John Lane published it in March 1915. The year of writing is unknown. The subtitle is A Tale of Passion. Ford had wanted the title The Saddest Story.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Dowell (The American narrator, whose account the reader cannot fully trust); Florence Dowell (John's wife, who fakes illness and hides affairs); Edward Ashburnham (The English officer called the good soldier, ruined by passion); Leonora Ashburnham (Edward's wife, who tries to control his money and his loves); Nancy Rufford (The Ashburnhams' young ward, who breaks down after Edward's death)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
John Dowell tells the story after the disaster, not in calendar order.
For nine years the Dowells and the Ashburnhams meet at a German spa.
Florence Dowell and Edward Ashburnham hide affairs behind false heart trouble.
Edward then loves his young ward, Nancy Rufford, and sends her away.
Florence dies by poison.
Edward cuts his throat.
Nancy loses her mind.
Dowell is left caring for Nancy and still unsure what the truth was.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three generations of the Brangwen family move from farm life toward a freer modern self.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1915 is correct for publication. Britain then suppressed the book for obscenity. Women in Love is the sequel, but it was not published in 1915.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tom Brangwen (The Marsh farmer who marries Lydia); Lydia Lensky (The Polish widow who becomes Tom's wife); Anna Brangwen (Tom and Lydia's daughter, later Will's wife); Will Brangwen (Anna's husband, pulled between desire and religion); Ursula Brangwen (The young woman who carries the novel into the modern age)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is his least autobiographical novel.
It shows how an individual can get satisfaction through marriage and also changing relations between the generations as well as the effect of modern civilization on human sensibility.
It follows three generations of Brangwen family living in Nottinghamshire.
The main character Tom Brangwen used to live at a farm.
A widow of Polish rebel named Lydia Lensky came to live in the village with her daughter Anna.
Both Tom and Lydia began to love each other and they were married soon.
Tom also started to love his step daughter Anna. She also loved him very passionately. But when Anna became young, she fell in love with Will, Tom's nephew.
Will was a Ruskinised young man and he was very fond of architecture of the church.
After the marriage of Anna and Will they had a daughter Ursula.
Ursula fell in love with a Polish young man Anton Skrebensky who also returned her love in equal way.
Later she left him, because one day she saw a rainbow in the sky and hoped that the god would send a new lover for her.
The Brangwens farm on the Marsh as industry rises around them.
Tom Brangwen marries Lydia, a Polish widow.
Their daughter Anna marries Will, and their marriage is a long struggle.
Ursula, the next generation, seeks work, study, and a larger life.
The book ends with Ursula seeing a rainbow as a sign of new life.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Rachel Vinrace sails to South America on a voyage of self discovery and tragic love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Begun around 1906 under the title Melymbrosia and published on 26 March 1915 by Duckworth.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rachel Vinrace (A sheltered young English woman and talented pianist); Terence Hewet (An aspiring writer who falls in love with Rachel); Helen Ambrose (Rachel's wise aunt who guides and protects her); St John Hirst (An intellectual Cambridge scholar who looks down on others); Clarissa Dalloway (A wealthy society woman traveling with her husband Richard)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Rachel Vinrace journeys by ship to Santa Marina in South America.
She meets other British travelers and explores life beyond her sheltered home.
She falls in love with an aspiring writer named Terence Hewet.
Rachel catches a tropical fever during a river trip and dies.

items.title: "A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man" (1916) — James Joyce

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young Irishman grows from a fearful child into an artist.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Joyce began sketching the book in 1904 and rewrote the earlier draft Stephen Hero. The Egoist serialized it in 1914. B. W. Huebsch published the New York book on 29 December 1916. The English Egoist Press edition followed. The database year 1916 is the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Stephen Dedalus (The young artist, based on Joyce but not his legal name); Simon Dedalus (Stephen's father, whose fortunes fall); Cranly (Stephen's university friend, who questions his leaving)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Stephen Dedalus is a sensitive boy at a strict Jesuit school.
A sermon on hell fills him with religious fear.
He later rejects the priesthood and the Catholic Church.
At university he chooses art over nation, family, and church.
He leaves Dublin to forge a conscience for his people.

items.title: "Prufrock and Other Observations" (1917) — T. S. Eliot

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: T. S. Eliot's first published book of twelve poems depicting modern city life and human loneliness.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It was published in June 1917 by The Egoist Press in London.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: J. Alfred Prufrock (The hesitant and self-conscious speaker of the opening poem); The Lady (An upper-class woman seeking sympathy and company in Portrait of a Lady)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The collection opens with the famous title poem about J. Alfred Prufrock.
It includes Portrait of a Lady, which describes an awkward friendship with an older woman.
The Preludes present dirty urban images of muddy streets, stale beer, and tired workers.
Rhapsody on a Windy Night follows a late night walk under flickering street lamps.
The poems capture the dull routines and psychological anxieties of early twentieth-century London and Boston.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Songs of love, death, and destiny, with poems of war and national waking.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1917 is correct for publication. The title page says the songs are of 1915 to 1916, and the copyright year is 1917. Do not answer 1915 as the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mother India (The speaking voice of The Gift of India, mourning sons who died abroad)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poems belong to 1915 and 1916, and the foreword is dated Hyderabad, 1916.
John Lane in New York and William Heinemann in London published the book in 1917.
The subtitle is Songs of Love, Death and Destiny.
The Gift of India asks the world to remember Indian soldiers killed in the First World War.
Awake, which she linked with a 1915 Congress speech, calls Indians to rise together.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Bertha Young feels perfect joy at a dinner, then sees her husband's secret.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1918 is the magazine date. The English Review printed the story in August 1918. It was collected in Bliss and Other Stories in 1920. The posthumous flag is wrong. Mansfield died in 1923. The move from magazine to book is real.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bertha Young (The hostess whose bliss hides a blind spot in her marriage); Harry Young (Bertha's husband, who is secretly involved with Pearl); Pearl Fulton (The guest Bertha idealizes, and Harry's lover); Eddie Warren (A nervous poet among the dinner guests)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bertha Young, aged thirty, feels a sudden blaze of bliss before her party.
She links that joy to the flowering pear tree in the garden.
Guests arrive, including the cool and beautiful Pearl Fulton.
Bertha thinks she and Pearl share a silent understanding.
She then sees Pearl and Harry planning a meeting, and the joy breaks.

items.title: "The Home and the World (English translation)" (1919 (English, London: Macmillan)) — Rabindranath Tagore

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Home and the World (English translation)

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: This is the English version of the Bengali novel Ghare Baire, made by Tagore's nephew in 1919.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database shows 1912; 1913; 1919 and calls it Drama. This is a novel. The English year 1919 is correct. The Bengali book is 1916.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bimala (Nikhil's wife, torn between home and the world); Nikhilesh (Her husband, a kind landlord who hates violence); Sandip (A fiery nationalist leader who attracts Bimala); Amulya (A young follower of Sandip)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ghare Baire came out in Bengali in 1915 and 1916.
Surendranath Tagore translated it into English.
Rabindranath Tagore helped with the English text.
Macmillan of London published it in 1919.
It is the same book as the Home and the World entry.

items.title: "The Wild Swans at Coole" (1917) — W. B. Yeats

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A middle volume on aging, Coole Park, war, and the fifty nine swans.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1919 is the enlarged Macmillan book, not the first printing. The Cuala Press published the first book in November 1917, with the play At the Hawk's Well. Macmillan published the larger poetry book in March 1919.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (An aging poet watching the swans at Coole Park); Robert Gregory (Lady Gregory's son, mourned among the war dead); The Irish airman (A pilot who foresees his death and weighs his motives)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title poem counts fifty nine swans on the water at Coole.
Nineteen years have passed since the speaker first heard them.
Their hearts have not grown old, while his has.
The 1919 book adds the airman poem and the elegy for Robert Gregory.
Irish loss in war sits beside personal loss and a colder style.

items.title: "“Tradition and the Individual Talent”" (1919) — T. S. Eliot

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A landmark critical essay arguing that great writers must possess a historical sense and write with artistic impersonality.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database lists genre as Poetry. That is a database error. This is a critical essay in prose. It was published in The Egoist in 1919.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: T. S. Eliot (The literary critic presenting a classical theory of art)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is an essay first published in "The Egoist" (1919) and later Eliot's first book of criticism "The Sacred Wood" (1920).
It is divided into three parts:.
The Concept of Tradition.
The Theory of Impersonal Poetry.
The Conclusion.
Eliot defines poetry as "Not a turning loose of emotion but an escape from emotion, not the expression of personality but an escape from personality".
In this essay Eliot presents his "Theory of Impersonality".
Eliot argues that tradition is not mere imitation of past writers.
Writers must obtain tradition by hard work and develop a historical sense.
The historical sense makes a poet feel that European literature from Homer exists simultaneously.
A new work of art alters the existing order of all past masterpieces.
Eliot proposes the impersonal theory of poetry, comparing the poet's mind to a shred of platinum.
The platinum acts as a catalyst (a substance that speeds up a reaction without changing itself).
Poetry is not a turning loose of emotion, but an escape from emotion.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her second story book, gathering Bliss, Prelude, and other mature tales.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1920 is correct for the Constable book. The unfinished flag is copied from The Dove's Nest and is wrong here. Prelude had a separate Hogarth Press printing in 1918. The title story is the 1918 magazine piece.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bertha Young (Heroine of the title story Bliss); The Burnell family (The New Zealand family in Prelude, including Kezia)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Constable published this collection in London in 1920.
The title story had already appeared in the English Review in 1918.
Prelude, first printed by the Hogarth Press in 1918, opens the family scenes.
Other stories study parties, artists, children, and strained couples.
This is a finished book issued in her lifetime, not an unfinished file.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A sequence that judges Pound's London years and calls the age a botched civilisation.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1920 is correct. The Ovid Press in London published the poem in June 1920. It is a finished sequence. It is not a section of the unfinished Cantos. Pound left England soon after.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: E. P. (The poet judged in the opening ode, a mask close to Pound); Hugh Selwyn Mauberley (A minor poet of refined but lifeless art in the second part)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poem is a sequence of short pieces in two main parts.
The first part begins as an ode for the burial of E. P.
It mocks a poet out of key with his time, and then mocks the age itself.
Pound attacks the war that killed a myriad for a botched civilisation.
Later portraits recall the London literary world he was leaving.
The Envoi praises beauty that might outlast change.
The second part shows Mauberley, a minor artist who perfects lifeless medallions.

items.title: "The Mysterious Affair at Styles" (1920) — Agatha Christie

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Christie's first detective novel, in which Poirot solves a poisoning at Styles Court.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1920 is the first publication, the United States edition of October 1920 from John Lane. Christie wrote most of the novel in 1916. The Bodley Head published the UK edition on 21 January 1921. At John Lane's request she moved Poirot's explanation from a courtroom to the library at Styles.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hercule Poirot (A Belgian detective who solves the Styles poisoning); Arthur Hastings (The narrator, a soldier on sick leave and Poirot's friend); Emily Inglethorp (The wealthy owner of Styles Court, who is murdered); Alfred Inglethorp (Emily's younger husband and one of the murderers)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
During the First World War, Hastings stays at Styles Court in Essex.
Emily Inglethorp, the rich owner, is poisoned with strychnine.
Hastings brings in Hercule Poirot, a Belgian refugee living nearby.
Suspicion falls on her young husband Alfred, and then on her stepson John.
Poirot shows that Alfred and Evelyn Howard planned the murder and tried to hide behind a false arrest.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A book of twenty critical essays examining Elizabethan drama, Renaissance poetry, and the methods of literary criticism.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database lists genre as Poetry. That is a database error. This is a volume of critical prose essays. It was published in November 1920 by Methuen.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: T. S. Eliot (The essayist arguing for disciplined, objective critical standards)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book collects critical essays and reviews published by Eliot between 1917 and 1920.
It includes Tradition and the Individual Talent as its central theoretical statement.
In Hamlet and His Problems, Eliot calls Hamlet an artistic failure.
In that essay, he introduces the famous term objective correlative.
The book also contains influential studies of Dante, Ben Jonson, Christopher Marlowe, and Algernon Swinburne.
Eliot demands close analysis of poetic text rather than emotional praise.

items.title: "This Side of Paradise" (1920) — F. Scott Fitzgerald

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A first novel about a Princeton youth chasing love, fame, and a self.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1920 is correct. Scribner's published the book on 26 March 1920. An early draft was called The Romantic Egotist. He finished this novel in his lifetime. The Last Tycoon, not this book, came out after his death.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Amory Blaine (A Princeton student who searches for love and a purpose); Isabelle Borge (A wealthy debutante (a young woman new to rich society) and Amory's early love); Rosalind Connage (A flapper (a young 1920s woman who broke old rules) who leaves Amory for a richer man)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Title is taken from the Rupert Brook's Tiare Tahiti 2. The Beautiful and Damned (1922)
Amory Blaine, a handsome Midwesterner, believes he has a great destiny.
At Princeton he falls in love with the rich debutante Isabelle.
After the war he loves Rosalind, who leaves him for a richer man.
He drifts through jobs, drink, and one more reckless romance.
The book made Fitzgerald famous and helped him marry Zelda Sayre.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ursula, Gudrun, Birkin, and Gerald test love, friendship, and modern industry.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1920 is the first publication year. Lawrence finished the novel in 1916. It was not published until 1920. It is the sequel to The Rainbow, not the same book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ursula Brangwen (The sister who pairs with Birkin); Gudrun Brangwen (The artist sister who pairs with Gerald); Rupert Birkin (The school inspector who wants a star equilibrium in love); Gerald Crich (The industrialist whose will hardens and then breaks); Hermione Roddice (The intellectual woman Birkin leaves behind)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
6- The Lost Girl (1920): It was revised and republished.
It was published as a sequel to "The Rainbow".
The early titles were "The Sisters" and "The Wedding Ring".
It is one of his novels showing his philosophy of life.
It shows the lives of two sisters named Ursula Brangwen and Gudrun who loved two men named Rupert Birkin and Gerald Crich respectively.
In this novel, the writer shows the conflict between mind and spirit against the Christian Gospels.
Birkin asks Ursula to marry him, she argues.
Gerald and Gudrun's relationship however becomes stormy.
The four holidays in the Alps, Gudrun begins an intense friendship with Loerke.
Gerald enraged by Loerke and most of Grudun verbal abuse, and tries to strange Gudrun.
Finally he leaves Gudrun and Loerke and climbs the mountain eventually slipping into a snowy valley and freezes to death.
The novel continues Ursula's life after The Rainbow.
Ursula moves toward Rupert Birkin, who wants a balance of two free people.
Gudrun is drawn to Gerald Crich, the coal owner.
Gerald's industrial will and Birkin's search for a new relation collide.
The Alpine ending leaves Gerald dead and the others facing that loss.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A shy young poet visits a clever country house party and fails in love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1921 is correct. Huxley wrote it in the summer of 1921. Chatto and Windus published it in London in November 1921. The American edition came in 1922. It is his first published novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Denis Stone (A shy young poet and the main observer); Anne Wimbush (The niece Denis loves); Henry Wimbush (The owner of Crome, who reads his history of the house); Priscilla Wimbush (Henry's wife, busy with spiritual fads); Mr Scogan (A cynical guest who sketches a cold future state)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Denis Stone, a young poet, joins a summer party at the house called Crome.
He loves Anne Wimbush, but she prefers the painter Gombauld.
The guests talk, flirt, and show off their private fads.
Priscilla Wimbush chases spiritual fashions.
Scogan mocks the age.
Scogan even pictures babies grown in bottles, a hint of Brave New World.
Denis reads Jenny's journal and sees a cruel sketch of himself.
He leaves on a false family call just when Anne might have liked him.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A critical essay reviewing Herbert Grierson's anthology and defending the unified sensibility of seventeenth-century poets.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database lists genre as Poetry. That is a database error. This is a critical review essay in prose. It was published on 20 October 1921 in the Times Literary Supplement.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: T. S. Eliot (The critic examining seventeenth-century verse and modern poetic diction)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Eliot reviews Herbert Grierson's book of metaphysical poetry from the seventeenth century.
He defends John Donne and George Herbert against old criticisms made by Samuel Johnson.
He argues that metaphysical poets possessed a unified sensibility (the ability to feel their thoughts directly).
In the seventeenth century, a dissociation of sensibility (a split between thinking and feeling) took place.
He blames John Milton and John Dryden for encouraging this harmful division in English poetry.
He concludes that modern poets must also be complex and difficult to reflect modern civilization.

items.title: "The Beautiful and Damned" (1922) — F. Scott Fitzgerald

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel about a young heir and his wife who waste their youth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1922 is the book year. Metropolitan serialized it from September 1921 to March 1922. Scribner's published the book on 4 March 1922. He finished it in his lifetime.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Anthony Comstock Patch (A Harvard man who waits for an inheritance and drinks it away); Gloria Gilbert (Anthony's beautiful wife, who fears growing old)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Anthony Patch lives idly in New York and waits for his grandfather's money.
He marries the beautiful Gloria Gilbert, and they live for parties.
The grandfather sees their wild life and cuts Anthony from the will.
Years of drink, debt, and a court fight wear them down.
Beauty and money do not save them from a spoiled middle age.

items.title: "The Garden Party and Other Stories" (1922) — Katherine Mansfield

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Garden Party and Other Stories

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her 1922 story book, led by The Garden Party and other studies of class and loss.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1922 is correct for the Constable book. The unfinished flag is wrong for this lifetime collection. The Poetry label is also wrong. This is Unit 3 fiction. The title story's magazine printing is also 1922.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Laura Sheridan (The young hostess in the title story); Miss Brill (A lonely woman whose Sunday ritual is broken in her own story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Constable published the collection in London in 1922.
The title story had just run in the Westminster Gazette in February 1922.
Stories include At the Bay, Miss Brill, and The Daughters of the Late Colonel.
Many pieces return to family life, parties, and small social cruelties.
The book is short fiction.
The database label Poetry is wrong.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A five-part modernist poem that portrays the spiritual collapse and fragmentation of Europe after World War I.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The poem was written in 1921-1922. It was first published in October 1922 in The Criterion and in November 1922 in The Dial. The first book edition appeared in December 1922.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tiresias (The blind prophet of Thebes who sees all the events in the poem); Madame Sosostris (A famous clairvoyant (fortune teller) with a wicked pack of Tarot cards); Phlebas the Phoenician (A drowned sailor whose body is picked clean by the deep sea currents); The Typist and the Clerk (Modern London city workers engaged in an unfeeling, mechanical romance)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a most important poem of T.S. Eliot.
The cinematographic technique was used in this poem.
The Greek and Latin epigraph of The Waste Land is taken from Gaius Petronius' The Satyricon.
It was published in 1922 as a 433 line poem and written in Free Verse.
The poem first appeared in UK in October issue of "The Criterion" and in United States in the November issue of "The Dial".
It was published in book form in December, 1922.
Allen Tate called this poem "a music of ideas".
It includes the famous phrases as:.
"April is the cruelest month"
"I will show you fear in a handful of dust"
"Shantih, Shantih, Shantih"
The poem follows the legend of the Holy Grail and the Fisher King combined with vignettes of contemporary British society.
The poem is divided in five sections: 1. The Burial of The Dead 2. A Game of Chess 3. The Fire Sermon 4. Death by Water 5. What the Thunder Said.
Weston and Frazer influenced him to write this poem. The Burial of the Dead:.
It takes its title from a line in the Anglican burial service, and expresses despair.
This section sets up the main theme of the poem by establishing the modern city as the real Wasteland of the poem.
The section is made up of four vignettes:.
First: The first speaker enters the poem as an unidentified person who drinks coffee and talks for the specific and artificial time increment of an hour.
Second: The second part launches into a description of a very dry, dusty and desolate world. A girl once known as "the hyacinth girl" speaks of how she is "neither living nor dead". The character Phoenician Sailor appears in this part.
Third: In this part Madam Sosostris reads tarot cards and makes predictions that will be fulfilled in later parts of the poem.
Fourth: This section mentions of the "Unreal city", the civilization portrayed in the poem, which has been undone by death.
The speaker sees a person he knows and cries out after him, asking if the corpse he has planted in his garden has begun to sprout and calling him a hypocrite reader, doppelganger and brother.
Part one, The Burial of the Dead, introduces a dead, dry landscape where April is cruel.
Part two, A Game of Chess, contrasts wealthy upper-class boredom with poor pub gossip about abortion.
Part three, The Fire Sermon, shows mechanical, lustful relationships along the polluted river Thames.
The blind prophet Tiresias witnesses a dull sexual encounter between a typist and a clerk.
Part four, Death by Water, depicts the drowned Phoenician sailor Phlebas rotting under the sea.
Part five, What the Thunder Said, travels through dry rock mountains waiting for rain.
The thunder speaks the Sanskrit words Datta, Dayadhvam, Damyata, ending with Shantih shantih shantih.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: One Dublin day in 1904 retells Homer's Odyssey in modern life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Joyce worked on the book from 1914. The Little Review serialized episodes from March 1918 until a ban in December 1920. Sylvia Beach published the full book in Paris, at Shakespeare and Company, on 2 February 1922. The database year 1922 is the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Leopold Bloom (The Dublin ad canvasser who stands for Odysseus); Molly Bloom (Leopold's wife, whose final monologue ends the book); Stephen Dedalus (The young writer who stands for Telemachus); Buck Mulligan (The medical student in the opening scene)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a modernist novel by James Joyce. It was first in parts in the American journal "The Little Review" from March 1918 to Dec 1920, and then published in its entirety by Sylvia Beach in Feb 1922 in Paris.
"Ulysses" was published in a serial form in a magazine "The Little Review". At a trial in 1921 the magazine was declared obscene and as a result Ulysses was banned in the United States throughout 1920's.
In 1933, it was decided by the district judge that the book was not pornographic and therefore could not be obscene. So the ban was lifted in 1933.
It is considered one of the most important works of modernist literature and has been called a "demonstration and summation of the entire movement".
He divided "Ulysses "into 18 chapters or episodes in three parts.
The book follows 16 June 1904, now called Bloomsday.
Stephen Dedalus teaches, walks, and argues about Shakespeare.
Leopold Bloom, a Jewish ad man, wanders the city on errands.
His wife Molly Bloom stays at home and ends the book with yes.
Each episode matches a book of Homer's Odyssey.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Laura's rich family holds a garden party on the day a poor neighbour dies.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Laura Sheridan (The daughter who feels the clash between the party and the death); Mrs Sheridan (Laura's mother, who insists the party go on); Laurie Sheridan (Laura's brother, who meets her after she leaves the Scotts); Mr Scott (The working man whose death shadows the party)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Sheridan family prepares a garden party on a perfect afternoon.
Laura enjoys the workmen, the lilies, and a new hat.
She hears that a neighbour, Mr Scott, has died by their lane.
Her mother and sister refuse to cancel the party.
Afterward Laura takes leftover food to the dead man's house and cannot explain life.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A chronicle play about Joan of Arc, from her voices to her trial and an epilogue.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Shaw wrote the play in 1923. It opened at the Garrick Theatre in New York on 28 December 1923. The London opening was on 26 March 1924, with Sybil Thorndike as Joan. Constable published the book in 1924. The database year 1923 is the first night. The book year is 1924.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Joan (The village girl who hears voices, leads France, and is tried); The Dauphin (The French prince Joan supports); The Earl of Warwick (An English lord who wants Joan removed as a political danger); The Bishop of Beauvais (A church judge at Joan's trial)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the last play of Shaw.
It is the "Only Tragedy" by Shaw and Michael Holroyd has characterized this play as "A tragedy without villain".
The play is based on the life and trial of "Joan of Arc".
Shaw himself characterized Saint Joan as "A chronicle play in six scenes and an epilogue".
The period is early 15th century when France was a vagal kingdom owing allegiance to English King Henry VI.
Joan, a French peasant girl saw divine visions and heard voices of St. Catherine, St. Margaret and Angel Michael, commanding her to dress and Don Armor as a soldier and drive the English out of France.
She is accused of arch heresy of Protestantism, i.e. protest against interference by church in a matter of personal faith.
She was burnt at Rouen on 30th May 1431.
The idea of the play was suggested to Shaw when in 1920, the Roman church canonized Joan of Arc as Saint Joan.
Joan, a village girl, says that saints' voices tell her to save France.
She leads soldiers and helps the Dauphin toward his crown.
Church courts and English power turn against her after the victories.
A court condemns her, and she is burned.
An epilogue brings the figures back years later to face what they did.
Shaw treats Joan as a brave mind that institutions fear.

Mansfield died in January 1923, with stories still unfinished.
John Middleton Murry gathered the papers for Constable.
The book came out in London in 1923.
Finished stories include The Doll's House and The Fly.
The title story and several others remain fragments.

items.title: "The Meaning of Meaning" (1923) — I. A. Richards

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1923 study of how words mean, written with C. K. Ogden.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.value: C. K. Ogden (Co writer who built the theory of signs with Richards); I. A. Richards (Co writer who links the sign theory to reading and criticism)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ogden and Richards ask how a word can stand for a thing.
They draw a triangle of symbol, thought, and referent, the real thing.
The word and the thing do not touch each other by themselves.
A word's meaning also depends on the situation around it.
Essays by Malinowski and Crookshank were printed with the book.

items.title: "A Passage to India" (1924) — E. M. Forster

5- Maurice (written in 1913-14 but published in 1971 posthumously and having homosexual theme)
Dr Aziz meets Mrs Moore in a mosque and they become friends.
Aziz takes Mrs Moore and Adela Quested to the Marabar Caves.
Adela flees and Aziz is charged with assaulting her.
At the trial Adela withdraws the charge, and Mrs Moore has died at sea.
Years later Aziz and Fielding meet in Mau, but true friendship is still blocked.

fields.value: Christopher Tietjens (A brilliant old fashioned Englishman, called the last Tory (an old conservative)); Sylvia Tietjens (His wife, who uses scandal to wound him); Valentine Wannop (A campaigner for peace and for women's votes, loved by Tietjens)

Some Do Not (1924) shows Tietjens in England before the war.
His wife Sylvia tries to shame him, while he loves Valentine Wannop.
No More Parades (1925) and A Man Could Stand Up (1926) follow him in the army.
The war is shown through his mind, not as a list of battles.
Last Post (1928) turns to peace.
Tietjens is mostly off the page.
The four books were first bound as one volume in 1950.

items.title: "Principles of Literary Criticism" (1924) — I. A. Richards

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1924 book on the value of literature and how readers respond.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: I. A. Richards (The critic explaining how and why readers value poems)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Richards asks what value a poem has for a reader.
He discusses form, rhythm, belief, and readings that disagree.
He wants criticism to be clearer than loose personal taste.
He treats the poem through the mind's responses, not gossip about the poet.
The book became a base for later close reading.

fields.value: A high society woman prepares for an evening party while a shell-shocked soldier ends his life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is called "Female Ulysses".
It is a novel of Woolf that details a day in the life of Clarissa Dalloway, a fictional high society woman in the post First World War England.
It is created from her own two short stories:.
Mrs. Dalloway in Bond Street.
The Prime Minister (Unfinished)
The novel addresses Clarissa's preparations for a party which she will host that evening.
This novel covers one day from morning to night in Mrs. Dalloway's life in June 1923.
Clarissa Dalloway walks through London in June to buy flowers for her party.
Septimus Warren Smith suffers from shell shock after fighting in World War I.
Old friends visit Clarissa and stir up memories of youth and missed choices.
Septimus leaps from a window to escape doctors, and Clarissa hears of his death at her party.

fields.value: A huge unfinished poem, published in parts from 1925 to 1969, that tries to include history.

fields.value: The poem's many speakers (Voices from Homer, history, economics, and Pound's own imprisonment)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Pound planned a long poem that would hold history, myth, and many voices.
It opens by going down to the ship, in the manner of Homer.
A Draft of XVI Cantos was printed in Paris in 1925.
Later books added the Chinese history cantos, the Adams cantos, and others.
The Pisan Cantos were written while he was held by the American army in Italy.
Those cantos won the Bollingen Prize, a US poetry award, in 1949.
Drafts and Fragments appeared in 1969. The whole poem was still unfinished at his death.

items.title: "The Common Reader" (1925 (First Series); 1932 (Second Series)) — Virginia Woolf

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Critical essays on English literary history written for everyday readers across two series (1925 and 1932).

fields.value: The Common Reader (An everyday book lover who reads for private enjoyment without scholarly bias)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
3- A Room of One's Own 4- On Being III (1930) 5- Three Guineas (1938); It is an indictment of Fascism 6- Granite and Rainbow (1958) 7- Profession for Women 8- Mr. Bennett and Mrs. Brown Drama 1- Freshwater: A Comedy (Performed in 1923, revised in 1935, published in 1976)
Woolf borrows the phrase common reader from Samuel Johnson to praise reading for pleasure.
The first series (1925) examines writers from Geoffrey Chaucer and Michel de Montaigne to Jane Austen.
In Modern Fiction, she argues that novels should capture the inner glow of the mind.
She criticizes materialist (focused only on physical objects) writers like Arnold Bennett and H. G. Wells.
The second series (1932) reviews John Donne, John Milton, Daniel Defoe, and Thomas Hardy.

Daisy is married to the rich and careless Tom Buchanan.
Gatsby is killed, and Nick learns how hollow the dream has become.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Hollow Men (A collective chorus of morally empty, paralyzed figures filled with straw)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a poem by T. S. Eliot.
The poem is divided into five parts and consists of 98 lines of which the last four are "probably the most quoted lines of any 20th-century poet writing in English". The Lines are: "This is the way the world ends This is the way the world ends This is the way the world ends Not with a bang but a whimper".
Eliot wrote that he produced the title "The Hollow Men" by combining the titles of the romance "The Hollow Land" by William Morris with the poem "The Broken Men" by Rudyard Kipling.
The speakers declare that they are hollow men stuffed with straw.
Their voices whisper quietly together like wind blowing through dry grass.
They wander through a dry cactus land under a fading star.
They are afraid to look into the eyes of souls in death's dream kingdom.
A shadow falls between idea and reality, conception and creation, desire and response.
The poem ends with a bleak chant that the world ends with a whimper.

fields.value: Gandhi's autobiography, a record of his experiments with truth.

A friend warned him that autobiography was a Western habit.
He still wrote short chapters about his experiments with truth.
He begins with childhood in Gujarat, marriage, and school.
He tells of law study in London and the long years in South Africa.
Diet, vows, religion, and political work are all tests of truth.
The English text is Mahadev Desai's translation from Gandhi's Gujarati.

The book also holds poems of rivers, mothers, and the claim I, too, sing America.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The Ramsay family vacations on the Isle of Skye before and after the grief of World War I.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The exact first publication date is 5 May 1927 by Hogarth Press.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mrs. Ramsay (A warm and beautiful mother who brings family and guests together); Mr. Ramsay (A demanding philosophy professor who fears his work will be forgotten); James Ramsay (The youngest son who resents his father and dreams of the lighthouse); Lily Briscoe (An unmarried painter who struggles against gender limits to make art); Charles Tansley (An insecure scholar who insists that women cannot paint or write)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Time passes is the subtitle of this novel.
The novel centers on the Ramsays and their visits to the Isle of Skye in Scotland between 1910 and 1920.
This novel is based on the stream of consciousness technique as the novel includes little dialogue and almost no action; most of it is written as thoughts and observations.
The novel recalls childhood emotions and highlights adult relationship.
It has three parts:.
Part I: The Window; Part II: Time passes; Part III: The Lighthouse Plot Part I: The Window.
The novel is set in the Ramsay's summer home in the Hebrides on the Isle of Skye. It begins with Mrs. Ramsay's remarks to her son- "Yes, of course, if it's fine tomorrow"
There is a tension between Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay and Mr. Ramsay and James (Ramsay's son).
The Ramsays had eight children and they all are joined by Lily Brisco, a painter who is attempting a portrait of Mrs. Ramsay and James.
Charles Tansley, another guest claims that - "Women can neither paint nor write"
The first section closes with a large dinner party.
In section one, young James Ramsay longs to visit the lighthouse, but bad weather stops them.
In section two, ten years pass quickly while World War I ravages Europe and Mrs. Ramsay dies.
In section three, Mr. Ramsay sails with his children to the lighthouse at last.
Lily Briscoe finishes her long-delayed painting on the lawn and finds artistic peace.

It is his most controversial novel dealt with sexual frustration of a young married woman Constance or Lady Chatterley whose husband has been paralyzed due to war injury.
Her sexual frustration leads her into an affair with the gamekeeper Oliver Mellors and later married to him.
It is most popular and most controversial novel of Lawrence.
It is the graphic and highly sexual novel, published in Italy in 1928, but was banned in the United States until 1959 and in England until 1960.
Sir Clifford Chatterley is wounded in the war and cannot father a child.
Connie feels dead inside the cold life of Wragby Hall.
She begins an affair with Oliver Mellors, the gamekeeper.
Their love crosses class and insists on tenderness of the body.
The private 1928 book was hard to sell openly in Britain.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An immortal English nobleman changes sex and lives through four centuries of literary history.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database 1928 is correct. Published on 11 October 1928 by Hogarth Press. The story ends on the exact day of publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Orlando (An immortal aristocrat and poet who changes sex from male to female); Princess Sasha (A Russian princess who breaks Orlando's heart during the Great Frost); Marmaduke Bonthrop Shelmerdine (A sea captain whom Orlando marries in the Victorian era); Nicholas Greene (A spiteful critic who survives across the centuries)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel describes the adventures of a poet who changes sex from man to woman and lives for centuries, meeting the key figures of the literary history.
The hero of the novel Orlando is born as a male nobleman in England during the reign of Elizabeth I.
He undergoes a mysterious change of sex at the age of about 30 and lives for more than 300 years into modern times without ageing perceptibility.
In the reign of Charles II, on a night of civil unrest and murderous riots, Orlando falls asleep for a period of days, resistant to all efforts to rouse him.
Upon awakening, he finds that he had metamorphosed into a woman, the same person, the same personality and intellect but in a woman's body.
Lady Orlando publishes her book in 1928 entitled "The Oak Tree", centuries after starting it and she wins a prize for it.
The novel ends with Orlando's husband's ship returns and she rushes to greet him.
Orlando begins as an Elizabethan nobleman and court favorite who loves poetry.
After a heartbreak with the Russian princess Sasha, Orlando serves as an ambassador in Turkey.
Orlando falls into a deep sleep and wakes up as a woman with the same identity.
Living through the Victorian age to 1928, Orlando publishes the poem The Oak Tree.

fields.value:
It is a book of poems by W.B. Yeats published in 1928.
It was the first major collection of Yeats after receiving Nobel Prize in 1923.
The title "The Tower" which the book shares with the second poem refers to Ballylee Castle, a Norman tower which Yeats purchased and restored in 1917.
The book includes several of Yeats poems that include:.
Sailing to Byzantium.
The Tower.
Leda and the Swan.
Among School Children.
Wisdom.
The Fool by the Roadside.
The Three Monuments.
All the poems appeared in The Tower had previously appeared somewhere else in print collection and periodicals.
Many of the poems featured in "Seven Poems and a Fragment", "The Cat and the Moon" and certain poems.
An extract from the poem "The Tower" "What shall I do with this absurdity O heart, O troubled heart- this caricature"
Sailing to Byzantium rejects the country of the young and the dying body.
The aged speaker asks the sages of Byzantium to gather him into art.
The Tower uses his restored Norman tower, Thoor Ballylee, as the main symbol.
Leda and the Swan and Among School Children sit in the same book.
Age, rage, history, and perfected art are held in one volume.

fields.value: An American ambulance officer loves an English nurse during the First World War.

fields.value: Frederic Henry (American lieutenant in the Italian ambulance service, and the narrator); Catherine Barkley (English nurse who loves Frederic and dies after giving birth); Rinaldi (Italian surgeon and Frederic's friend)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel of Hemingway is set during Italian campaign of World War I.
The title of the novel is taken from a poem by 16th century dramatist George Peele (English).
It is about a love affair between the expatriate American, Frederic Henry serving as a Lieutenant in the "Ambulance Corpse" of the Italian Army and Catherine Barkley, an English Nurse.
It is set against the backdrop of the First World War, cynical soldiers, fighting and the displacement of populations.
The novel is divided into five books.
Frederic and Catherine live a quiet life in the mountains until she goes into labor.
After a long and painful birth their son is stillborn.
Catherine begins to hemorrhage and soon dies. Frederic returns to his hotel in rain when the novel ends.
Famous Quotes from Farewell to Arms: 1. "When you love you wish to do things for. You wish to sacrifice for. You wish to serve." 2. "But life's not hard to manage when you have nothing to lose." 3. "All thinking men are atheist."
Frederic Henry serves in the Italian ambulance corps.
He falls in love with the English nurse Catherine Barkley.
He is wounded, and their love grows while he heals in Milan.
During the retreat at Caporetto he leaves the army and flees with her.
In Switzerland, Catherine dies after childbirth, and he walks out in the rain.

fields.value: A feminist essay arguing that women need financial independence and private space to write fiction.

fields.value: The book was published on 24 October 1929 by Hogarth Press, based on 1928 lectures.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mary Beton / Mary Seton / Mary Carmichael (The narrator persona (a voice used by an author)); Judith Shakespeare (The imaginary, equally talented sister of William Shakespeare who commits suicide)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is an extended essay by Woolf published on 24 October 1929.
The essay was based on a series of lectures she delivered at Newnham College and Girton College in 1928.
It is seen as a feminist text.
The themes of the essay are:.
Women's access to education.
Building a history of women's writing.
The four Marys.
Lesbianism Women's Access to Education.
The title of the essay comes from the conception that "a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fictions"
The essay examines whether women were capable of producing work of the quality of William Shakespeare, addressing the limitations that past and present women writers face.
In one section Woolf had invented a fictional character "Judith", Shakespeare's sister, to illustrate that a woman with Shakespeare's gifts would have been denied the same opportunities to develop them because the doors were closed for the women. Building a History of Women's Writing:.
In this essay Woolf constructs a critical and historical account of women writers such as: Aphra Behn, Jane Austen, Bronte Sisters, Anne Finch, Countess of Winchilsea and George Eliot.
Woolf gets inspiration from Jane Allen Harrison and introduces him in the essay as J…. H….. The Four Marys:.
In this essay Woolf sees the following 4 women as powerless impoverished women everywhere:.
Judith Shakespeare.
Mary Seton.
Mary Carmichael and.
Mary Beaton Lesbianism.
It describes the works of a fictional woman writer, Mary Carmichael.
Woolf deliberately invokes lesbianism: "Then may I tell you that the very next words I read were these 'Chloe liked Olivia', Do not start, do not blush. Let us admit in the privacy of our own society that these things sometimes happen. Sometimes women do like women".
Woolf investigates why women produced far less literature than men throughout history.
She invents Judith Shakespeare to show how society crushes female artistic talent.
She contrasts the rich food at a men's college with the plain meals at a women's college.
She urges women to earn five hundred pounds a year and secure a room with a lock.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1929 report on students reading poems with titles and authors removed.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1929 is correct. Kegan Paul published it in London in 1929. A revised edition came in 1930.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: I. A. Richards (The teacher who set the poem test and studied the answers); The student readers (Undergraduates whose unsigned comments showed common misreadings)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Richards gave Cambridge students poems with names and titles taken off.
The students wrote comments, and many of them misread the poems.
He studied stock response, a ready feeling that ignores the actual words.
He also studied tone, metaphor, and belief that is only half thought out.
The experiment pushed teachers toward close reading of the text itself.

items.title: "The Sound and the Fury" (1929) — William Faulkner

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The fall of the Compson family is told by three brothers and then by an outside narrator.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1929 is correct. Jonathan Cape and Harrison Smith published the novel on 7 October 1929. Faulkner first called the story Twilight. Malcolm Cowley's Portable Faulkner in 1946 later widened his fame.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Benjy Compson (The youngest brother, mentally disabled, who narrates the first part); Caddy Compson (The sister whose loss haunts the brothers. She is seen more than she speaks); Quentin Compson (The oldest brother, who drowns himself at Harvard); Jason Compson (The harsh middle brother who narrates the third part); Dilsey Gibson (The black servant who endures and cares for the family)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The once proud Compson family of Jefferson is breaking apart.
Benjy, who cannot speak and mixes past with present, tells the first part.
His sister Caddy is the centre he loves and loses.
Quentin tells the day of his suicide at Harvard in 1910.
Jason, bitter and cruel, tells a day in April 1928 and steals Caddy's money.
On Easter Sunday, Dilsey holds the house together while Jason fails.
The four parts are 7 April 1928, 2 June 1910, 6 April 1928, and 8 April 1928.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The Bundren family hauls Addie's body to Jefferson, and fifteen voices tell the journey.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1930 is correct. Jonathan Cape and Harrison Smith published it on 6 October 1930. Faulkner said he wrote it in about six weeks on night duty. The title is from Homer in Marris's English, not from scripture.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Addie Bundren (The mother whose burial wish drives the journey. She narrates after death); Anse Bundren (Her selfish husband, who wants teeth and a new wife); Cash Bundren (The eldest son, a carpenter who builds the coffin); Darl Bundren (The thoughtful son who narrates nineteen chapters and is sent to an asylum); Jewel Bundren (Addie's son by Reverend Whitfield, not by Anse); Dewey Dell Bundren (The daughter, pregnant, who fails to get an abortion); Vardaman Bundren (The youngest child, who says his mother is a fish)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Addie Bundren is dying and wants to be buried in Jefferson.
Her son Cash builds her coffin while she watches.
After she dies, flood and a broken bridge delay the wagon.
Vardaman, the youngest, says his mother is a fish.
The rotting body, a broken leg, a barn fire, and selfish aims pile up.
Darl, who narrates most, is taken away as insane.
Anse buries Addie, takes Dewey Dell's money, gets new teeth, and remarries at once.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A six-part religious poem depicting the difficult turn from worldly despair to Christian humility and prayer.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It is Eliot's first major long poem after his 1927 conversion to Anglo-Catholicism.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Penitent Speaker (A struggling Christian convert seeking spiritual forgiveness); The Lady of Silences (A silent, veiled mediator symbolizing divine grace and the Virgin Mary)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the first long poem of Eliot.
It is also referred as his conversation poem.
It is based on Dante's Purgatorio.
Vladimir Nabokov parodied Ash Wednesday in his Novel "Lolita"
His doctrine is identical with that of Gaeta or Vedantic Philosophy.
The speaker renounces earthly hope and material ambition.
Three white leopards feast on his flesh under a juniper tree.
He climbs three winding staircases, leaving behind sloth and sensual temptation.
He glimpses a veiled Lady of Silences who honors the Virgin Mary.
He meditates on the lost Word of God that the noisy world cannot hear.
The poem concludes with a humble prayer between rocks, asking not to be separated from God.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Auden's first regular book of poems, the 1930 Faber volume that made his name.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1930 is correct for the Faber book. The 1928 Spender printing is a different Poems, of about thirty copies. The 1933 second edition substitutes seven poems. The database edition trap is real.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Stephen Spender had hand printed a different, tiny Poems in 1928 for friends.
Faber published this new book in London in 1930, and it is the one exams mean.
It includes the charade Paid on Both Sides, a short play in verse.
The poems draw on Old English rhythm, saga, school life, Marx, and Freud.
A second edition in 1933 took out seven poems and put seven others in their place.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Six friends speak their inner thoughts from childhood to old age against the backdrop of crashing ocean waves.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database 1931 is correct. First published on 8 October 1931 by Hogarth Press. Database incorrectly flagged it as posthumous.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bernard (A phrasemaker and storyteller who provides the final summary); Louis (An Australian outsider who craves social order and historical continuity); Neville (An intellectual scholar and poet who seeks perfection in love); Jinny (A vivacious woman focused on physical beauty and movement); Susan (A woman of the countryside who loves nature and domestic motherhood); Rhoda (A shy and anxious dreamer who feels detached from the physical world); Percival (The idolized heroic friend who never speaks and dies by falling from a horse in India)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Six childhood friends grow up, take different life paths, and mourn the dead Percival.
Bernard tells stories, Neville loves poetry, and Louis seeks order in business.
Jinny chases bodily pleasure, Susan chooses farm life and motherhood, and Rhoda suffers from anxiety.
Bernard delivers an epic final monologue summing up identity and defying death.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A controlled future state makes people happy with breeding, sleep teaching, and a drug, until John the Savage rejects it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1932 is correct. Huxley wrote the novel in 1931 while living in France. Chatto and Windus published it in London in February 1932. He later answered it with the essay Brave New World Revisited in 1958 and with the novel Island in 1962.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John the Savage (Linda's son, raised outside the state and devoted to Shakespeare); Bernard Marx (An unhappy man of the top caste who brings John to London); Lenina Crowne (A contented hatchery worker whom John both desires and rejects); Mustapha Mond (The World Controller for Western Europe); Helmholtz Watson (A gifted writer who is exiled for wanting real thought)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel is written by Aldous Huxley in 1931 and published in 1932.
It is set in London of AD 2540.
The novel anticipates developments in Reproduction Technology, sleep - learning, psychological manipulation and classical conditioning that combine profoundly to change society.
Huxley answered this book with a re-assessment in an essay, Brave New World - Revisited (1958)
Its title is derived from Miranda's speech in William Shakespeare's The Tempest. Act V, scene I. "...wonder! How many godly creatures are There here! How beauteous mankind is! O Brave New World, That has such people in it".
It is fifth but first dystopian (dystopian means- the land that is not ideal) novel of Huxley.
This novel was inspired by the utopian novels of H.G. Wells' "A Modern Utopia" and "Men Like Gods" (1923).
In the year 632 After Ford, London breeds babies in bottles and sorts them into castes.
Sleep teaching and the drug soma keep people calm and cheerful.
Bernard Marx and Lenina Crowne visit a Savage Reservation in New Mexico.
They meet Linda and her son John, who knows the world mainly through Shakespeare.
John is taken to London, hates the empty pleasures, and argues with Mustapha Mond.
Mond defends stability and says John is asking for the right to be unhappy.
John withdraws, is hunted by crowds, and hangs himself.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Lena Grove searches for her baby's father while Joe Christmas is destroyed by a town's fear of race.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1932 is correct. Smith and Haas of New York published it in 1932. The London edition from Chatto and Windus came in 1933. The working title was Dark House.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lena Grove (A pregnant woman walking to Jefferson in trust that Burch will marry her); Joe Christmas (An orphan of uncertain race whose rage ends in a killing and his own death); Joanna Burden (A white woman from an abolitionist family, murdered after her affair with Christmas); Byron Bunch (A quiet mill worker who loves Lena and helps her); Gail Hightower (A disgraced former minister haunted by his grandfather's war); Lucas Burch (The father of Lena's child, living in Jefferson as Joe Brown)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Pregnant Lena Grove walks to Jefferson to find Lucas Burch.
Burch is there under the name Joe Brown, and Byron Bunch falls in love with Lena.
Joe Christmas, who believes he may be of mixed race, lives as an outcast.
He has an affair with Joanna Burden, and she is murdered.
Brown points the hunt at Christmas by calling him black.
