Percy Grimm, a cruel local captain, shoots Christmas and maims him.
Byron stays with Lena and the baby after Burch runs away again.

items.title: "New Bearings in English Poetry" (1932) — F. R. Leavis

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A critical book that maps a new path for modern English poetry.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1932 is the first edition. Chatto and Windus of London published it in 1932. A new edition followed in 1950. Do not learn 1950 as the first year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: F. R. Leavis (The critic who judges modern English poetry)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Leavis argues that much Victorian poetry sounds pretty but feels unreal.
He praises Gerard Manley Hopkins for hard and living language.
He studies T. S. Eliot and Ezra Pound as the new masters.
He also writes on W. B. Yeats and the younger poet Ronald Bottrall.
He asks readers to judge a poem by the life in its words.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1932 mix of prose and verse that studies English public life like a campaign.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1932 is correct. Faber, London, 1932. A slightly revised edition followed in 1934, and a further revision with a new preface in 1966. One Auden Society line that says 1930 is a slip. Britannica and the bibliography both say 1932.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The orator voices (Speakers who address England as if it were a troop, a school, or a sick body)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Faber published The Orators in London in 1932.
The subtitle is An English Study, and the book is dedicated to Stephen Spender.
The voices address England like leaders speaking to a group.
Prose and poems sit together and diagnose a sick public world.
Auden revised it in 1934 and again, with a new preface, in 1966.

items.title: "Down and Out in Paris and London" (1933) — George Orwell / Eric Blair

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Down and Out in Paris and London

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1933 memoir of hunger, cheap rooms, and odd jobs in Paris and London.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1933 is correct for publication. Victor Gollancz published it in London on 9 January 1933. The database calls the book poetry and places it in the poetry unit. That is wrong. It is prose report. The name Orwell comes from the River Orwell in East Anglia.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Narrator (Eric Blair writing as George Orwell, reporting his own hard months)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The narrator lives among the poor in a Paris lodging house.
He works as a dishwasher in hotel kitchens and stays nearly broke.
He returns to London and stays in spikes, which are poor shelters.
He walks with tramps and records how poverty shapes a day.
The book asks readers to see the very poor as full people.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first book, eighteen dense poems of body, birth, sex, and death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1934 is correct. The Poetry Foundation dates the book to December 1934. It is also called Eighteen Poems. The Sunday Referee and the Parton Bookshop issued it. He was twenty.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book came out in December 1934, just after he turned twenty.
Many pieces were rewritten from notebooks of his teen years.
The poems bind the human body to the processes of nature.
Creation and destruction sit inside the same images.
Readers found a new voice, often hard to follow at first.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Prison letters that teach world history to his daughter Indira.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1934 is correct. Wikipedia and Encyclopedia.com both date the book 1934. The letters were not posted from jail. He released them after he came out in 1933.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jawaharlal Nehru (The father writing history from prison); Indira Gandhi (His daughter, the reader the letters address)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nehru wrote 196 letters between 1930 and 1933 in several jails.
He addressed them to Indira, but he kept them until his release.
They continue an earlier set of letters published in 1929.
With few library books, he used notes and his own reading.
H. G. Wells helped shape the plan, but Nehru also stresses Asia.
The letters run from ancient times to the troubled 1930s.

items.title: "Murder on the Orient Express" (1934) — Agatha Christie

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poirot finds that every passenger helped to kill a man on a snowbound train.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1934 matches the UK book. Collins Crime Club published it on 1 January 1934. Dodd, Mead published the US edition on 28 February 1934 as Murder in the Calais Coach. That title avoided a clash with Graham Greene's Stamboul Train, which was called Orient Express in the United States. Britannica lists 1933. Keep 1934 for the UK book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hercule Poirot (The detective who is a passenger on the train); Ratchett (The murdered man, whose real name is Cassetti); Bouc (A director of the train company and Poirot's friend)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Poirot boards the Orient Express on his way back from the Middle East.
Snow stops the train.
The American Ratchett is found stabbed in his berth.
Ratchett is really Cassetti, a criminal tied to a kidnapped child's death.
Each suspect seems to have an alibi, and the clues point in too many directions.
Poirot concludes that the passengers shared the murder, each striking once.

items.title: "Tender Is the Night" (1934) — F. Scott Fitzgerald

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel about a brilliant doctor whose marriage and gift both fail.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1934 is correct for the first book. Scribner's Magazine serialized it from January to April 1934. The book appeared on 12 April 1934. Malcolm Cowley later rearranged it into time order, and that version came out in 1948. Learn 1934 as the first publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dick Diver (A gifted psychiatrist whose charm and strength wear out); Nicole Diver (Dick's wealthy wife, once his patient); Rosemary Hoyt (A young film actress who loves Dick)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dick and Nicole Diver seem to be the perfect couple on the French Riviera.
Young actress Rosemary Hoyt falls in love with Dick.
A flashback shows that Nicole was Dick's patient before she was his wife.
As Nicole grows stronger, Dick sinks into drink and loses his gift.
The marriage ends, and Dick fades into a small, failed life.

items.title: "Murder in the Cathedral" (1935) — T. S. Eliot

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A verse drama recounting the 1170 martyrdom of Archbishop Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database lists genre as Literary Criticism and unit as unit-8-literary-criticism. Those are database errors. This is a verse drama play. It premiered in June 1935 at Canterbury Cathedral and was published that same year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Becket (The Archbishop of Canterbury who dies for church authority); Chorus of Women of Canterbury (Working-class women whose chants represent common suffering and spiritual witness); The Four Tempters (Spiritual voices testing Becket with pleasure, power, political conspiracy, and glory); The Four Knights (King Henry II's barons who assassinate Becket and rationalize their act)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Archbishop Thomas Becket returns to Canterbury after seven years of exile in France.
The Chorus of Canterbury women expresses dread and foresees coming disaster.
Four tempters test Becket with worldly pleasures, high office, baronial alliance, and the pride of martyrdom.
Becket rejects all four temptations, recognizing that spiritual pride is the deadliest trap.
In an interlude on Christmas morning, Becket preaches on Christian peace and martyrdom.
Four knights sent by King Henry II murder Becket before the altar.
The knights step forward and address the audience like modern politicians to justify their crime.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A schoolboy novel about Swami, his friends, and cricket in colonial Malgudi.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1935 is correct. A biography says he wrote the draft in 1930. Hamish Hamilton published it in 1935 after Graham Greene recommended it. Greene also changed the title from Swami, the Tate.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Swaminathan (The schoolboy hero, usually called Swami); Mani (Swami's strong, careless classmate and old friend); Rajam (A wealthy police officer's son and captain of the cricket club); W. T. Srinivasan (Swami's father, a lawyer)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the first novel of the trilogy written by R.K.Narayan.
The novel is set in British India in a fictional town Malgudi. Graham Greene helped to publish this book.
Malgudi Schooldays is a slightly abridged version of Swami and Friends and it includes two additional stories featuring Swami from Malgudi Days and Under the Banyan Tree.
Swaminathan is a lazy ten year old at Albert Mission School.
His close friend is Mani.
A rich new boy, Rajam, joins the class.
Swami is drawn into a town protest and is later moved to another school.
The boys form a Malgudi Cricket Club.
Swami skips class for a match, is expelled, and runs away.
He comes home, but Rajam leaves town and their friendship breaks.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: One day in the life of Bakha, a young sweeper, shows the cruelty of untouchability.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1935 is correct. Wishart in London published the novel in 1935. Anand marks the writing time as 1933 at the end of the book. Forster, his friend, wrote the preface. The book was inspired by an aunt punished for eating with a Muslim woman.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bakha (A young sweeper and the centre of this one day novel); Sohini (Bakha's sister, assaulted by the temple priest); Lakha (Bakha's father and head of the local sweepers); Pundit Kali Nath (The priest who wants Sohini and then cries pollution); Mahatma Gandhi (Appears at the end to speak against untouchability)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel was inspired by his aunt's experience when she had a meal with a Muslim women and was treated as an outcast by his family.
It depicts a day in the life of 'Bakha', a young sweeper, who is untouchable due to his work of cleaning latrines.
The entire plot gives us the account of events happening in a single day in the life of Bakha. He doesn't like to do toilet cleaning but wants to do study and be a learned man. Lakha is the father of Bakha, who is a bit of antagonist in the novel, his profession is sweeper.
The outcasts were not allowed to draw water from wells, enter temples or basically touch anything, as it would make anything impure and corrupt.
In the end of the novel, Anand presents three answers to the malpractice of untouchability.
Bakha in offered to accept Christianity that has no caste system and so he will be no longer an outcaste. But Bakha fears changing his religion.
Sohini is the sister of Bakha.
Mahatma Gandhi comes to the village and educates everyone on untouchability.
In the concluding paragraph, a person randomly comes into the scene and informs everyone about a machine (perhaps toilet flush) that will clean faecal matters automatically.
Bakha thinks that this will be a solution to all his problems.
Bakha, son of the sweeper Lakha, cleans latrines in an army town.
A high caste man slaps him because Bakha forgot the warning call.
The priest Kali Nath assaults Bakha's sister Sohini, then accuses her.
Colonel Hutchinson tries to draw Bakha to Christianity, and Bakha slips away.
Bakha hears Gandhi speak against untouchability.
A poet then mentions the flush toilet, which could end the sweeper's filthy task.
Bakha goes home with that small hope.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Years later, several tellers rebuild the rise and bloody fall of Thomas Sutpen's design.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1936 is correct. Random House published the novel in New York in 1936. The London edition from Chatto and Windus came in 1937. Quentin's presence links it to The Sound and the Fury, but this book tells the Sutpen story.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Sutpen (A poor white man who tries to found a great house and is destroyed by his design); Rosa Coldfield (Ellen's younger sister, who first tells Quentin the story); Quentin Compson (The listener and reteller, also a main figure in The Sound and the Fury); Shreve (Quentin's Harvard roommate, who helps imagine the missing parts); Henry Sutpen (Sutpen's son, who kills Charles Bon); Charles Bon (Sutpen's rejected son from the West Indies marriage); Judith Sutpen (Sutpen's daughter, who was to marry Bon)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Thomas Sutpen comes to Mississippi to build a plantation and a dynasty.
He marries Ellen Coldfield and has Henry and Judith.
Henry's friend Charles Bon is engaged to Judith.
Sutpen reveals that Bon is his son from an earlier marriage, and that Bon is part black.
Henry kills Bon at the gate to stop the marriage, then disappears.
Sutpen later insults Wash Jones's granddaughter and is killed by Jones.
Quentin Compson retells the story to his Harvard roommate Shreve, and the house burns.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prison memoir of his mind, his family, and India's freedom struggle.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1936 is correct. John Lane, The Bodley Head, London, issued the first edition. Encyclopedia.com lists that 1936 book. A New York edition titled Towards Freedom appeared in 1941. A 1942 reprint added a chapter called Five years later.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jawaharlal Nehru (The narrator examining his life and the national movement); Mahatma Gandhi (The leader whose nonviolent methods shape Nehru's politics); Motilal Nehru (His father, a rich lawyer and Congress leader); Kamala Nehru (His wife, seriously ill while the book was being written)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nehru wrote almost the whole book in jail, from June 1934 to February 1935.
He says he wrote first to trace his own mental growth.
He begins with the family move from Kashmir toward Delhi and Agra.
Chapters cover Harrow, Cambridge, and his turn to Gandhi.
His wife Kamala's illness hangs over the writing.
London published it in 1936, and it sold widely in English.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1936 speech, printed as a book, that demands an end to caste.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1936 is correct. He published it himself on 15 May 1936. The 1937 edition adds his reply to Gandhi. The 1944 edition adds the 1916 paper Castes in India.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: B. R. Ambedkar (The speaker, addressing Hindus who still defend caste); Mahatma Gandhi (The critic answered in the 1937 edition, not in the first printing)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A Lahore reform group invited him to speak on caste in 1936.
He sent the text ahead, and the group asked him to cut harsh parts.
He refused to change a comma, and the meeting was cancelled.
He published the speech himself on 15 May 1936.
He says shared meals are not enough.
The religious idea of caste must go.
Gandhi answered in 1936. Ambedkar replied in the 1937 edition.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The orphan Munoo is worked to death as a poor servant and labourer.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1936 is correct. Lawrence and Wishart of London published it in 1936 as The Coolie. Later editions usually drop the word The. Munoo dies of tuberculosis at about fifteen. He is not Bakha.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Munoo (The orphan hero who is exploited from town to city and dies young)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book is highly critical of British rule in India and India's caste system.
The plot revolves around a 14-year old boy Munoo and his plight due to poverty and exploitation aided by social and political structure in place.
Munoo who at his early stage gets into obscurity of his own existence.
Munoo is a poor orphan boy pushed out to work.
He moves through jobs in Daulatpur, Bombay, and Simla.
Masters use his labour and pay him too little to live on.
The cruelty here is mainly poverty and greed, not the sweeper's caste.
City mills, servants' work, and a rickshaw life wear his body down.
He dies of tuberculosis while he is still a boy of about fifteen.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Anthony Beavis moves from empty society life toward pacifism, in chapters that jump across years.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1936 is correct. Chatto and Windus published the novel in 1936. The title is Milton's line, not a phrase Huxley invented. The chapters move back and forth in time.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Anthony Beavis (A sociologist who is the novel's centre); Brian Foxe (Anthony's kind school friend, whom Anthony betrays); Mary Amberley (An older woman and Helen's mother); Helen Amberley (Mary's daughter, with whom Anthony has an affair); Mark Staithes (A harsh, cynical friend drawn to political struggle)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel follows Anthony Beavis from boyhood into the middle of the 1930s.
Chapters jump among about 1902, 1914, 1928, and 1934.
He mourns his mother, betrays his friend Brian Foxe, and drifts through love affairs.
Mary Amberley and her daughter Helen draw him into a shallow social world.
His cynical friend Mark Staithes pulls him toward hard politics.
Anthony grows sick of violence and upper class emptiness.
He turns toward pacifism and a mystical search for meaning.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The late poems of 1936 to 1939, including Under Ben Bulben and his own epitaph.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates Last Poems and Two Plays to 1939. The Nobel list dates Macmillan's Last Poems and Plays to 1940. Yeats died on 28 January 1939, so both books are posthumous (printed after the writer's death).

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet (The aged speaker who addresses Irish poets and designs his grave)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
These poems were written in his last years, from 1936 to his death.
Under Ben Bulben tells Irish poets to learn their trade.
The same poem sets his epitaph (the words for his grave): cast a cold eye, horseman, pass by.
Politics, lust, rage, and a final plain ballad voice mix in the group.
The books of these poems appeared only after he died.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A critical book that rethinks the main line of English poetry.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1936 is correct. Chatto and Windus published it in London in 1936. It is a poetry book, not the novel book of 1948.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: F. R. Leavis (The critic who revalues the English poetic line)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Leavis looks again at English poetry from the seventeenth century onward.
He traces a witty line from Donne and the later poets.
A chapter on Milton questions Milton's effect on later verse.
He also writes on Pope and on eighteenth century poetry.
The book owes a debt to T. S. Eliot, yet the judgments are his own.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His second book, still drawn mostly from early notebooks, with a religious turn.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1936 is correct. The Poetry Foundation places publication in September 1936. A Welsh timeline gives 10 September 1936. Dent was the publisher. Only a few poems were wholly new.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dent published the book in September 1936.
Most poems were revised notebook pieces, not brand new work.
The ten sonnets called Altarwise by owl light use Christian story.
The book ends on the hopeful poem And death shall have no dominion.
Edith Sitwell's praise in the Sunday Times helped it sell.

items.title: "The Bachelor of Arts" (1937) — R. K. Narayan

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Chandran leaves college, loses a marriage plan, lives as a wandering holy man, and then returns.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1937 is correct. Nelson published The Bachelor of Arts in 1937. It follows Swami and Friends (1935).

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Chandran (A young graduate whose love, wanderings, and return fill the novel); Malathi (The woman he hopes to marry, until horoscopes block the match); Sushila (The woman he meets after he comes home)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Chandran finishes college in Malgudi and falls in love with Malathi.
Her family rejects him because of a horoscope fear called Mangala Dosha.
Malathi marries someone else.
Chandran goes to Madras, lives roughly, and becomes a sanyasi (a wandering holy man).
After eight months he remembers his parents and comes home.
He then agrees to meet Sushila and loves her at first sight.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A quiet hobbit joins dwarves and a wizard to face a dragon and come home changed.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1937 is correct. Wikipedia dates the Allen and Unwin edition 21 September 1937. The Tolkien Society also dates publication 1937. He had finished the tale by late 1932.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bilbo Baggins (A hobbit who loves his quiet home and becomes the company's burglar); Gandalf (The wizard who pushes Bilbo into the quest); Thorin Oakenshield (The dwarf leader who claims the mountain and its gold); Smaug (The dragon who stole the dwarf kingdom); Gollum (A cave creature who loses a magic ring to Bilbo)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bilbo Baggins lives a safe life until Gandalf arrives.
Thorin and twelve other dwarves want their mountain treasure back.
The dragon Smaug sleeps on that gold under the Lonely Mountain.
Lost underground, Bilbo finds a ring and wins a riddle game with Gollum.
Bilbo sees a gap in the dragon's hide, and Bard kills Smaug.
The Battle of Five Armies follows.
Thorin dies, and Bilbo goes home.

items.title: "Two Leaves and a Bud" (1937) — Mulk Raj Anand

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A peasant who comes to an Assam tea estate is shot while defending his daughter.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1937 is correct. Lawrence and Wishart of London published it in 1937. The story is set on an Assam tea estate. A later Hindi film, Rahi, was based on it and was also released in English as The Wayfarer.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gangu (A Punjabi peasant who is killed while protecting his daughter); Leila (Gangu's daughter, pursued by the British officer); Sajani (Gangu's wife, who dies of cholera on the estate); Budhu (Gangu's son); Reggie Hunt (The British officer who shoots Gangu); John de la Harve (The estate doctor who protests against the workers' conditions)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gangu, a peasant of Hoshiarpur, loses his land to debt.
He takes his wife Sajani, daughter Leila, and son Budhu to a tea estate in Assam.
The promised good pay is a trap.
The family lives in filth and debt.
The doctor John de la Harve begs the manager to improve the workers' lot.
Cholera kills Sajani.
Gangu cannot even borrow for her rites.
The British officer Reggie Hunt chases Leila.
Gangu tries to stop him and is shot.
A court of Englishmen finds Hunt not guilty.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An old woman tells how Gandhi's call changes a South Indian village bound by caste.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1938 is correct. George Allen and Unwin published Kanthapura in London in 1938. Oxford University Press reprinted it in Bombay in 1947. That reprint is not the first edition. The foreword is the usual source of the line about not writing like the English.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Achakka (The old woman who narrates the whole village tale); Moorthy (A young Brahmin who brings Gandhi's teaching into Kanthapura); Rangamma (A widow who shelters Moorthy and leads the women); Narasamma (Moorthy's mother, who dies after he is cast out); Bade Khan (The policeman at the coffee estate); Kenchamma (The village goddess whom the people trust)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel is narrated by Achakka in the form of "Sthalapurana". Achakka is an old village woman.
Kanthapura is a traditional caste ridden Indian village which is away from all modern ways of living.
The village is believed to have protected by a local deity called "Kenchamma"
The protagonist of the novel "Moorthy" is a Brahmin who discovered a half-burried 'Linga' from the village and installed it. A temple is built there which became the center point of village life.
Hari-Katha was a traditional form of storytelling practiced in the village.
A man named 'Jayaramachar' narrated Hari-Katha based on Gandhi and his ideals.
The narrator was arrested because of political propaganda instilled in the story.
The novel begins its course of action when Moorthy leaves for the city where he got familiar with Gandhian philosophy through pamphlets and other literatures.
He followed Gandhian spirit, discarded foreign cloths and fought against untouchability.
At the end of the novel, it is mentioned that the people of Kanthapura are settled in Kashipur and Kanthapura was occupied by people from Bombay.
Achakka, an old village woman, tells the story of Kanthapura.
The village goddess is Kenchamma.
Caste still divides the streets.
Moorthy, a young Brahmin, returns from the city as a follower of Gandhi.
He wears khadi (cloth made at home), rejects foreign goods, and is cast out.
Women led by Rangamma keep the struggle going while Moorthy is in prison.
Police burn and break the village.
Moorthy later loses his simple faith in Gandhi's way.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A political essay arguing that women's education and public freedom are essential to stop war and fascism.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1938 is correct, but misclassified as Poetry. First published on 2 June 1938 by Hogarth Press. Sequel in spirit to A Room of One's Own.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Narrator (An educated woman responding to a male lawyer's letter about world peace)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Woolf receives a letter from an educated gentleman asking how to prevent war.
She donates one guinea to help rebuild a women's college.
She donates a second guinea to help professional women find jobs.
She gives the third guinea to an anti-war society while founding a Society of Outsiders for women.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1938 textbook, written with Robert Penn Warren, that teaches the poem as a poem.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Their earlier booklet grew into An Approach to Literature. This poetry book came out in 1938.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Cleanth Brooks (Co author who presses readers to study the poem's own words); Robert Penn Warren (Co author, poet, and partner in the textbook and The Southern Review)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Brooks and Warren saw that students read poems like ads or news notes.
They built a textbook of poems, questions, and close readings.
They tell teachers to start from the poem, not from a life story.
A paraphrase or a moral lesson can help, but it is not the end.
The book carried New Criticism into American college classrooms.

items.title: "And Then There Were None" (1939) — Agatha Christie

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ten guilty strangers are killed one by one on an island, with no detective to save them.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1939 is the UK book year. Collins Crime Club published it on 6 November 1939 under an older title that is now rejected as racist. The first US edition, in 1940, was called And Then There Were None from the start. Later editions in both countries use that title. Use And Then There Were None in exam answers.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Justice Wargrave (A retired judge who plans the murders and then kills himself); Vera Claythorne (A former governess who is the last of the guests to die); Dr Armstrong (A doctor tricked into helping Wargrave fake his death); Philip Lombard (A soldier of fortune whom Vera shoots near the end)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ten people are invited to a lonely island off the Devon coast.
A record accuses each of them of causing a death that the law did not punish.
They die in turn, and each death matches a line of a nursery rhyme.
Justice Wargrave seems to die with the others, but he is the killer.
A confession in a bottle tells how he faked his death and then killed himself.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dream book in invented language about a Dublin family and all history.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Joyce began the book in 1923 and worked on it for about sixteen years. Parts appeared as Work in Progress from 1924. Faber and Faber published the book in May 1939. The database year 1939 is the book year. The title has no apostrophe.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker (The father, often called HCE, who dreams the book); Anna Livia Plurabelle (The mother, whose flow is like the river Liffey); Shem (One son, the writer and outcast); Shaun (The other son, the public man and rival); Issy (The daughter, who appears in split and teasing forms)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
7- Stephan Hero (1944): It is the first edition of the novel A Portrait of an Artist as a Young Man.
It is considered as Joyce's most comprehensible novel. Harold called it "Masterpiece of Joyce".
Joyce invented a unique polyglot language or idioglossia solely for the purpose of this work. Posthumous Publications: Stephan Hero (1944): It is a precursor to "A Portrait of an Artist as a Young Man", written in 1904-06 and it is an autobiographical novel. Giacomo Joyce: It is written in 1907 but published in 1968 in Faber and Faber.
The book is a night dream, not a daytime story like Ulysses.
Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker, a pub keeper, is the dreaming father.
Anna Livia Plurabelle is the mother, linked with the river Liffey.
Their sons Shem and Shaun fight as rivals through history.
The last sentence runs into the first, so the book is a circle.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A vast epic in blank verse on Savitri's victory over Death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database says book editions 1939-40. Those years belong to The Life Divine, not to Savitri. The earliest known manuscript is 1916. Separate cantos appeared from 1946. Part One of the first edition was published in 1950, shortly before his death on 5 December 1950. The rest of the poem came out in 1951. A single volume edition followed in 1954.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Savitri (The heroine who confronts Death to save her husband); Satyavan (Her husband, doomed to die young); Aswapati (Savitri's father, a king on a long spiritual search); Death (The power that claims Satyavan and debates with Savitri)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The earliest known manuscript is dated 1916.
Aurobindo turns the Mahabharata legend into a symbol of spiritual victory.
King Aswapati seeks a higher consciousness for the earth.
Savitri marries Satyavan, who is fated to die within a year.
She faces Death and wins her husband back.
The poem also pictures a divine life on earth.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: General Sternwood hires Philip Marlowe to stop a blackmailer and to face a family murder.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1939 is right for the Knopf book. A first draft existed by May 1938. Parts reuse stories from 1935 and 1936. The title is a soft name for death.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Philip Marlowe (The private detective who tells the story in his own voice); General Sternwood (A rich, ill old man who hires Marlowe); Carmen Sternwood (The wild younger daughter who killed Rusty Regan); Vivian Regan (The older daughter who helps hide that killing)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Old General Sternwood asks Marlowe to handle a blackmail threat against his daughter Carmen.
Marlowe finds the blackmailer, Arthur Geiger, shot dead, and Carmen drugged beside a camera.
The Sternwood chauffeur, Owen Taylor, is found dead in a car in the water.
Marlowe traces nude photos, a casino owner named Eddie Mars, and more killings.
He learns Carmen killed Rusty Regan, and Vivian helped hide the body.
The book never answers who killed the chauffeur.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A verse drama about Harry, Lord Monchensey, who returns to his family home haunted by the Furies.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database lists genre as Literary Criticism and unit as unit-8-literary-criticism. Those are database errors. This is a verse drama play. It premiered in March 1939 at the Westminster Theatre and was published in March 1939 by Faber and Faber.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Harry, Lord Monchensey (A nobleman haunted by guilt who seeks spiritual cleansing); Amy, Dowager Lady Monchensey (Harry's controlling mother who wishes to keep the family past unchanged); Agatha (Harry's perceptive aunt who guides him toward truth and spiritual freedom)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The family gathers at their English estate Wishwood to celebrate the birthday of Amy, Dowager Lady Monchensey.
Amy hopes her eldest son Harry will return to take charge of the family estate.
Harry arrives in deep torment, believing he pushed his wife off a passenger ship.
He is constantly pursued by the unseen Furies (ancient Greek spirits of vengeance).
His insightful Aunt Agatha reveals that Harry's father had once wished to murder Amy.
Harry realizes that he is carrying the inherited guilt of his family.
He chooses spiritual pilgrimage, transforming the Furies into guiding angels of redemption.
Amy dies from the shock of Harry's departure.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Auden's 1940 book of songs and public poems from the edge of the Second World War.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1940 is correct for both the London and New York editions. The edition trap is real because Auden revised many of these poems later. Musee des Beaux Arts and Spain 1937 are inside this book, but each also has an earlier printing.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Faber in London and Random House in New York published it in 1940.
It is dedicated to Chester Kallman.
It collects lyrics and topical poems written as war began.
Musee des Beaux Arts and the revised Spain 1937 both stand in this book.
Auden later revised or dropped some of these poems, so editions differ.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Marlowe follows huge Moose Malloy, who is searching Los Angeles for his old love Velma.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1940 is right. Chandler worked from June 1939, destroyed a draft, and finished in spring 1940. Knopf published the book in 1940.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Philip Marlowe (The detective who follows both the Malloy case and a jewel murder); Moose Malloy (A huge ex-convict looking for Velma); Velma Valento (Malloy's old girlfriend, now living as Mrs Lewin Lockridge Grayle); Anne Riordan (A policeman's daughter who helps Marlowe)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Moose Malloy storms into a club, kills the owner, and hunts for Velma Valento.
Marlowe is hired around a jewel ransom and is knocked out beside a dead man.
Anne Riordan helps him, and the trail leads to rich Mrs Grayle.
Crooked Bay City police drug Marlowe, and he later finds Moose again.
Mrs Grayle is Velma.
She shoots Moose and later kills herself when cornered.

items.title: "For Whom the Bell Tolls" (1940) — Ernest Hemingway

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An American volunteer tries to blow up a bridge in the Spanish Civil War.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1940 is correct. Charles Scribner's Sons published the novel on 21 October 1940. Hemingway finished the draft in July 1940. The database posthumous badge is wrong. He died in 1961. The Pulitzer board gave no novel prize in 1941 after a dispute over this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Robert Jordan (American volunteer and explosives expert); Maria (Young Spanish woman whom Jordan loves); Pilar (Strong woman who leads the hidden fighting group in practice); Pablo (Leader who first fears the bridge attack)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel tells the story of Robert Jordan, a young American in the International Brigades attached to a republican guerrilla unit during Spanish Civil War.
Robert is assigned to blow up a bridge during an attack on the city.
The Book's title is taken from the metaphysical poet John Donne's Devotions upon Emergent Occasions.
Robert Jordan, an American teacher, joins a small hidden fighting group.
He is ordered to destroy a bridge before an attack.
He loves Maria, a young woman hurt by the war.
Pilar supports the plan, while Pablo first resists and then returns.
Jordan is wounded after the blast and stays behind so the others can escape.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Villagers stage an outdoor historical play at a country manor on the eve of World War II.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1941 is correct. Posthumously published by Hogarth Press on 17 July 1941. Woolf finished the manuscript just before her death in March 1941.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bartholomew Oliver (The elderly retired Indian Civil Service officer of Pointz Hall); Mrs. Swithin (Lucy) (Bartholomew's religious, daydreaming sister who reads an outline of history); Giles Oliver (Bartholomew's anxious stockbroker son); Isa Oliver (Giles's wife who secretly writes poetry and feels trapped in her marriage); Miss La Trobe (The passionate, troubled director and author of the village pageant)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Oliver family and their neighbors gather at Pointz Hall in June 1939.
Miss La Trobe directs an outdoor pageant reviewing English history from Chaucer to the present.
During the final act, actors turn mirrors onto the audience to reveal modern human confusion.
Night falls, warplanes rumble overhead, and Giles and Isa Oliver prepare to speak in the dark.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A suite of four meditative poems reflecting on time, human history, mystical experience, and the Christian Incarnation.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The four poems appeared individually between 1936 and 1942. They were first published together as a single volume in 1943 by Harcourt, Brace and Company.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Meditative Speaker (A mature poet contemplating the mystery of time and spiritual devotion); The Compound Ghost (A composite dead master poet encountered on London streets during a bombing raid)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
13- Criterion: An Imperial Epic.
Burnt Norton explores time present and time past, visiting a quiet English rose garden.
East Coker meditates on family ancestry, cyclic history, and human mortality in rural England.
The Dry Salvages uses the Mississippi river and Massachusetts coastal rocks to explore human journey and memory.
Little Gidding reflects on prayer, war, and the burning love of the Holy Spirit during air raids.
The poet encounters a compound ghost (a composite master poet) walking in ruined London streets.
The sequence resolves with the mystical vision that all shall be well when fire and rose become one.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His most famous Spanish story collection, first gathered in 1944 and enlarged in 1956.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The 1944 book joins The Garden of Forking Paths with Artifices. The 1956 edition adds three stories. Grove Press published the English Ficciones in 1962.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator Borges (A voice that often shares the author's name but is not a plain confession); Pierre Menard (A modern writer who attempts to produce Don Quixote anew); Funes (A man who remembers every detail and cannot think in general ideas)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The 1941 book The Garden of Forking Paths supplied the first group of tales.
In 1944 Borges added a second group, Artifices, and called the whole Ficciones.
Stories invent false books, infinite libraries, and detectives who misread clues.
Pierre Menard tries to write Don Quixote again, word for word.
The 1956 edition adds three tales, including The South.
An English translation of the whole book appeared in 1962.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Farm animals drive out the farmer and then fall under a pig dictator.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1945 is correct for the British book. Secker and Warburg published it on 17 August 1945. The title page of the first printing says May 1945, but copies were not issued then. The United States edition followed in 1946. Several publishers had refused the book during the war.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Napoleon (Pig who becomes the tyrant, often read as Stalin); Snowball (Pig rival who is expelled, often read as Trotsky); Boxer (Hardworking horse who trusts the leaders too long); Squealer (Pig who rewrites the rules and spreads propaganda (lies that serve power)); Old Major (Old boar whose speech starts the rebellion)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
vi)
It was published after War World II in 1945 in England and in 1946 in United States.
It is a dystopian novella having the original title "Animal Farm: A Fairy Story". (Utopia means: An ideal place; Dystopia means: a not good place)
It is an allegorical novella, which according to Orwell, reflects events leading up to the Russian Revolution of 1917, and then into the Stalin era in the Soviet Union.
Orwell wrote this book from Nov 1943 to Feb 1944 when the wartime alliance with the Soviet Union was as its height and Stalin was regarded highly by the British people, a circumstance that Orwell hated.
Its publication was delayed because it was rejected by various publishers.
It won Hugo Award in 1996.
Famous Quote: "All animals are equal, but some are more equal than others"
"Napoleon" stands for Stalin and "Snowball" stands for Trotsky. Plot:.
One night all the animals assembled in a barn at Mr. Jones Manor Farm, to hear Old Major, a pig, to describe his dream he had about a world where all animals live free from tyranny of their human masters.
Old Major dies soon after the meeting but all the animals were inspired by his philosophy of animalism, plot a rebellion against Jones.
Two pigs Snowball and Napoleon prove themselves important figures and planners of this dangerous enterprise.
The revolution occurs when Jones forgets to feed the animals, as a result Mr. Jones and his men are chased off the farm.
Manor farm was renamed as "Animal Farm" and the "Seven Commandments of Animalism" are painted on the barn wall.
Initially the rebellion was a great success and animals used to meet every Sunday to debate the farm policy.
The pigs become the supervisors because of their intelligence.
Napoleon along with another pig Squealer, persuades the other animals that the pigs are always moral and correct in their decisions.
Jones and his men return to Animal Farm to retake it but with the tactics of Snowball, animals defeat Jones and his battle became known as "The Battle of Cowshed".
Mollie, a vain horse is lured off the farm by another human.
Snowball plans to bring electricity in the farm but Napoleon opposes it.
Napoleon summons a pack of ferocious dogs who chase Snowball off the farm forever.
Napoleon announces that Windmill (for producing electricity) will be built in the farm and he lies that it is his own idea (actually it was Snowball's idea).
Boxer, a horse proves himself to be most valuable in building the windmill. He represents Working Class.
Mr. Pilkington represents the Capitalists. Mr. Fredrick represents Hitler in it.
Jones forsakes the farm and moves to another part of the country.
Napoleon hires a solicitor and begins trading with neighboring farms.
A heavy storm topples the windmill and Napoleon blames Snowball for this but the animals re-build it.
Now Napoleon has become a dictator and kills innocent animals in front of the entire farm.
Napoleon and other pigs move into Jones' house and sleep in his bed.
The other animals receive less and less food while the pigs grow fatter.
When the windmill is completed in August he sells a pile of timber to Jones; Frederick, a neighboring farmer who pays him forged notes.
Frederick and his men attack the windmill and explode it but they are defeated.
The seven commandments of animalism are broken by pigs and the language of the commandments are changed, as "No animal shall drink alcohol" is changed to "No animal shall dink alcohol to excess"
Boxer, horse again puts his strength in building the windmill but he is exhausted, Napoleon sells him to a knacker (glue boiler).
Squealer makes the animals believe that Boxer had died a peaceful death.
Year passes and Napoleon expands the farm boundaries by purchasing two more fields, but the life of all animals except pigs, went worse.
Eventually pigs begin to walk in their hind legs and take many qualities of their farmer human oppressors.
Seven commandments are reduced to a single law: "All animals are equal, but some are more equal than others"
The novel ends with Pilkington sharing drinks with the pigs in Jones' house.
Napoleon changes the farm name to Manor Farm.
Napoleon quarrels with Pilkington in a cards game and other animals watch them from outside the window. The following characters represents:.
Old Major - Karl Marx.
Napoleon - Stalin.
Snowball - Leon Trotsky.
Mr. Pilkington - Winston Churchill "1984" (1949)
Old Major teaches the animals to rebel against Mr Jones.
Snowball and Napoleon lead the new farm after the rebellion.
Napoleon drives Snowball out and rules with the help of Squealer.
Boxer, the loyal horse, is sold when he is no longer useful.
The pigs walk like men, and the old equality slogan is twisted.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An English lecturer loses his wife and slowly finds peace through grief and a spiritual link.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1945 is correct. Eyre and Spottiswoode published it in 1945. Rajam died in 1939. The book uses that grief, but 1939 is not the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Krishna (The English teacher and narrator, close to Narayan himself); Susila (Krishna's wife, whose death drives the story); Leela (Their young daughter); The headmaster (A school leader who cares more for pupils than for his own home)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Krishna teaches English at Albert Mission College in Malgudi.
His wife Susila and their child Leela come to live with him.
Susila dies of typhoid, and Krishna is broken by grief.
A stranger claims he can carry messages from Susila.
Krishna also learns from a headmaster who puts pupils first.
He ends with a moment of rare immutable joy.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His best known poetry book, clearer lyrics of war, childhood, and Wales.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1946 is correct. Britannica and the Poetry Foundation both give 1946. Dent published it. Do not go gentle is not in this book. That poem was printed in 1951.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dent published the book in 1946, and it sold quickly.
The poems are less packed than the work of the 1930s.
Fern Hill and Poem in October recover a childhood in Wales.
A Refusal to Mourn answers the death of a child in the London bombing.
The Hunchback in the Park remembers a lonely figure from Swansea.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prison search for India's past, culture, and unity under British rule.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1946 is correct. Wikipedia says he wrote it in Ahmednagar Fort and that Signet Press, Calcutta, issued it in March 1946. The same page's box also prints 14 November 1946. Encyclopedia.com lists the 1946 Signet Press edition. The safe exam year is 1946.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jawaharlal Nehru (The prisoner narrator searching India's past); India (The culture he treats as a living presence, not only a map); Abul Kalam Azad (A fellow prisoner whose talk helped the book)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nehru wrote it at Ahmednagar Fort after the Quit India call of 1942.
He reads India's story from the Indus valley to his own time.
He asks what still binds many different people into one India.
Fellow prisoners, including Abul Kalam Azad, helped him think and correct pages.
The book sees India as both a real country and an old idea.
Signet Press in Calcutta published it in 1946, before independence.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1947 novel of the Bengal famine and the Quit India struggle.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1947 is correct. South Asian Britain lists a London edition from Victor Gollancz in 1947. Wikipedia lists Hind Kitabs in 1947. The exam year is 1947 either way. The slug omits the exclamation mark of the printed title So Many Hungers!

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kajoli (A village girl who rejects being sold and later sells newspapers); Rahoul (A Cambridge trained scientist who chooses the nationalist path); Devata (Rahoul's grandfather, a Gandhian who lives among the peasants of Baruni)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story is set in Bengal during the 1943 famine and the Quit India movement.
Kajoli, a village girl, is driven toward shame by hunger and then refuses that life.
She turns instead to selling newspapers in the city.
Rahoul, a scientist trained at Cambridge, leaves pure study for the national struggle.
His grandfather Devata, a Gandhian, brings satyagraha (nonviolent protest) to the village of Baruni.
The title joins the hunger for food with the hunger for freedom.

items.title: "The Age of Anxiety" (1947) — W. H. Auden

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long wartime poem of lonely voices, which won the Pulitzer Prize.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1947 is correct for the first edition, New York, Random House. The London Faber edition is 1948. The Pulitzer Prize followed in 1948. Do not answer 1948 as the first publication year.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Random House published it in New York in 1947.
Faber published the London edition in 1948.
Auden calls it a baroque eclogue, meaning an ornate poem of speaking parts.
The speaking parts explore isolation and spiritual emptiness in the modern age.
It won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1948.
The title later became a common name for modern worry itself.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1947 book of close readings that attacks the heresy of paraphrase.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1947 is correct. Many essays had appeared earlier. The book gathers them and states the paraphrase argument.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Cleanth Brooks (The critic who reads each poem from the inside)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Brooks reads famous English poems as whole structures, not as messages.
The first chapter treats poetic language as the language of paradox.
He reads Donne, Shakespeare, Pope, Wordsworth, Keats, Tennyson, and Yeats.
He says a poem cannot be swapped for a plain prose summary.
The closing chapter names that mistake the heresy of paraphrase.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A critical book that names a short line of great English novelists.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1948 is correct. The subtitle names George Eliot, Henry James, and Joseph Conrad. Austen opens the line, and Lawrence is added in the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: F. R. Leavis (The critic who draws the line of the English novel)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In The Great Tradition Leavis names Jane Austen, George Elliot, Henry James and Joseph Conrad as the great novelists. He said that Charles Dickens, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Herman Melville and Edgar Allen Poe are their successors.
By the end of the essay. Leavis amended the list of the greatest novelists and included D. H. Lawrence as their successor.
He stressed the importance of these novelists placed on 'a reverent openness before life.'
In this essay Leavis dismisses significant British authors as:.
Henry Fielding: His subject matter and interests are too limited.
Samuel Richardson: His subject matter is also limited and his work demands too much of the readers time.
George Moore: He is too concerned with style.
The Trollopes (Frances and Anthony) - They couldn't understand and appreciate Austen.
James Joyce: His works lack an organic form.
Charlotte Bronte: She couldn't see why any value should be attached to Jane Austen.
Emily Bronte: Wuthering Heights seems like 'a kind of sport' to Leavis and she only inspired a minor tradition.
Leavis says the great English novelists form one moral tradition.
He names Jane Austen, George Eliot, Henry James, and Joseph Conrad.
He adds D. H. Lawrence as the great modern novelist in that line.
He praises Dickens as a genius, but calls him a great entertainer.
He leaves Thomas Hardy outside this central line of the novel.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Winston Smith rebels against a state that watches, rewrites, and tortures.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1949 is correct. Secker and Warburg published the novel in London on 8 June 1949. It was his last novel. He died on 21 January 1950, so the book is not posthumous. The printed title joins the two number words with a hyphen.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Winston Smith (Outer Party worker who tries to resist); Julia (Young woman who becomes Winston's lover); O'Brien (Inner Party man who pretends to help and then tortures Winston); Big Brother (Face of the Party, whether a real man or a symbol)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Non Fictions: 1- Down and Out in Paris and London (1933)
Winston Smith lives in Airstrip One under the Party and Big Brother.
He works at the Ministry of Truth, changing old records.
He loves Julia and tries to join a secret resistance.
O'Brien traps him, and the Ministry of Love breaks him by torture.
Winston ends by loving Big Brother, and the rebellion fails.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A verse comedy about an unhappy married couple and their guests guided by an enigmatic psychiatrist-priest.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database lists genre as Literary Criticism and unit as unit-8-literary-criticism. Those are database errors. This is a verse drama play. It premiered at the Edinburgh Festival in August 1949 and was published in March 1950 by Faber and Faber.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sir Henry Harcourt-Reilly (The mysterious psychiatrist who acts as a spiritual healer and moral guide); Edward Chamberlayne (A self-absorbed barrister (lawyer) who cannot experience true love); Lavinia Chamberlayne (Edward's sharp wife who fears she is unlovable); Celia Coplestone (A young poet who gives up society life to become a Christian martyr in Africa)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Elements of the play are based on Alcestis, by ancient Greek playwright Euripides.
It is the most popular play of Eliot in his lifetime (total 7 plays).
It received the 1950 Tony Award for best play.
The comedy centers round the fortunes of Mr. Edward Chamberlayne and Lavinia Chamberlayne, who are separated after five years of marriage.
Their problem is a usual conflict between husband and wife.
Edward Chamberlayne hosts a London cocktail party alone because his wife Lavinia has just left him.
An Unidentified Guest at the party drinks gin and offers Edward unexpected advice on marriage.
The Unidentified Guest is later revealed to be the famous psychiatrist Sir Henry Harcourt-Reilly.
Reilly brings Edward and Lavinia together in his consulting room to face their mutual flaws.
Edward and Lavinia choose the common path of reconciliation and tolerance in ordinary domestic life.
Edward's former lover Celia Coplestone chooses the higher spiritual path of Christian devotion and missionary martyrdom.
Two years later, the Chamberlaynes host another cocktail party in peace.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Prose essays that explain the teaching of the Bhagavad Gita.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It is wrong here. The first series ran in the Arya from August 1916 to July 1918. The book of that series came out in Madras in 1922. The second series ran from August 1918 to July 1920, and its revised book came out in 1928. Britannica dates the essays 1922, which is the first book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Krishna (The divine teacher whose words the essays explain); Arjuna (The warrior disciple who hesitates before the battle); Sri Aurobindo (The commentator who interprets the Gita for modern readers)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The essays ran in the Arya in two series, from 1916 to 1920.
The first series covers the opening six chapters of the Gita.
Arjuna shrinks from killing his kinsmen on the field of Kurukshetra.
Krishna teaches duty without desire for reward, and a divine birth in age after age.
Aurobindo reads the battle as the soul's struggle, not only as a war story.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Linked stories about Americans settling Mars while Earth slides toward ruin.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1950 is correct for the Doubleday book. The British edition of 1951 is titled The Silver Locusts and changes some stories. A 1997 edition moves the inner dates forward by 31 years, from 1999-2026 to 2030-2057. The database calls the book non fictional prose. That label is wrong. It is fiction, Unit 3.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ylla (A Martian woman who dreams of the coming Earth men); Spender (An Earth man on a later expedition who turns against the settlers); The automated house (The empty house in There Will Come Soft Rains, still keeping its routine)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Doubleday published the book in the United States in 1950.
An editor urged Bradbury to join older Mars stories, as Anderson joined town tales.
Early expeditions meet Martians, and human disease destroys most of them.
Settlers try to rebuild American towns on Mars.
Nuclear war wrecks Earth.
A few humans remain to start again.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A romantic verse play on the princess Vasavadutta and King Vuthsa.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database says early 20th century and sorts the play at 1950. The manuscript says it was written between 18 and 30 October 1915 and revised from 8 to 17 April 1916. He declined to print it when publication was proposed. The first edition appeared in 1957, in the Sri Aurobindo Mandir Annual and as a separate book. That is seven years after his death.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Vasavadutta (The princess whose love changes a political plot); Vuthsa (The king of the Kathasaritsagara legend, also called Udayana)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Aurobindo takes the plot from Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara, a Sanskrit story cycle.
He wrote the play in Pondicherry in October 1915 and revised it in April 1916.
A rival king tries to master Vuthsa by a trick rather than by open war.
Princess Vasavadutta is drawn into that plan, but she and Vuthsa fall in love.
Love, not force, joins the two sides.
The first printed book came only in 1957.

items.title: "Montage of a Dream Deferred" (1951) — Langston Hughes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1951 book length poem of one Harlem day, cut like a bebop record.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1951 is correct. Holt published Montage of a Dream Deferred in 1951. The poem Harlem, also called A Dream Deferred, appears in this book. Lorraine Hansberry took her play title from that poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Harlem voices (Neighbors, lovers, preachers, and street speakers across one day); The speaker of Harlem (The voice that lists what a delayed dream might do)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Henry Holt published the book in 1951.
Hughes asks the reader to take about ninety short poems as one long poem.
The day runs from dawn to the next dawn in Harlem.
Bebop breaks, shouts, and street voices interrupt one another.
The famous short poem Harlem asks what happens to a dream deferred.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A study of how racism and colonial rule wound a person's mind and language.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Editions du Seuil published the French book in 1952. Charles Lam Markmann translated it, and Grove Press issued that English text in 1967. A later English version by Richard Philcox appeared in 2008. Exams usually want 1952 and 1967.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Frantz Fanon (The essayist, speaking as a psychiatrist and a colonized man)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Fanon asks how a black person is taught to desire a white world.
He studies language, because colonial speech can make people feel inferior.
He uses stories from psychiatry to show shame, anger, and desire.
He rejects the idea that black people have one fixed nature.
He ends by asking the body to keep him a man who questions.

items.title: "The Old Man and the Sea" (1952) — Ernest Hemingway

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Old Man and the Sea

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An old Cuban fisherman hooks a giant marlin and then loses it to sharks.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1952 is correct. He wrote it in Cuba from December 1950 to February 1951. Life magazine printed the whole story on 1 September 1952. Scribner's published the book on 8 September 1952. It won the Pulitzer Prize in 1953. The database calls it posthumous. That is wrong. He died in 1961.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Santiago (Old Cuban fisherman who will not give up); Manolin (Boy who loves Santiago and looks after him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He got Pulitzer Prize for this novel in 1953.
It was the last work of Hemingway of fiction.
The novel is centered upon Santiago, an aging fisherman who struggles with a giant Marlin far out in the gulf Stream.
Santiago assistant is Manolin. Famous Quote from 'Old Man and the Sea' "A man can be destroyed but not defeated."
Santiago has caught nothing for 84 days.
The boy Manolin still cares for him, though he must fish on another boat.
On the next day Santiago hooks a huge marlin far out at sea.
He kills the fish after a long fight, then sharks eat the meat.
He returns with the skeleton, and the boy promises to fish with him again.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In a future state, fireman Guy Montag burns books, then chooses to save them.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1953 is the novel. Galaxy Science Fiction printed the shorter The Fireman in February 1951. Ballantine Books published the novel in October 1953. From 1967 a school edition cut words. Bradbury forced a return to the full text in 1980. The Martian Chronicles note does not belong on this novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Guy Montag (The fireman who stops burning books and starts hiding them); Clarisse McClellan (The curious neighbor who makes Montag question his life); Mildred Montag (Montag's wife, lost in television and sleeping pills); Captain Beatty (The fire chief who defends censorship and is burned by Montag); Faber (A former professor who helps Montag understand books); Granger (Leader of the exiles who remember books by heart)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Guy Montag is a fireman whose job is to burn hidden books.
His neighbor Clarisse and a woman who dies with her books unsettle him.
His wife Mildred lives inside wall sized television shows.
Captain Beatty explains how speed, media, and fear killed reading.
Montag kills Beatty, flees, and joins exiles who memorize books.
War destroys the city.
The exiles walk back to rebuild.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An adult story collection whose polite people commit strange, funny, and cruel acts.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1953 is right for the Knopf collection. Some stories are older magazine pieces. A revised edition appeared in 1961. This is not a children's book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mary Maloney (The pregnant wife in Lamb to the Slaughter who hides a murder as dinner); The old gambler (The man in Man from the South who wagers cars against fingers); Claud (A recurring country figure in the four Claud's Dog tales)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The 1953 book gathers eighteen stories, and the last four sit under the title Claud's Dog.
In Lamb to the Slaughter, Mary Maloney kills her husband with a frozen leg of lamb.
She cooks the lamb, and the policemen eat the weapon while they search for it.
In Man from the South, an old man bets a finger against a car and a lighter.
Other tales include Taste, Poison, Skin, and The Sound Machine.
The book won the Edgar Award in 1954.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Marlowe helps his friend Terry Lennox, then uncovers two deaths among the rich in Idle Valley.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1953 matches the British first book, from Hamish Hamilton in November 1953. The United States edition, from Houghton Mifflin, is March 1954. The text is the same apart from spelling.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Philip Marlowe (The detective whose loyalty to Lennox drives the book); Terry Lennox (A scarred, rich drunk who fakes his death); Roger Wade (A blocked, alcoholic novelist); Eileen Wade (Roger's wife, and Lennox's earlier wife, who commits the murders)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Marlowe befriends Terry Lennox and drives him to the Mexican border.
Police say Lennox's wife Sylvia was murdered and that Lennox confessed, then died.
Marlowe is asked to watch the drunken writer Roger Wade and Wade's wife Eileen.
He works out that Eileen killed Sylvia and Roger, then Eileen kills herself.
Lennox returns alive, with a new face, and Marlowe sends him away.

items.title: "He Who Rides a Tiger" (1954) — Bhabani Bhattacharya

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A blacksmith fakes a holy miracle during the famine, then confesses the fraud.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1954 is correct for the first edition, Crown Publishers, New York. Kirkus reviewed it in October 1954. Some lists give an Indian Jaico edition in 1955. That later listing is not the first publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kalo (A blacksmith who poses as a Brahmin priest); Chandralekha (Kalo's daughter, also called Lekha, whom he rescues and then involves in the fraud); Biten (A fellow prisoner, formerly a Brahmin, whose conscience presses Kalo)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
During the Bengal famine, the low caste blacksmith Kalo goes to the city.
He is jailed for stealing food, and in jail he meets Biten, once a Brahmin.
He finds his daughter Chandralekha forced into prostitution and rescues her.
To live, he pretends to be a high Brahmin and stages a false appearance of Shiva.
The lie brings money and honour, but it also traps him.
At the end he tells the truth, destroys the false holiness, and steps off the tiger.

items.title: "The Lord of the Rings" (1954-1955) — J. R. R. Tolkien

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Hobbits try to destroy one ruling ring before the Dark Lord Sauron can use it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates The Fellowship of the Ring to 29 July 1954. It dates The Two Towers to 11 November 1954. It dates The Return of the King to 20 October 1955. The Tolkien Society agrees the parts appeared in 1954 and 1955.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Frodo Baggins (The hobbit who bears the One Ring toward destruction); Sam Gamgee (Frodo's gardener and loyal companion); Gandalf (The wizard who identifies the Ring and returns after Moria); Aragorn (The ranger who is heir to the old kingdoms of men); Sauron (The Dark Lord who made the One Ring)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book began as a sequel to The Hobbit and grew much larger.
Frodo inherits Bilbo's ring, which Gandalf proves is the One Ring.
A fellowship of hobbits, men, an elf, a dwarf, and Gandalf sets out.
The company breaks.
Frodo and Sam go toward Mordor with Gollum.
Other friends defend Rohan and Gondor while the quest continues.
The ring is destroyed in Mount Doom, and Sauron falls.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A play for voices about one day and night in a small Welsh town.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database calls 1954 a posthumous broadcast and publication. That is right for the BBC and the full book. A short first half appeared in Botteghe Oscure in 1952. The first public reading was in New York on 14 May 1953, while Thomas was alive. He died on 9 November 1953. The BBC Third Programme broadcast it on 25 January 1954. Dent published the full text in February 1954. New Directions followed in April 1954.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: First Voice (A narrator who leads the listener through the town); Captain Cat (A blind old sailor who dreams of the dead); Polly Garter (A young mother who sings of lost loves); Mrs Ogmore-Pritchard (A fussy widow who nags her two dead husbands in her dreams); Reverend Eli Jenkins (The poet preacher of the town)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Night opens on the dreams of the people of Llareggub.
Blind Captain Cat dreams of drowned sailors and of Rosie Probert.
Morning brings the post, gossip, Polly Garter's song, and the Reverend Eli Jenkins.
Lovers such as Mog Edwards and Myfanwy Price meet mainly in letters and dreams.
Night returns, and the town goes back to sleep.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A boy's summer of 1928 in Green Town, bottled like dandelion wine.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1957 is correct for the Doubleday book. A short story also called Dandelion Wine appeared in Gourmet in June 1953. Farewell Summer, a sequel, came only in 2006. The Martian Chronicles note does not belong on this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Douglas Spaulding (The twelve year old hero, based on the boy Bradbury); Tom Spaulding (Douglas's younger brother, more skeptical than Douglas); Grandfather Spaulding (The man who makes and stores the dandelion wine)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book is set in the summer of 1928 in Green Town, Illinois.
Green Town is a dream version of Bradbury's Waukegan.
Twelve year old Douglas Spaulding learns he is alive, and that people die.
His grandfather bottles each summer day as dandelion wine.
Many chapters began as separate stories, the earliest in 1946.
Doubleday published the joined book in 1957.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Short essays on everyday French culture, plus a theory of how myth works.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Seuil published the French book in 1957. Annette Lavers translated an abridged English edition in 1972. A fuller English edition appeared in 2012. The catalog calls it poetry. It is cultural theory.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Roland Barthes (The critic reading everyday French signs)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Most essays first appeared in Les Lettres nouvelles between 1954 and 1956.
Barthes reads wrestling, ads, toys, wine, and photos as modern myths.
A myth is a second level of meaning laid on a simple sign.
The closing essay, Myth Today, explains the method.
A Paris Match cover of a saluting soldier is his example of empire as myth.

items.title: "The Buddha and His Dhamma" (1957) — B. R. Ambedkar

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His last book, a life of the Buddha retold as a religion of morality.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He died on 6 December 1956. The book appeared the next year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Buddha (The teacher whose life and Dhamma the book retells); B. R. Ambedkar (The author, who shapes the story for a modern equal society)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He finished the manuscript in 1956, the year he became a Buddhist.
The book retells the Buddha's life and his Dhamma (his teaching).
He rejects a creator God and puts morality in that place.
He also rejects caste, ritual, and the idea of a fixed soul.
The book came out in 1957, after he had died.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Railway Raju, a corrupt tourist guide, is mistaken for a holy man and fasts for rain.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1958 is correct. Narayan worked on it during a 1956 visit to the United States. Viking published the American edition and Methuen the British edition in 1958. The Sahitya Akademi Award followed in 1960. Vijay Anand's film Guide came out in 1965 and changes the ending.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Raju (A tour guide who becomes a prisoner and then an unwilling holy man); Rosie (A dancer married to Marco, later helped and used by Raju); Marco (Rosie's husband, an archaeologist who cares more for his work than for her dancing); Velan (The villager who first believes Raju is a holy man)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel is also based on the fictional town Malgudi, in South India.
The novel describes the transformation of the protagonist Raju, from a tour guide to a spiritual guide and then of the greatest holy man of India.
Narayan, won the Sahitya Akademi Award for this novel.
Raju guides tourists at Malgudi station and is called Railway Raju.
He falls in love with Rosie, a dancer married to the scholar Marco.
Marco leaves.
Raju manages Rosie's career and then forges her signature.
He goes to prison.
After release, villagers take him for a sadhu (a holy man).
In a drought they ask him to fast.
He confesses to Velan, but the fast continues.
On the eleventh day he sinks by the river as rain seems to come in the hills.
The ending stays uncertain.
