items.title: "A Raisin in the Sun" (1959) — Lorraine Hansberry

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Chicago family fights over insurance money and a house in a white neighborhood.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1959 is correct. Hansberry finished the play in 1957. It opened at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre on 11 March 1959, directed by Lloyd Richards. Random House published the book in 1959. It is not posthumous. The note about Les Blancs does not belong on this play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lena Younger (Mama) (The mother who holds the insurance money and buys the house); Walter Lee Younger (Her son, a driver who wants the money for a business); Ruth Younger (Walter's wife, tired by the cramped flat); Beneatha Younger (Walter's sister, who hopes to study medicine); Joseph Asagai (A Nigerian student who courts Beneatha); Karl Lindner (The white neighbor who offers to keep the Youngers out)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Younger family shares a cramped flat on Chicago's South Side.
Mama Lena waits for a ten thousand dollar insurance check after Big Walter's death.
Walter Lee wants a liquor store.
Beneatha wants to be a doctor.
Mama wants a house.
Mama buys a house in white Clybourne Park, then trusts Walter with the rest.
Willy runs off with the money.
Karl Lindner offers to buy the family out.
Walter almost accepts, then refuses.
The family chooses the house.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Eleven adult stories about nasty marriages, strange bodies, and cruel last turns.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1960 matches the Roald Dahl Museum and the Knopf and Michael Joseph books. A Britannica scholars note has said 1959, which is the magazine year of The Landlady, not the collection year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Separate story narrators (Speakers of eleven different adult tales, not one shared hero); The landlady (The keeper of a lodging house in the story The Landlady)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Knopf published this second major adult collection in 1960.
The eleven tales include The Landlady, Royal Jelly, Parson's Pleasure, and Pig.
Several had already appeared in magazines, including The Landlady in 1959.
The Champion of the World is a short form of the later children's book Danny, the Champion of the World.
The mood is menace inside ordinary homes.
A 1979 television series, Tales of the Unexpected, reused many of these plots.

items.title: "The Serpent and the Rope" (1960) — Raja Rao

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Brahmin scholar moves between India and France, seeking truth as his marriage fails.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1960 is correct. John Murray published it in London in 1960. The New York Pantheon edition is 1963. Wikiquote and the novel page date the Sahitya Akademi Award to 1964. Another Rao page says 1963. Do not use either award year as the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ramaswamy (The Brahmin narrator, close to Rao's own years in France); Madeleine (His French wife, whose marriage to him breaks down); Savithri (A young Indian woman in Cambridge whom he loves); Little Mother (His stepmother, who shares the family rites in India)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is written in the biographical style and it deals with the concepts of existence, reality and fulfillment of one's capabilities.
The protagonist of the novel, Ramaswamy's thought process in the novel is said to be influenced by Vedantic philosophy and Adi-Shankara's non-dualism.
It won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1964.
It is a story for the search of spiritual truth.
Ramaswamy, a South Indian Brahmin, studies in France and marries Madeleine.
Their baby son dies.
Ramaswamy goes home when his father is dying.
He meets Savithri, a Cambridge student, and cannot forget her.
Madeleine turns toward Buddhism and away from him.
A second child also dies.
The marriage ends.
Ramaswamy looks for a guru (a spiritual teacher).
The serpent in the title is illusion.
The rope is reality.

items.title: "To Bedlam and Part Way Back" (1960) — Anne Sexton

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: To Bedlam and Part Way Back

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her first book, poems on mental illness and the slow return toward ordinary life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1960 is correct. Houghton Mifflin, 1960. This is the first book, not a posthumous one.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker of Her Kind (A woman who says she has gone out like a witch and has been her kind)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Houghton Mifflin published the book in 1960.
The poems come from her time in hospital and from the work of getting well.
The poems tell of hospital, treatment, and the slow return to ordinary ties.
Her Kind is the famous poem, spoken by a woman who calls herself a witch.
The title means a journey into madness and only part of the way back.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The 1960 Penguin printing of the complete Lady Chatterley's Lover in Britain.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database title UK unexpurgated edition and year 1960 name an edition, not a new novel. Penguin's complete text was first published in Great Britain in 1960. The Old Bailey acquitted Penguin on 2 November 1960.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Constance Chatterley (The same heroine as in the 1928 novel); Oliver Mellors (The same gamekeeper as in the 1928 novel); Sir Clifford Chatterley (The same paralysed husband as in the 1928 novel)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This row is a publication event, not a new story.
Lawrence had died in 1930, so he never saw this edition.
Penguin issued the unexpurgated text (the text with nothing cut) in Britain in 1960.
The publisher was tried at the Old Bailey from 20 October to 2 November 1960.
The jury acquitted Penguin, and the complete text could be sold.

items.title: "The Man-Eater of Malgudi" (1961) — R. K. Narayan

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A quiet printer is invaded by a violent taxidermist who destroys himself.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1961 is correct. Viking published the book in 1961.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nataraj (A gentle printer whose house and press are taken over); Vasu (A huge taxidermist and bully, the human man eater); Sastri (Nataraj's employee, who reads Vasu as a demon); Rangi (A temple dancer who warns Nataraj about the elephant); Kumar (The elephant Vasu wants to kill)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel tells the story of a painter Natraj, who lives in Malgudi and spends his time in the company of his two friends a poet and a journalist. The theme of the novel is self-destruction.
Vasu- a taxidermist, villain of the novel, and the man eater of Malgudi.
Kumar is the name of the elephant.
Rangi- a prostitute who has an affair with Vasu.
Narayan's depiction, about Vasu : "Every demon carries within him unknown to himself, a tiny seed of self-destruction and goes up in thin air the most unexpected moment".
Nataraj runs a small press in Malgudi and likes his quiet friends.
Vasu, a taxidermist (a man who stuffs dead animals), takes the attic.
Vasu bullies customers, kills creatures, and behaves like a rakshasa (a demon).
He plans to shoot Kumar, a temple elephant.
Nataraj finds him dead.
Vasu had struck a mosquito on his own forehead.
The tale recalls Bhasmasura, a demon ruined by his own power.

items.title: "The Wretched of the Earth" (1961) — Frantz Fanon

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1961 argument about colonial violence, revolt, and the new nation after empire.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The French book appeared in 1961, with a preface by Sartre, shortly before Fanon died. Constance Farrington's English translation was published in 1963. Do not treat 1963 as the first publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Frantz Fanon (The author, writing as a psychiatrist who joined the Algerian struggle); Jean Paul Sartre (French philosopher who wrote the preface, not the book itself)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Fanon says decolonization (the ending of colonial rule) begins in violence.
He describes the colonial world as split between settler and native.
He studies how revolt can rebuild a damaged sense of self.
He warns that a new elite may copy the old colonial rulers.
Jean Paul Sartre added a famous preface to the book.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A cynical journalist is shipwrecked on Pala, a small society that tries to join science with kindness.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1962 is correct. Chatto and Windus published the British edition in 1962. Harper published the American edition in 1962. The database files this book under Drama. It is a novel, not a play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Will Farnaby (A cynical journalist who learns how Pala lives)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Will Farnaby, a cynical journalist, is shipwrecked on the island of Pala.
Pala has built a society that wants freedom rather than control.
Its people use science, teaching, and a drug called moksha with care.
The story is thin on purpose, so Huxley can explain the island's ideas.
Pala is the hopeful opposite of the World State in Brave New World.
The novel was Huxley's last, published the year before he died.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1962 English selection of his stories and other writings, not a Spanish original.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: This is not the year of a Spanish original. An augmented edition followed in 1964, and Penguin reissued the book in 1970.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Selected narrators (Voices from several stories, including the librarian of Babel and other masks of Borges)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Editors Donald A. Yates and James E. Irby chose the pieces for English readers.
New Directions in New York published the book in 1962.
Many tales come from Ficciones and from other Spanish books.
Essays sit beside stories, so the book is not one plot.
Penguin issued another English edition in 1970.
Borges did not write a Spanish book with this title.

items.title: "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory" (1964) — Roald Dahl

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poor Charlie Bucket finds a golden ticket and becomes the heir of Willy Wonka's factory.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1964 is right. Knopf published the United States book on 17 January 1964. Allen and Unwin published the British book on 23 November 1964. The sequel, Charlie and the Great Glass Elevator, is 1972.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Charlie Bucket (A poor, kind boy who wins the factory); Willy Wonka (The secretive chocolate maker who tests the children); Grandpa Joe (Charlie's grandfather, who goes on the tour); The Oompa-Loompas (The factory workers who sing after each child fails)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Willy Wonka hides five Golden Tickets in chocolate bars.
Augustus Gloop, Veruca Salt, Violet Beauregarde, and Mike Teavee find four tickets.
Charlie Bucket finds the fifth and enters with Grandpa Joe.
Each greedy child breaks a rule and is removed in a comic disaster.
The Oompa-Loompas sing a warning after each disaster.
Wonka gives the factory to Charlie, the one child who stayed kind.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short metaphysical comedy in which a cat stands for divine grace.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1965 is correct. Macmillan in New York published it in 1965. The subtitle is often A Tale of India. One bibliography uses A Tale of Modern India. Both agree on 1965. It is not a study of Shakespeare the playwright.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ramakrishna Pai (The clerk who narrates this odd tale); Govindan Nair (Pai's neighbor, who trusts divine grace like a kitten carried by a cat); The cat (A figure of grace that carries the soul, not a pet story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a gentle, almost teasing fable of two friends. The setting is famine of 1942.
Govinda Nair is an astute, down-to-earth philosopher and clerk who tackles the problems of routine living with extra-ordinary common sense and Gusto and whose refreshing and unorthodox conclusions, continually panic.
Ramkrishna Pai, is Nair's friends, neighbor and narrator of the story.
This novel brings the live texture of life in Trivandrum.
This short book takes up questions left by The Serpent and the Rope.
Ramakrishna Pai, a quiet clerk, tells the story.
His neighbor Govindan Nair laughs at fear and trusts a larger order.
Nair trusts a cat the way a kitten trusts its mother to carry it.
Indian philosophy calls this the mother cat's hold of grace.
The tone is comic, but the question is still how grace acts in daily life.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her 1966 book about the choice between death and life, which won the Pulitzer Prize.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1966 is correct for publication by Houghton Mifflin. The Pulitzer Prize was awarded in 1967. Do not merge those two years into one date.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Houghton Mifflin published Live or Die in 1966.
The poems are arranged as a record moving through a hard stretch of years.
They face illness, grief, and the hard choice in the title.
The title itself sets that choice between living and dying.
It won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1967.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A study of how European knowledge ordered the world before modern human sciences.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Gallimard published the French book in 1966. Pantheon and Tavistock published The Order of Things in 1970. The catalog calls it poetry. It is theory.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Michel Foucault (The historian who compares systems of knowledge)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The French title is Les Mots et les choses, meaning words and things.
Foucault compares three ages of knowledge, called epistemes (ways a culture orders truth).
In the Renaissance, people linked things by likeness.
In the Classical age, they sorted the world into tables and classes.
He ends by calling man a recent figure in knowledge, and a figure that may pass.

items.title: "The Vendor of Sweets" (1967) — R. K. Narayan

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Gandhian sweet seller clashes with his son back from America, then steps away.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1967 is correct. Viking published the American edition in 1967.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jagan (A sweet seller and former Gandhi follower, the father at the center); Mali (Jagan's son, who returns from America with new business plans); Grace (The young woman Mali brings home and calls his wife); The cousin (A cousin who carries news between Jagan and Mali)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jagan sells sweets in Malgudi and tries to live by Gandhi's rules.
His wife Ambika is dead.
He has spoiled his son Mali.
Mali takes hidden money and goes to America to study writing.
He returns with Grace and a plan for a machine that writes stories.
Jagan refuses to fund the machine.
After Mali is arrested, Jagan moves toward giving up the shop.

items.title: "A Wizard of Earthsea" (1968) — Ursula K. Le Guin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The boy wizard Ged releases a shadow and must name it with his own name.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1968 is right. Parnassus Press in Berkeley brought out the book in 1968. It is the first Earthsea novel, before The Tombs of Atuan in 1971.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ged (A young wizard from Gont, also called Duny and Sparrowhawk); Ogion (The quiet mage who teaches Ged balance); Vetch (Ged's loyal friend from the school on Roke); The shadow (The nameless thing Ged releases and must face)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Duny, called Sparrowhawk, shows power on the island of Gont.
The mage Ogion gives him his true name, Ged, and teaches balance.
At the wizard school on Roke, pride makes Ged call up a shadow.
The shadow scars him, and the old Archmage dies driving it off.
Ged hunts the shadow to the edge of the map with his friend Vetch.
He names the shadow with his own name and becomes whole.

items.title: "The Left Hand of Darkness" (1969) — Ursula K. Le Guin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Envoy Genly Ai asks the ambisexual people of Gethen to join a league of worlds.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1969 is right. Ace published the paperback in 1969, and a hardcover also appeared in 1969. The awards came in 1970. Do not date the book 1970.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Genly Ai (A man from Earth, sent as the first envoy to Gethen); Estraven (A Gethenian leader who believes Ai and dies helping him); King Argaven (The ruler of Karhide, who can both father and bear children)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Genly Ai is sent to the ice world Gethen, also called Winter.
People there have no fixed sex except during a brief fertile time called kemmer.
Prime minister Estraven is exiled, and King Argaven rejects the league.
In Orgoreyn, Ai is betrayed and sent to a prison camp.
Estraven frees him, and they cross the ice for eighty days.
Estraven is killed at the border, and Gethen agrees to join the Ekumen.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Mr Fox tunnels under three cruel farmers and steals a feast for the hungry animals.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1970 is right. Allen and Unwin in Britain and Knopf in the United States both published it in 1970. Wikipedia dates the book 1 June 1970.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mr Fox (A clever fox who steals to feed his family); Mrs Fox (His wife, who prepares the underground feast); Boggis, Bunce, and Bean (Three mean farmers who besiege the fox hole); Badger (A friend who helps raid the stores and invite the other animals)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mr Fox steals food from farmers Boggis, Bunce, and Bean.
The farmers shoot off his tail, then dig up the fox hole.
The fox family digs deeper, and the farmers wait above to starve them.
Mr Fox, his children, and Badger tunnel into the farms' stores.
They hold a feast and plan a secret underground village.
The three farmers are still waiting at the hole.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her African play about colonialism and revolt, finished and staged after her death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The play opened at the Longacre Theatre on 15 November 1970 and closed on 19 December 1970. Random House published the text in 1972 in Les Blancs: The Collected Last Plays, edited by Robert Nemiroff. Hansberry died in 1965, so both the staging and the book are posthumous. Nemiroff supplied some dialogue.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tshembe Matoseh (An educated African who must choose between Europe and the revolt); Abioseh Matoseh (Tshembe's brother, training to be a Catholic priest); Charlie Morris (A white American journalist who wants to understand the struggle); Madame Neilsen (The blind wife of the mission reverend, long settled in Africa); The Woman (A silent dancer who embodies the call to resist)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hansberry began the play about 1960, after seeing Jean Genet's Les Negres.
Tshembe Matoseh returns from Europe for his father's funeral.
A mission hospital, a colonial officer, and an American journalist share the crisis.
A silent woman calls Tshembe toward the revolt he hoped to avoid.
She died in 1965 with the script unfinished.
Robert Nemiroff completed it.
Broadway saw it in 1970, and the book came in 1972.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A slow reading of Balzac's story Sarrasine, cut into small units of meaning.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Seuil published the French book in 1970. Richard Miller's English translation appeared from Hill and Wang in 1974. The catalog calls it poetry. It is theory.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Roland Barthes (The critic dividing Sarrasine into codes); Sarrasine (The sculptor in Balzac's story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Balzac's Sarrasine tells of a sculptor who loves a singer.
Barthes cuts the story into lexias (short bits of text for reading).
He tracks five codes: puzzle, action, character hint, symbol, and cultural reference.
A readerly text asks only to be consumed.
A writerly text asks the reader to help make it.
He argues that the reader produces meaning and does not only receive it.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The physicist Shevek moves between anarchist Anarres and rich Urras and shares his theory of time.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1974 is right. Harper and Row published it in 1974. In the story's own timeline it comes before The Left Hand of Darkness, though it was published later. The awards are 1975.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Shevek (An Anarresti physicist who invents a general theory of time); Takver (Shevek's partner on Anarres); Sabul (A senior physicist who controls publication and blocks Shevek)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Shevek leaves Anarres, a poor anarchist moon, for the rich planet Urras.
Chapters switch between his past on Anarres and his present on Urras.
On Anarres, custom and a jealous senior, Sabul, block his work.
On Urras he sees luxury, war, and a state that wants his science.
He gives the theory to all worlds through the Terran embassy.
The theory makes the ansible possible, an instant link between stars.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A history of how punishment moved from public torture to the modern prison.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Gallimard published Surveiller et punir in 1975. The English book came from Pantheon and Allen Lane in 1977.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Michel Foucault (The historian of punishment and discipline)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The French title is Surveiller et punir, meaning to watch and to punish.
It opens with a public execution in 1757, then a prison timetable.
Foucault says punishment shifted from hurting the body to training the person.
The panopticon (cells around a central watchtower) is his model of discipline.
He argues that schools, factories, and hospitals use similar watching.

items.title: "The Awful Rowing Toward God" (1975) — Anne Sexton

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her last religious book, published in 1975 after she had died.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: She died on 4 October 1974. The book appeared the next year. Do not date the publication 1974.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The rower (The speaker who rows a small boat toward God)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poems picture the soul rowing toward God in a small boat.
Faith, doubt, and the tired body fill the sequence.
She finished the manuscript before she died in October 1974.
Houghton Mifflin published the book in 1975.
Because it came out after her death, the book is posthumous.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A posthumous book of creation myths and early wars, edited by Tolkien's son.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Tales began in the First World War. Tolkien died in 1973. Wikipedia dates the Allen and Unwin book 15 September 1977. The Tolkien Society agrees that Christopher Tolkien's edition appeared in 1977.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Eru (The One, the creator in the opening myth); Morgoth (Melkor after his fall, the first great enemy); Feanor (The elf craftsman who made the Silmarils); Beren and Luthien (A man and an elf maiden whose love story Tolkien linked with his own marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Holy powers sing the world into being, and Melkor brings discord.
Feanor makes three great jewels, the Silmarils, and Morgoth steals them.
Elves fight long wars, and the land of Beleriand is broken.
The island kingdom of Numenor grows proud and is drowned.
The last section sketches the rings and the later age of the other novels.
Christopher Tolkien, with Guy Gavriel Kay, shaped unfinished papers into this book.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1978 study of how the West imagined and ruled the East.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1978 is correct. Pantheon Books published it in 1978. The library class on the record uses 1979. Learn 1978 as the first year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edward Said (The critic who defines Orientalism as a Western system of knowledge and power)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Said studies Western writing about Asia, North Africa, and the Arab world.
He says that writing made the East seem strange, weak, and stuck in time.
He separates a school subject, a way of seeing, and a tool of rule.
Those pictures helped empires, because knowledge was tied to power.
The book became a base text for postcolonial studies.

items.title: "Ain’t I a Woman?" (1981) — bell hooks / Gloria Jean Watkins

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A study of how racism and sexism together shaped the lives of Black women in America.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1981 is right. She began drafting it at Stanford around 1971 and South End Press published it in 1981. The database genre Poetry is wrong. This is prose theory.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: bell hooks (The critic speaking in her own analytical voice); Sojourner Truth (The nineteenth century speaker whose question supplies the title)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title comes from Sojourner Truth's 1851 speech Ain't I a Woman?
hooks argues that slavery left Black women with the lowest standing.
She says old stereotypes of Black women still shape later decades.
She criticizes sexism inside Black nationalist politics.
She also criticizes a feminist movement built around white middle class women.
She began the book at Stanford and published it in 1981.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A collection of short stories about ordinary people in the fictional town of Malgudi.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1982 is the later Penguin edition sold outside India, not the first book. Indian Thought Publications issued Malgudi Days in 1943. One Narayan biography paragraph says 1942, but Britannica and the collection record say 1943. A revised Penguin book in 1982 added further stories. The television series began in 1986.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The astrologer (A fake fortune teller who recognizes a man from his criminal past); Talkative Man (A recurring storyteller in several Malgudi tales); Swami (The boy from Swami and Friends, who returns in Father's Help)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Each story shows one small crisis in Malgudi.
In An Astrologer's Day, a street astrologer meets a man he once tried to kill.
The Doctor's Word shows a doctor who lies to save a friend.
Father's Help brings back the schoolboy Swami.
Other stories follow a postman, a blind beggar, and the Talkative Man.
The stories were later filmed for the television series Malgudi Days.

items.title: "The World, the Text, and the Critic" (1983) — Edward Said

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The World, the Text, and the Critic

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Essays of 1983 that keep criticism tied to history, power, and the world.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1983 is correct. Harvard University Press published the book in 1983. The essays come from the years before that. A later reprint is not the first edition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edward Said (The critic arguing for worldly, secular reading)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book collects essays written from about 1969 to 1981.
The opening essay is called Secular Criticism.
Said says a text stays tied to history and to human lives.
He argues with theory that lifts a book out of the world.
Essays treat Swift, Conrad, traveling theory, and religious criticism.

items.title: "Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center" (1984) — bell hooks / Gloria Jean Watkins

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A call to build feminist theory from the lives of women at the margin, not only from the center.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1984 is right for the first South End Press book. A second edition is 2000 in one library record and 1999 in an older encyclopedia note. Exam questions want the first year, 1984.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: bell hooks (The theorist arguing from the position of Black women at the margin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
hooks says 1960s women's liberation often centered white women with class privilege.
She criticizes Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique for that narrow view.
Friedan's picture, she argues, misses poor women, Black women, and women without homes.
The margin means lives hidden from mainstream America and from mainstream feminism.
She asks men to join the fight, and she wants a changed society, not a small reform.
She uses the phrase white-supremacist capitalist patriarchy for the whole system.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her first full poetry book, spoken in the voices of outsiders.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1985 is correct. Anvil Press Poetry published the book in London in 1985. It won a Scottish Arts Council award.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The model (A poor woman who poses naked and judges the painting.); Georges (The painter who treats her body as a study in shape.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This 1985 book is made of dramatic monologues.
The speakers are often poor, angry, or ignored.
In the title poem, a model poses naked for a painter named Georges.
He pays her only a few francs for many hours of work.
She knows the grand painting does not show her real life.
The book asks who gets to define art and beauty.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dream, also called Morpheus, is captured by a human magician.
He escapes, finds his tools, and rebuilds his kingdom, the Dreaming.
His siblings are the Endless, beings such as Death, Desire, and Despair.
Single issues tell tales drawn from many world myths.
The series follows Dream toward change, mercy, and an end.
It ran for 75 issues and is not one ordinary novel.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A theory book arguing that repeated acts create the appearance of a natural gender.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1990 is correct. Routledge published Gender Trouble in 1990. It is theory, so there is no performance date.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Butler reads feminist and psychoanalytic writers, including Simone de Beauvoir and Michel Foucault.
The book says gender is not a stable identity behind our gestures.
Repeated acts, clothes, and speech make gender look natural.
Butler calls this gender performativity.
Drag can show that the link between sex, gender, and desire is not fixed.
The book became a founding text of queer theory (theory of sex and gender norms).

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A later book on how bodies and sex are also shaped by repeated social norms.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1993 is correct. Routledge published the book in 1993. It continues the argument of Gender Trouble (1990).

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Some readers thought Gender Trouble made the body unimportant.
This book answers them.
Butler says sex is also formed by rules, language, and repetition.
A birth announcement such as the cry that a baby is a girl helps start that process.
The body is material, but that materiality is shaped by power.
Performativity here means forced repetition, not a free daily choice.

fields.value: A 1993 book that reads classic novels beside the history of empire.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1993 is correct. Chatto and Windus published the book in 1993. It continues the argument begun in Orientalism.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edward Said (The critic connecting novels to conquest and resistance)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Said extends Orientalism from the Arab world to empire more widely.
He reads Defoe, Austen, Conrad, Forster, and Kipling with imperial history.
He says a story can support rule, or it can block other stories.
He defines imperialism as a center that rules a distant land.
He argues that empire's cultural habits continued after formal colonies ended.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Essays on excited, freeing teaching, where class is a place to cross old limits.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: bell hooks (The teacher-writer reflecting on classrooms she has known); Paulo Freire (The educator whose idea of freedom shapes the book)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The subtitle calls education the practice of freedom.
hooks draws on Paulo Freire, who used that idea of freeing education.
She remembers segregated schooling and later integrated classrooms.
She wants teachers and students to share excitement, not only to pass facts.
Essays link class, race, gender, and the body to how people learn.
The aim is to transgress, meaning to step across unjust limits.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Richard Mayhew helps a wounded girl named Door.
After that, London Above can no longer see him.
He enters London Below, a magical city tied to Underground station names.
Door is hunted, and Richard joins her quest.
Allies include the Marquis de Carabas and the fighter Hunter.
The angel Islington is not the helper he seems.

fields.value: Mrs Darwin (Charles Darwin's wife, who speaks a tiny zoo diary.); Mrs Midas (The wife who suffers when her husband's touch turns life to gold.); Little Red Cap (A girl who retells the wolf story as a lesson about poets.); Medusa (The woman with snakes for hair, speaking in her own voice.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Each poem gives the stage to a woman from an old story.
Some speakers are wives, such as Mrs Darwin and Mrs Midas.
Others are figures like Medusa, Eurydice, and Little Red Cap.
The women correct, mock, or mourn the famous men.
Humor and anger sit side by side.
The book asks what history hides when only men speak.

fields.value: A freed prisoner is hired for a war between old gods and new ones.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Shadow Moon leaves prison and learns that his wife, Laura, is dead.
Mr. Wednesday hires him as a guard and driver.
Wednesday is Odin, an old god brought to America by believers.
New gods of media, roads, and money are pushing the old gods out.
Wednesday's plan is a trick as well as a war.
Shadow learns the truth as the battle comes.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The lover (The I of the poems, speaking to a beloved you.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker falls in love and tells the joy in plain words.
Poems such as You and Text follow letters, calls, and longing.
Time, the body, and absence become the main images.
The joy fades as the affair breaks.
The book ends in loss, not in mythic costume.
It won the T. S. Eliot Prize.

The bee flies through the poems as a sign of what humans must protect.
Some poems are public and some are private.
The opening poem, Bees, treats poet bees as makers of honey and art.
The book won the Costa Poetry Award in 2011.
It was also named on the short list for the T. S. Eliot Prize.

Full name: Thomas Ernest Hulme.
He was a War Poet.
He was an English poet and critic. He was born at Gratton Hall, Endon, and Staffordshire. He rejected Romanticism.
He was expelled from St. John' College, Cambridge for rowdy behavior.
In 1909, Hulme arranged meetings of a group of poets which included Ezra Pound and F.S. Flint. He was a member of Imagist Movement.
He had a lasting influence on T.S. Eliot.
Five of Hulme's poems were published in 'The New Age' in 1912 as "The Complete Poetical Works of T.E. Hulme".
In 1913, he translated Henri Bergson's "Introduction to Metaphysics" which was a major influence on his thought.
Hulme joined the army in 1914 and his "War Notes" were published in "New Age".
His essays were edited posthumously by Sir Herbert Read in "Speculations" (1924) and "Notes on Language and Style".
(1883 - 1917)
Thomas Ernest Hulme was an English critic and poet who had notable influence on modernism. He is also called Lawrence of Arabia. He is an Imagist Poet.
He contributed critical articles to The New Age.
He was made secretary of the Poet's club. In 1908, he delivered his paper A Lecture on Modern Poetry to the Club.
His poems Autumn and City Sunset both published in 1909 in a poet's club anthology and had the distinction of being the first imagist poem.
Further five poems were published in The New Age in 1912 as the complete poetical works of T.E Hulme.
Robert Frost met Hulme in 1913 and was influenced by his ideas.
In his critical writings Hulme distinguished between 'Romanticism', a style informed by a belief in the infinite in man and nature, characterised by Hulme as split religion and 'Classicism', a made of art stressing human finitude, formal restraint concrete imagery and in Hulme's words "Dry Hardness".
Hulme's politics was conservatives. Notable Works of Hulme: 1. Notes on Language and Style (1929)

(1873 - 1956)
He was an English poet and short story writer and best known for his children's verse.
He was born in Kent, England and educated at St. Paul's Cathedral School.
He left school at 16 and began working in an Anglo American oil company and remained there for 18 years.
He was married in 1899. He was a Georgian Poet.
He published his first story, "Kismet" (1895) in the journal Sketch under the pseudonym Walter Ramal.
His first book was a collection of poems called "Songs of Childhood" which appeared in 1902. It is regarded as a significant example of Children's Literature and was applauded for his creative imagery.
In 1908, when he got Civil List Pension he devoted himself entirely to writing.
Mare also wrote Ghost Stories as "Eight Tales", "The Riddle and Other Stories" etc.
He also wrote super natural novels like "Henry Brocken" (1904), "The Return" (1910)
He died in Twickenham in 1956.
His play "Crossing" has an important role in Robertson Davies' "The Manticore".
His Ariel poems include:.
Alone (1927)
Self to Self (1928)
The Snowdrop (1929)
News (1930)
To Lucy (1931)
Doris Ross McCrosson is the biographer of De la Mare.
In his lecture "Rupert Brooke and the Intellectual Imagination", Mare explained that "Children are not bound in by their groping senses. Facts to them are the liveliest chameleons".
Gary William Crawford has described De la Mare's supernatural fiction for adults as being "among the finest to appear in the first half of this century". Major Works of De la Mare Novels 1- Henry Brocken (1904)
